Competency: Describe how paired endocardial tubes from splanchnic mesoderm fuse into the primitive heart tube by the end of week 3 and loop to the right in week 4, and relate defective ciliary dynein (Kartagener syndrome) to dextrocardia.

Trace atrial septation through the septum primum, ostium primum, ostium secundum, septum secundum, and foramen ovale, and predict the defect when each step fails (patent foramen ovale, ostium secundum ASD, ostium primum ASD).

Explain how fused endocardial cushions divide the atrioventricular canal and help form the membranous septum and the mitral and tricuspid valves, and relate endocardial cushion defects to Down syndrome.

Describe how neural crest cells build the spiral aorticopulmonary septum, and predict transposition of the great vessels from failed spiraling, persistent truncus arteriosus from failed septation, and tetralogy of Fallot from anterosuperior infundibular septum displacement.
Trace fetal circulation through the umbilical vein, ductus venosus, foramen ovale, ductus arteriosus, and umbilical arteries, and explain why the best oxygenated blood reaches the brain.

Explain closure of the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus at birth (falling pulmonary resistance, rising left atrial pressure, rising O2, falling prostaglandin E2) and name the adult remnants of fetal vessels.

Relate the aortic arch derivatives (third arch to common and proximal internal carotid, fourth to aortic arch and right subclavian, sixth to proximal pulmonary arteries and ductus arteriosus) to the different paths of the right and left recurrent laryngeal nerves.
Describe the endocardium, myocardium, epicardium, and fibrous cardiac skeleton, and explain how the skeleton electrically insulates the atria from the ventricles except at the AV bundle.

Identify the features of cardiac muscle cells (branched, one or two central nuclei, intercalated discs with fascia adherens, desmosomes, and gap junctions, diads at the Z line) and contrast them with skeletal muscle.
Distinguish Purkinje fibers (large, pale, glycogen rich, few myofibrils, subendocardial) from working myocytes, and identify the atrial granules that store atrial natriuretic peptide.

Compare the tunica intima, media, and adventitia of elastic arteries, muscular arteries, arterioles, continuous, fenestrated, and sinusoidal capillaries, and veins, and relate each wall structure to its function.

Identify endothelial products (nitric oxide, prostacyclin, endothelin-1, and von Willebrand factor and P-selectin stored in Weibel-Palade bodies) and predict how endothelial dysfunction shifts vessel tone and clotting.

Locate the heart in the middle mediastinum with its apex at the left fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, and identify the chambers that form the right border, left border, and anterior surface on a chest radiograph.

Relate chamber position to clinical findings: the right ventricle lies most anterior behind the sternum, and the left atrium lies most posterior against the esophagus, so left atrial enlargement can cause dysphagia.

Describe the fibrous and serous (parietal and visceral) pericardium and the transverse and oblique sinuses, and explain why pericardial pain refers to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).

Identify the great vessels (SVC, IVC, pulmonary trunk and arteries, four pulmonary veins, aortic arch branches from right to left) and the ligamentum arteriosum with the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking under the arch.

Identify the internal features of each chamber (crista terminalis, pectinate muscles, fossa ovalis, coronary sinus opening, trabeculae carneae, papillary muscles, moderator band, conus arteriosus) and compare left and right ventricular wall thickness.

Predict injuries from blunt and penetrating chest trauma: aortic tear at the isthmus near the ligamentum arteriosum after sudden deceleration, myocardial contusion, ventricular puncture, and hemopericardium causing tamponade.

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Identify the cusps of each heart valve, the anchoring of atrioventricular cusps by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, and the chest wall site where each valve is best heard.

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Relate valve opening and closing to pressure differences across each phase of the Wiggers diagram (isovolumetric contraction, ejection, isovolumetric relaxation, rapid and reduced filling, atrial systole) and to the timing of S1 and S2.

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Interpret a left ventricular pressure-volume loop, identifying mitral and aortic valve opening and closing, and predict how the loop changes in aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, and mitral regurgitation.

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Explain the jugular venous a, c, and v waves and x and y descents, and predict cannon a waves in AV dissociation and large v waves in tricuspid regurgitation.

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Explain physiologic, wide, fixed, and paradoxical splitting of S2 and give a cause of each (right bundle branch block or pulmonic stenosis, atrial septal defect, left bundle branch block or aortic stenosis).

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Distinguish S3 (rapid filling of a volume-overloaded ventricle) from S4 (atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle), and identify functional flow murmurs in pregnancy, anemia, fever, and childhood.

Unit name: Heart valves and the cardiac cycle
Competency: Classify murmurs by timing and location (systolic ejection, holosystolic, early diastolic, mid-diastolic, continuous), match each to its lesion, and predict changes with inspiration, squatting, handgrip, and Valsalva.

Explain the phases of the ventricular myocyte action potential (fast Na+ upstroke, transient K+ outflow, L-type Ca2+ plateau, K+ repolarization, inward rectifier resting potential near -90 mV) and why the long refractory period prevents tetany.
Trace excitation-contraction coupling from T-tubule L-type Ca2+ channels through calcium-induced calcium release by ryanodine receptors (RyR2) to Ca2+ binding of troponin C and cross-bridge cycling.
Explain relaxation by SERCA (regulated by phospholamban), the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, and the sarcolemmal Ca2+-ATPase, and predict why ATP loss in ischemia impairs both contraction and relaxation.
Explain how beta-1 adrenergic stimulation acts through cAMP and protein kinase A to phosphorylate L-type Ca2+ channels, phospholamban, and troponin I, raising contractility and speeding relaxation.
Explain the cardiac length-tension relationship at the sarcomere level (filament overlap and troponin C Ca2+ sensitivity) and contrast how force is graded in cardiac versus skeletal muscle.

Calculate cardiac output, stroke volume, ejection fraction, and mean arterial pressure from given values, and use the Fick principle to calculate cardiac output from O2 consumption and arteriovenous O2 content.
Predict how changes in preload, afterload, and contractility alter stroke volume, end-systolic volume, and the position of the Frank-Starling curve.

Interpret combined cardiac function and venous return curves and predict the new operating point after hemorrhage, volume infusion, venoconstriction, increased contractility, or a change in total peripheral resistance.

Apply the law of Laplace to explain why concentric hypertrophy normalizes wall stress and a dilated ventricle needs more O2, and list the determinants of myocardial O2 demand (heart rate, contractility, wall stress).

Trace the baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus through CN IX, aortic arch through CN X, nucleus tractus solitarius) and predict heart rate and vascular resistance changes after standing, hemorrhage, and carotid sinus massage.
Explain hormonal control of blood volume and pressure by the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, ADH, and the natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP.

Explain the mechanisms of orthostatic hypotension (volume depletion, autonomic failure such as diabetic neuropathy, prolonged bed rest) and define it as a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing.
Locate the SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers, trace an impulse through them, and explain why AV nodal delay allows the atria to finish filling the ventricles.
Explain the pacemaker action potential (funny current through HCN channels, T-type and L-type Ca2+ currents, K+ repolarization) and how norepinephrine and acetylcholine change the slope of phase 4.
Relate the blood supply of the SA and AV nodes (from the RCA in most hearts) to sinus bradycardia and AV block during an inferior myocardial infarction.
Interpret a normal ECG: identify the P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment, T wave, and QT interval, calculate heart rate, and estimate the mean QRS axis from leads I and aVF.
Distinguish first degree, Mobitz I, Mobitz II, and third degree AV block and right and left bundle branch block on ECG, and predict which AV blocks arise in the AV node and which arise below it.

Identify premature beats, atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, multifocal atrial tachycardia, paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, ventricular tachycardia, torsades de pointes, and ventricular fibrillation on ECG, and relate each to its mechanism and risk of cardiac arrest.

Explain how an accessory pathway in Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome produces a short PR interval and delta wave, and describe sick sinus syndrome as SA node dysfunction causing sinus bradycardia, sinus pauses, or alternating bradycardia and tachycardia.
Trace the origins and courses of the right coronary artery, left main, left anterior descending, and circumflex arteries, and identify the myocardial regions each supplies.

Define coronary dominance by the origin of the posterior descending artery and predict why the posteromedial papillary muscle, with its single supply, is the one that ruptures after an inferior infarction.
Trace cardiac venous drainage through the great, middle, and small cardiac veins to the coronary sinus, and the anterior cardiac and smallest cardiac veins that bypass it.

Explain why left ventricular perfusion occurs mainly in diastole, why the myocardium extracts about 70% of arterial O2 at rest, and why tachycardia and high wall stress make the subendocardium ischemic first.
Explain local metabolic control of coronary flow by adenosine and other metabolites and why increased myocardial O2 demand must be met by increased flow rather than greater extraction.
Explain how an anomalous left coronary artery arising from the pulmonary artery causes myocardial ischemia in infancy once pulmonary artery pressure falls after birth.

Identify the branches of the aortic arch, descending thoracic aorta, and abdominal aorta with their vertebral levels (celiac trunk T12, superior mesenteric L1, renal about L1, inferior mesenteric L3, bifurcation L4).
Trace the arterial supply of the brain through the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems and identify the vessels that form the circle of Willis.

Trace the main arteries of the upper limb (subclavian, axillary, brachial, radial, ulnar) and lower limb (external iliac, femoral, popliteal, anterior and posterior tibial, fibular, dorsalis pedis) and locate the palpable pulse points.

Trace venous return through the SVC and IVC, the left renal vein crossing anterior to the aorta, and the hepatic portal vein, and identify the portosystemic anastomoses that dilate in portal hypertension.
Identify watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction, border zones between cerebral artery territories) and explain why they infarct first during systemic hypotension.
Compare the share of resting cardiac output received by the gut and liver, kidneys, skeletal muscle, brain, and heart, and relate each to its O2 extraction.

Describe the structure of lymphatic capillaries (blind ends, overlapping endothelial flaps, anchoring filaments) and explain how they return about 2 to 3 L of filtered fluid and protein to the blood each day.
Trace lymph from collecting vessels through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct to the left venous angle, and identify the regions drained by the right lymphatic duct.
Explain the forces that move lymph forward: valves, rhythmic contraction of lymphangions, the skeletal muscle pump, breathing, and rising interstitial fluid pressure.

Describe the structure and functions of lymph nodes, spleen (red and white pulp), thymus (cortex and medulla), and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, including where B and T cells mature and are selected.

Explain the causes and features of lymphedema (node dissection, radiation, tumor, Wuchereria bancrofti filariasis), including swelling that becomes firm and nonpitting as fibrosis develops, and chylothorax from thoracic duct injury.
Apply the relationship flow equals pressure gradient divided by resistance, and Poiseuille's law, to predict how changes in vessel radius, length, and blood viscosity alter resistance and flow.
Calculate total resistance for vessels arranged in series and in parallel, and explain why arterioles set total peripheral resistance and why parallel organ circuits can adjust flow independently.
Relate blood velocity to total cross-sectional area, and predict turbulence, bruits, and flow murmurs from Reynolds number factors such as anemia, high velocity, and stenosis.
Explain how arterial compliance and stroke volume set pulse pressure, and predict isolated systolic hypertension with a wide pulse pressure from arterial stiffening with age.
Apply the Starling equation to predict edema from raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, low plasma oncotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, or lymphatic obstruction.

Distinguish metabolic, myogenic, endothelial, neural, and hormonal control of arteriolar tone, and identify the main control of flow in the coronary, cerebral, skeletal muscle, skin, and pulmonary beds.
Explain how central command and muscle mechanoreceptor and metaboreceptor reflexes start the exercise response, with early vagal withdrawal followed by rising sympathetic drive.
Predict changes in heart rate, stroke volume, cardiac output, arteriovenous O2 difference, and O2 uptake during graded exercise using the Fick principle.
Explain the redistribution of cardiac output during exercise: metabolic dilation in active muscle, sympathetic constriction in gut and kidney, rising skin flow for heat loss, and stable brain flow.
Compare blood pressure and total peripheral resistance responses in dynamic (aerobic) exercise and static (isometric) exercise, and relate each to volume or pressure load on the heart.

Distinguish the trained endurance athlete's heart (eccentric remodeling, larger stroke volume, resting bradycardia from vagal tone, higher maximal O2 uptake) from pathologic hypertrophy such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

Trace the exogenous and endogenous lipoprotein pathways (chylomicrons with apo B-48, VLDL, IDL, LDL with apo B-100, HDL with apo A-I) and the roles of lipoprotein lipase, apo C-II, apo E, LCAT, and CETP.

Classify familial dyslipidemias by defect and lipid pattern: lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II deficiency (type I, chylomicrons, pancreatitis), LDL receptor defects (type II), apo E2 (type III, remnants), and hepatic VLDL overproduction (type IV).

Explain how HMG-CoA reductase controls cholesterol synthesis, how SREBP raises LDL receptor and HMG-CoA reductase expression when cell sterol is low, and how LDL enters cells by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

Explain the fuels of the heart (mostly fatty acid beta-oxidation through the carnitine shuttle at rest, plus glucose, lactate, and ketones) and the switch to anaerobic glycolysis with lactate build-up during ischemia.

Explain the role of thiamine pyrophosphate in pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and relate thiamine deficiency to wet beriberi (high-output heart failure, vasodilation, edema) in alcohol use disorder and malnutrition.
Explain how deficiency of B6, B12, or folate raises homocysteine and vascular risk, and how vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) and copper deficiency (lysyl oxidase, Menkes disease) weaken vessel walls.

Predict ECG changes of hypokalemia (U waves, flat T waves), hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, wide QRS), hypocalcemia (long QT), and hypercalcemia (short QT), and relate hypomagnesemia to torsades de pointes.

Explain the genetics of familial hypercholesterolemia: autosomal dominant LDLR, APOB, or gain-of-function PCSK9 variants, the gene-dosage difference between heterozygotes and homozygotes, and loss of feedback on liver cholesterol synthesis.
Relate hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to autosomal dominant sarcomere gene mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3), myocyte disarray, and the variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance seen among relatives.

Relate Marfan syndrome (FBN1 on chromosome 15, increased TGF-beta signaling), Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1 or TGFBR2), and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1) to aortic dilation, dissection, mitral valve prolapse, and arterial rupture.

Explain congenital long QT syndrome (loss of KCNQ1 or KCNH2, gain of SCN5A), compare Jervell and Lange-Nielsen and Romano-Ward inheritance, and relate Brugada syndrome (SCN5A loss) to sudden cardiac death.

Associate genetic syndromes with heart defects: Down syndrome (endocardial cushion defects), Turner syndrome (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation), 22q11.2 deletion (tetralogy, truncus arteriosus), Williams syndrome (supravalvular aortic stenosis), and VACTERL association.

Relate Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin), Friedreich ataxia (frataxin GAA repeat), and mitochondrial DNA disorders with heteroplasmy (Kearns-Sayre syndrome) to cardiomyopathy or conduction block.

Explain why adult cardiomyocytes, which have largely left the cell cycle, respond to pressure or volume load by hypertrophy with reactivated fetal genes (ANP, BNP, beta-myosin heavy chain), and why infarcts heal by scar.
Compare pressures and resistance in the pulmonary and systemic circuits, and explain how recruitment and distension lower pulmonary vascular resistance as cardiac output rises.
Contrast hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with hypoxic vasodilation in systemic arterioles, and predict pulmonary hypertension from chronic global hypoxia in COPD or at high altitude.
Explain how breathing changes venous return and ventricular filling, including normal S2 splitting, pulsus paradoxus, and the drop in cardiac output with positive pressure ventilation.

Predict pulmonary edema when pulmonary capillary pressure exceeds plasma oncotic pressure in left heart failure or mitral stenosis, and right ventricular failure (cor pulmonale) from chronic lung disease or pulmonary embolism.
Explain the gravity-dependent distribution of blood flow and ventilation from apex to base, the resulting V/Q ratios, and the conditions that create zone 1 (no flow).

Explain why hypoxemia from a right-to-left shunt barely improves with 100% O2, and identify nonrespiratory roles of the pulmonary circulation (ACE conversion of angiotensin I, bradykinin breakdown, filtering of small clots).

Explain atherosclerosis as chronic inflammation: endothelial VCAM-1, monocyte and T-cell recruitment, oxidized LDL uptake by scavenger receptors into foam cells, IL-1 beta release, and metalloproteinases that thin the fibrous cap.

Explain acute rheumatic fever as molecular mimicry between group A streptococcal M protein and cardiac antigens, and identify Aschoff bodies, Anitschkow cells, pancarditis, ASO titers, and the Jones major criteria.

Classify vasculitides by immune mechanism: immune complex (polyarteritis nodosa with hepatitis B, IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia), ANCA-associated (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA), and granulomatous T-cell (giant cell and Takayasu arteritis).

Explain immune-mediated pericardial, valvular, and conduction disease: Dressler syndrome after infarction, Libman-Sacks endocarditis in lupus, and congenital heart block from maternal anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies.
Distinguish hyperacute, acute cellular, acute antibody-mediated, and chronic heart transplant rejection (cardiac allograft vasculopathy) by immune mechanism and timing.

Describe how viral myocarditis moves from direct myocyte injury to a cytotoxic T-cell response and dilated cardiomyopathy, and identify eosinophilic hypersensitivity myocarditis and rare myocarditis after mRNA COVID-19 vaccination.

Explain how lost T-cell surveillance in AIDS or transplant immunosuppression lets HHV-8 driven Kaposi sarcoma grow and why lesions often regress when immunity returns, and relate atrial myxoma IL-6 release to fever and weight loss.

Compare endocarditis bacteria by morphology and virulence factors: Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase, protein A, clumping factor), viridans streptococci (cocci in chains, alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant, dextran), Enterococcus faecalis, and Staphylococcus epidermidis (biofilm on prosthetic material).
Identify causes of culture-negative endocarditis (HACEK organisms, Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella) and relate Streptococcus gallolyticus endocarditis to colon cancer.

Describe the Trypanosoma cruzi life cycle (triatomine bug feces, nondividing blood trypomastigotes, intracellular amastigotes in heart and smooth muscle) and its transmission by transfusion, transplant, pregnancy, and food.

Describe Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete, Ixodes tick, white-footed mouse reservoir, OspA to OspC switching, VlsE variation) and Rickettsia rickettsii (Dermacentor tick, obligate intracellular, endothelial infection, actin-based spread).

Compare flaviviruses (yellow fever, dengue; Aedes mosquitoes; positive-sense RNA) with filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg; negative-sense RNA; fruit bat reservoir; body fluid spread), and explain antibody-dependent enhancement in dengue.

Explain how coxsackie B virus (nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus, fecal-oral spread) enters cardiomyocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor and cleaves dystrophin with protease 2A, and name other myocarditis viruses (adenovirus, parvovirus B19, HHV-6).

Identify other microbial causes of heart and vessel disease: diphtheria toxin myocarditis, tuberculous constrictive pericarditis, and tertiary syphilis aortitis from obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum.

Define stage 1 (130 to 139 or 80 to 89 mmHg) and stage 2 (140/90 mmHg or higher) hypertension, and explain primary hypertension as polygenic with risk factors such as age, obesity, sodium intake, and alcohol.

Identify secondary causes of hypertension (renal artery stenosis from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation, sleep apnea) and the key clue for each.

Describe hypertensive damage: hyaline arteriolosclerosis, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction and atrial enlargement, nephrosclerosis, retinopathy, and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms causing intracerebral hemorrhage.

Distinguish hypertensive emergency (severe elevation, often 180/120 mmHg or higher, with acute organ damage) from chronic hypertension, and identify hyperplastic onion-skin arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis.

Define pulmonary hypertension (mean pulmonary artery pressure over 20 mmHg at rest) and classify its causes, including left heart disease (most common), lung disease and hypoxia, chronic thromboembolism, and heritable BMPR2 pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Explain pulmonary arterial hypertension pathogenesis (low NO and prostacyclin, high endothelin-1, smooth muscle proliferation, plexiform lesions) and predict a loud P2, right ventricular heave, right axis deviation, and cor pulmonale.

Explain the causes of left-sided heart failure and relate pulmonary venous congestion to dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, basal crackles, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells) in the lung.

Explain the causes of right-sided heart failure (most often left-sided failure; also cor pulmonale and right ventricular infarction) and relate systemic venous congestion to raised JVP, hepatojugular reflux, pitting edema, and nutmeg liver.

Distinguish heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (40% or lower, systolic) from preserved ejection fraction (50% or higher, diastolic), and interpret an S3, raised BNP, and chest radiograph signs of congestion.

Explain how sympathetic activation, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and ADH first support output but then drive fluid retention, remodeling, and progression, while natriuretic peptides partly oppose them.

Predict complications of heart failure: acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias, mural thrombi with embolism, cardiorenal syndrome, and cardiac cachexia.

Explain high-output heart failure in severe anemia, thyrotoxicosis, arteriovenous fistula, wet beriberi, and Paget disease of bone, and contrast its low systemic vascular resistance with low-output failure.
Predict sudden cardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypotension from acute mitral regurgitation after rupture of chordae tendineae or a papillary muscle.

Identify coronary atherosclerosis as the cause of most ischemic heart disease, list its risk factors, and name other causes (vasospasm, emboli, vasculitis, increased demand from tachycardia, hypertrophy, or aortic stenosis).

Distinguish stable angina (fixed stenosis of about 70% or more, exertional, ST depression), unstable angina (plaque disruption with partial thrombus, rest pain, no troponin rise), and Prinzmetal angina (vasospasm, transient ST elevation).

Trace the pathogenesis of myocardial infarction from plaque rupture and occlusive thrombus to irreversible injury after about 20 to 40 minutes, and distinguish transmural (often STEMI) from subendocardial (often NSTEMI) infarction.
Predict the occluded coronary artery from ECG lead changes (LAD in V1 to V4; circumflex in I, aVL, V5, V6; RCA in II, III, aVF) and interpret the timing of troponin and CK-MB rise and fall.

Relate the microscopic timeline of infarction (wavy fibers and coagulative necrosis in day 1, neutrophils at 1 to 3 days, macrophages at 3 to 7 days, granulation tissue by 1 to 2 weeks, scar by 2 months) to complications.

Predict complications of infarction by timing: early arrhythmia and cardiogenic shock, fibrinous pericarditis, papillary muscle, septal, or free wall rupture (most often 3 to 7 days), ventricular aneurysm with mural thrombus, and Dressler syndrome.

Describe chronic ischemic heart disease (ischemic cardiomyopathy): healed infarct scars, hypertrophy of surviving myocardium, left ventricular dilation, progressive heart failure, arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death.

Explain the causes of aortic stenosis (age-related calcification, bicuspid valve, rheumatic disease) and its findings: crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids, pulsus parvus et tardus, concentric hypertrophy, syncope, angina, and dyspnea.

Explain the causes of aortic regurgitation (aortic root dilation from hypertension, Marfan, or syphilis; bicuspid valve; endocarditis; rheumatic disease) and its findings: early decrescendo diastolic murmur, wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses, eccentric hypertrophy.

Explain mitral stenosis (almost always rheumatic) and its findings: opening snap with diastolic rumble, left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation with mural thrombus, pulmonary hypertension, and dysphagia or hoarseness from atrial compression.

Explain the causes of mitral regurgitation (prolapse, papillary muscle ischemia or rupture, left ventricular dilation, rheumatic disease, endocarditis) and its holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla, S3, and left atrial volume overload.

Distinguish acute (Staphylococcus aureus, normal valves) from subacute (viridans streptococci, damaged valves) infective endocarditis, identify the valves most involved, and interpret Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, Roth spots, and splinter hemorrhages.

Distinguish nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis in cancer and hypercoagulable states and Libman-Sacks endocarditis in lupus (small sterile vegetations on either or both leaflet surfaces) from infective endocarditis.

Explain mitral valve prolapse (myxomatous degeneration, links to Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, and ADPKD), its mid-systolic click and late systolic murmur that move earlier with standing or Valsalva, and its complications.

Explain how repeated rheumatic fever produces chronic rheumatic heart disease, with commissural fusion, thickened and shortened chordae, fish-mouth mitral stenosis, and combined mitral and aortic involvement.

Explain carcinoid heart disease: serotonin from liver metastases of a neuroendocrine tumor reaches the right heart, causing tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis, while lung monoamine oxidase spares the left heart; urine 5-HIAA is high.

Identify complications of prosthetic heart valves: valve thrombosis and embolism, mechanical hemolysis with schistocytes, structural failure of bioprosthetic valves, and endocarditis, often from Staphylococcus epidermidis.

Explain dilated cardiomyopathy causes (familial TTN variants, alcohol, prior myocarditis, doxorubicin, peripartum, Chagas, thiamine deficiency, hemochromatosis) and findings: four-chamber dilation, systolic dysfunction, S3, and functional mitral and tricuspid regurgitation.

Explain hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: asymmetric septal hypertrophy, myocyte disarray, outflow obstruction from systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, a murmur louder with Valsalva and softer with squatting, and sudden death in young athletes.

Explain restrictive cardiomyopathy causes (amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, radiation, endomyocardial fibrosis, Loeffler endocarditis) and its diastolic filling failure with right-sided congestion, and identify the low-voltage ECG despite a thick ventricular wall in amyloidosis.
Compare dilated, hypertrophic, and restrictive cardiomyopathy by chamber size, wall thickness, ejection fraction, and type of dysfunction (systolic versus diastolic).

Explain the causes of myocarditis (coxsackie B and other viruses, Chagas, Lyme, diphtheria, drug hypersensitivity, lupus, giant cell myocarditis) and its lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis, raised troponin, arrhythmia, and progression to dilated cardiomyopathy.

Explain stress (takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, a catecholamine-linked transient apical ballooning with near-normal coronary arteries, usually in postmenopausal women after acute stress, and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy that improves once the rate is controlled.
Explain acute (primary) pericarditis, usually viral such as coxsackie B, and its sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

Identify causes of secondary pericarditis (early post-infarction, Dressler syndrome, uremia, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, radiation, tuberculosis, bacteria, cancer, cardiac surgery) and match them to serous, fibrinous, purulent, hemorrhagic, or caseous exudate.

Explain constrictive pericarditis (tuberculosis, prior viral pericarditis, surgery, radiation) and its Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, and calcification, and distinguish it from restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Explain the causes of serous and hemorrhagic pericardial effusion and its findings (muffled heart sounds, low-voltage QRS, electrical alternans, enlarged globular heart on radiograph), and why the rate of fluid build-up matters more than volume.

Explain cardiac tamponade, including traumatic or post-rupture hemopericardium, and predict Beck triad (hypotension, distended neck veins, distant heart sounds), pulsus paradoxus, and equal diastolic pressures in all chambers.

Identify metastatic disease as far more common than primary cardiac tumors, name the usual sources (lung, breast, melanoma, lymphoma, leukemia), and relate pericardial spread to bloody effusion with malignant cells and tamponade.

Explain left-to-right shunt physiology and Eisenmenger syndrome: pulmonary vascular remodeling raises pressure until the shunt reverses, causing late cyanosis, clubbing, polycythemia, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

Explain ventricular septal defect (most often membranous) and predict its harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, the spontaneous closure of many small defects, and heart failure with large defects.
Distinguish ostium secundum ASD (most common), ostium primum ASD (Down syndrome), and patent foramen ovale, and predict a fixed split S2, pulmonic flow murmur, and paradoxical embolism.

Explain patent ductus arteriosus (sixth arch derivative; risk with prematurity and congenital rubella) and its continuous machine-like murmur, bounding pulses, and differential cyanosis of the toes once Eisenmenger syndrome develops.

Explain tetralogy of Fallot (pulmonary infundibular stenosis, right ventricular hypertrophy, overriding aorta, VSD) from anterosuperior infundibular septum displacement, its link to 22q11.2 deletion, boot-shaped heart, and relief of tet spells by squatting.

Explain bicuspid aortic valve (about 1 to 2% of people, linked to Turner syndrome and coarctation) and predict early calcific aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, endocarditis, and ascending aortic dilation or dissection.

Explain coarctation of the aorta (linked to Turner syndrome and bicuspid valve) and predict arm hypertension, weak delayed femoral pulses, and rib notching from enlarged intercostal collateral arteries.
Explain transposition of the great vessels (failed spiraling of the aorticopulmonary septum, linked to maternal diabetes) and why survival depends on mixing through a PDA, ASD, or VSD.

Apply Virchow triad to explain thrombus formation, distinguish pale arterial thrombi from red venous thrombi, identify lines of Zahn, and predict thrombus fates (propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization and recanalization).

Identify inherited hypercoagulable states (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C or S deficiency) and acquired ones (antiphospholipid syndrome, cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, immobility, surgery).

Classify emboli: venous thromboemboli to the lung, systemic emboli from mural thrombi to brain, legs, gut, kidney, and spleen, fat embolism 1 to 3 days after long-bone fracture, amniotic fluid embolism, and gas embolism.

Distinguish white infarcts (solid organs with end-arterial supply) from red infarcts (venous occlusion, loose tissue, dual supply, reperfusion), coagulative from liquefactive necrosis, and the factors that decide infarct size.
Define petechiae, purpura, ecchymosis, and hematoma, and predict the effect of hemorrhage by volume and site, including shock after acute loss of more than about 20% of blood volume.
Distinguish transudate from exudate edema, relate each to Starling forces or inflammation, and contrast pitting edema with nonpitting edema of lymphedema.

Classify shock as hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, or distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) and predict cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure in each.

Explain the stages of shock (compensated, progressive with lactic acidosis, irreversible), septic shock mediators (endotoxin, TNF, IL-1, nitric oxide), and resulting multiorgan dysfunction (acute tubular necrosis, ARDS, DIC).
Distinguish the three patterns of arteriosclerosis: atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis (hyaline and hyperplastic), and Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis, which does not narrow the lumen.

Trace atherosclerosis from endothelial injury to fatty streak to fibrous plaque, identify the arteries most affected (abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal, carotid), and predict complications (rupture, thrombosis, embolism, aneurysm).

Explain familial hypercholesterolemia findings: LDL often above 190 mg/dL in heterozygotes, coronary disease in childhood or the teens in homozygotes, tendon xanthomas, xanthelasma, and early corneal arcus.

Distinguish abdominal aortic aneurysm (atherosclerosis, older male smokers, infrarenal, rupture risk rising with diameter) from thoracic aneurysm (cystic medial degeneration, tertiary syphilis), berry aneurysms, and mycotic aneurysms.

Explain aortic dissection (intimal tear into the media; hypertension, Marfan, bicuspid valve, Turner, cocaine), its tearing back pain, unequal arm pressures, widened mediastinum, Stanford A versus B, and complications such as tamponade and aortic regurgitation.

Explain peripheral arterial disease (claudication, rest pain, ulcers, ankle-brachial index 0.90 or lower, Leriche syndrome) and atheroembolic disease with blue toes and cholesterol clefts after arterial catheterization.

Explain pulmonary embolism from deep leg vein thrombi and predict sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia with raised A-a gradient, acute right ventricular strain, and why most emboli do not cause lung infarction.

Explain deep vein thrombosis risk factors through Virchow triad and its unilateral warm, swollen, painful leg, and distinguish it from superficial thrombophlebitis, including migratory thrombophlebitis with cancer (Trousseau sign).

Explain varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency (incompetent valves, risk with age, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged standing) and predict edema, stasis dermatitis, and ulcers near the medial malleolus.
Distinguish primary Raynaud phenomenon (benign vasospasm in young women) from secondary Raynaud with scleroderma, lupus, or Buerger disease, and explain the white, blue, red color sequence.

Explain thromboangiitis obliterans (heavy smokers, often young men; segmental thrombosing inflammation of medium and small arteries extending to veins and nerves) and predict digital ulcers and gangrene unless tobacco use stops.

Explain giant cell arteritis (age over 50, granulomatous inflammation of carotid branches, headache, jaw claudication, high ESR, skip lesions on biopsy), its risk of blindness, and its link to polymyalgia rheumatica.
Explain Takayasu arteritis (granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis of the aortic arch and branches, usually young Asian women) and predict weak upper limb pulses and unequal arm blood pressures.

Explain polyarteritis nodosa (hepatitis B link, transmural necrotizing inflammation of medium arteries with lesions of different ages, renal and mesenteric microaneurysms, lung sparing, ANCA negative).

Identify Kawasaki disease in a child under 5 (fever, conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, swollen hands and feet, cervical lymphadenopathy) and predict coronary artery aneurysm as its key complication.

Distinguish ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA, sinus, lung, and kidney), microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA, no granulomas), and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (asthma, eosinophilia, MPO-ANCA).

Identify IgA vasculitis (palpable purpura on buttocks and legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, IgA nephropathy, often after an upper respiratory infection in children) and Behcet syndrome (oral and genital ulcers, uveitis).

Distinguish capillary hemangioma, including the infantile (strawberry) type that appears in the first weeks of life, grows fast, regresses, and is GLUT1 positive, from cavernous hemangioma, which does not regress and is the most common benign liver tumor.

Distinguish pyogenic granuloma (including the pregnancy gingival form), cherry hemangioma, and bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella in immunocompromised hosts, neutrophilic infiltrate) from hemangiomas and Kaposi sarcoma.

Explain Kaposi sarcoma pathogenesis: HHV-8 infection, spindle cells forming slit-like vascular spaces, viral cyclin D homolog and LANA effects on p53 and Rb, and growth favored by immune suppression; lesions progress from patch to plaque to nodule.
Compare the classic, endemic African, transplant-associated, and AIDS-associated forms of Kaposi sarcoma by population, sites, and course.

Identify atrial myxoma as the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults (pedunculated, usually left atrial, ball-valve obstruction, emboli, constitutional symptoms) and cardiac rhabdomyoma with tuberous sclerosis in children.
Identify angiosarcoma risk factors (vinyl chloride, arsenic, Thorotrast for liver tumors; chronic lymphedema after mastectomy) and its aggressive course.

Explain how bacteremia seeds damaged endothelium or fibrin-platelet deposits to form vegetations, and predict the likely organism by setting: native valve, IV drug use, prosthetic valve, dental work, or GI and GU procedures.

Predict complications of bacterial endocarditis: valve destruction and ring abscess, septic emboli (systemic in left-sided, lung in right-sided disease), immune complex glomerulonephritis, and mycotic aneurysm.

Distinguish acute Chagas disease (often mild; Romana sign) from chronic Chagas years later (dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and conduction block, megaesophagus, megacolon) in people from Latin America.

Distinguish the stages of Lyme disease (erythema migrans; then facial palsy, meningitis, and carditis with AV block; then large joint arthritis and late neurologic disease) and relate risk to Northeast and upper Midwest exposure.

Explain Rocky Mountain spotted fever as rickettsial vasculitis and predict fever, headache, a rash spreading from wrists and ankles to the trunk with palms and soles involved, thrombocytopenia, and possible shock and multiorgan failure.
Compare yellow fever (midzonal liver necrosis, Councilman bodies, jaundice, black vomit) with dengue (fever, severe muscle and joint pain, thrombocytopenia, plasma leak in severe dengue).
Explain the shared mechanism of viral hemorrhagic fevers (endothelial damage, cytokine storm, consumptive coagulopathy) and the high fatality and body fluid spread of Ebola and Marburg filoviruses.

Predict viral myocarditis in a young adult after a respiratory or GI illness (chest pain, arrhythmia, raised troponin, heart failure) and identify lymphocytic infiltrate with myocyte necrosis on biopsy.

Trace thyroid development from an endodermal diverticulum at the foramen cecum of the tongue, its descent along the thyroglossal duct anterior to the hyoid bone, and relate failed descent to a lingual thyroid.

Identify the pharyngeal pouch origins of the inferior parathyroids (third pouch, with the thymus), superior parathyroids (fourth pouch), and parafollicular C cells (ultimobranchial body, neural crest), and predict ectopic inferior parathyroid locations in the mediastinum.

Distinguish the origin of the anterior pituitary (Rathke pouch, oral ectoderm) from the posterior pituitary (infundibulum, diencephalic neuroectoderm), and relate Rathke pouch remnants to craniopharyngioma.
Compare the mesodermal origin of the adrenal cortex with the neural crest origin of the adrenal medulla, and relate the medulla's neural crest origin to pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.

Explain how failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches in 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome produces neonatal hypocalcemic tetany together with thymic hypoplasia and T cell deficiency.
Describe development of the pancreatic islets from foregut endoderm of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds.

Identify thyroid follicles (cuboidal follicular cells surrounding colloid) and parafollicular C cells, and relate tall columnar cells with scalloped, scant colloid to an actively stimulated gland, as in Graves disease.

Distinguish the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis, and medulla of the adrenal gland by histology and principal product (aldosterone, cortisol, adrenal androgens, catecholamines from chromaffin cells).

Distinguish anterior pituitary acidophils (GH, prolactin), basophils (FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH), and chromophobes from the posterior pituitary, which contains pituicytes and Herring bodies formed by axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons.
Identify parathyroid chief cells (PTH secretion) and oxyphil cells, and identify pancreatic islet alpha, beta, and delta cells by their hormones (glucagon, insulin, somatostatin).

Classify endocrine cells by derivation (neural crest: chromaffin cells and C cells; endoderm: thyroid follicular cells, parathyroids, islets; ectoderm: adenohypophysis) and relate neuroendocrine origin to chromogranin and synaptophysin staining of neuroendocrine tumors.
Locate the thyroid lobes and the isthmus anterior to the second and third tracheal rings, and explain why the gland, enclosed in pretracheal fascia, moves upward on swallowing.

Describe the relationship of the recurrent laryngeal nerve (tracheoesophageal groove) and external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (with the superior thyroid artery) to the thyroid, and predict voice changes after injury during thyroidectomy.

Locate the four parathyroid glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, and explain why their variable position, especially of the inferior glands, matters in thyroid and parathyroid surgery.

Locate the pituitary in the sella turcica beneath the diaphragma sellae, relate it to the optic chiasm above and cavernous sinuses laterally, and predict bitemporal hemianopia from suprasellar tumor extension.

Locate the retroperitoneal adrenal glands within the renal fascia superomedial to the kidneys, contrasting the pyramidal right gland behind the inferior vena cava with the crescent-shaped left gland along the medial border of the left kidney.

Trace the thyroid's arterial supply (superior thyroid artery from the external carotid, inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk, occasional thyroid ima artery) and venous drainage (superior and middle to internal jugular, inferior to brachiocephalic).

Trace the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system from superior hypophyseal arteries through the median eminence plexus and portal veins to the anterior pituitary, and explain why the anterior lobe is vulnerable to ischemic necrosis.

Trace the adrenal arteries (superior from inferior phrenic, middle from aorta, inferior from renal) and veins (right to inferior vena cava, left to left renal vein), and explain how cortical blood reaching the medulla induces PNMT for epinephrine synthesis.
Explain why the parathyroids depend mainly on the inferior thyroid artery, and predict hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy from devascularization or removal of parathyroid tissue.
Explain why insulin and glucagon draining into the hepatic portal vein reach the liver at high concentration first, and relate this to hepatic first-pass extraction of insulin.

Match each hypothalamic hormone (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) to its anterior pituitary target, and predict the effect of pituitary stalk section (rising prolactin, falling other anterior pituitary hormones, diabetes insipidus).

Explain control of ADH release by plasma osmolality (hypothalamic osmoreceptors) and blood volume (baroreceptors), and its action on V2 receptors inserting aquaporin-2 channels into collecting duct principal cells.

Explain calcium homeostasis: calcium-sensing receptor control of PTH, PTH effects on bone resorption, distal tubule calcium reabsorption, proximal tubule phosphate excretion, and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and the opposing action of calcitonin.

Explain regulation of aldosterone by angiotensin II and hyperkalemia (ACTH having a minor role), and its collecting duct actions: sodium reabsorption (ENaC, Na/K-ATPase) and potassium secretion by principal cells, and hydrogen ion secretion by alpha intercalated cells.

Trace glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GLUT2 entry, glucokinase, rising ATP closing K-ATP channels, depolarization, calcium influx, exocytosis), and explain why oral glucose releases more insulin than intravenous glucose through incretins (GLP-1, GIP).
Explain glucose counterregulation during fasting and hypoglycemia, comparing the rapid effects of glucagon and epinephrine with the slower effects of cortisol and growth hormone.

Classify hormones by signaling pathway: Gs/cAMP (ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, PTH, glucagon), Gq/IP3-calcium (GnRH, TRH, oxytocin), intrinsic tyrosine kinase (insulin, IGF-1), JAK/STAT (GH, prolactin), and intracellular receptors (steroids, thyroid hormone, calcitriol).

Explain plasma transport of thyroid hormone (thyroxine-binding globulin) and cortisol (cortisol-binding globulin), why only free hormone is active, and predict raised total T4 with normal free T4 when binding globulin rises in pregnancy.

Interpret paired trophic and target hormone levels (for example, high cortisol with low ACTH, or low free T4 with high TSH) to localize an endocrine disorder to the target gland, pituitary, or hypothalamus by negative feedback logic.

Describe actions of thyroid hormone (raised basal metabolic rate and Na/K-ATPase, beta-1 adrenergic receptor upregulation, bone growth, CNS maturation) and its activation by peripheral deiodinase conversion of T4 to T3.

Explain direct GH actions (lipolysis, insulin antagonism) and indirect actions through hepatic IGF-1 (linear growth, protein synthesis), and GH regulation by GHRH, somatostatin, IGF-1 feedback, sleep, exercise, and hypoglycemia.

Explain cortisol's effects (gluconeogenesis, proteolysis, lipolysis, anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions, permissive effect on catecholamine vasoconstriction, reduced collagen synthesis) and the morning peak of ACTH and cortisol secretion.
Explain tonic dopamine inhibition of prolactin secretion and TRH stimulation of prolactin, and predict hypogonadism from hyperprolactinemia through suppression of GnRH.

Contrast insulin's effects (GLUT4 uptake in muscle and adipose, glycogen synthesis, glycolysis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis) with glucagon's effects (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis) on fuel metabolism in the fed and fasting states.

Explain how insulin deficiency with glucagon excess increases lipolysis, hepatic fatty acid oxidation, and conversion of acetyl-CoA to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing an anion gap metabolic acidosis.
Relate dietary iodine to thyroid hormone synthesis and selenium to the deiodinases that convert T4 to T3, and explain how iodine deficiency raises TSH and causes goiter.

Trace vitamin D activation (UVB conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin, hepatic 25-hydroxylation, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation stimulated by PTH and low phosphate) and predict rickets, osteomalacia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism from deficiency.
Explain how hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and end-organ PTH action, producing hypocalcemia that does not correct until magnesium is replaced.

Explain how leptin from adipocytes (satiety) and ghrelin from the stomach (hunger) act on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to regulate appetite, and relate leptin resistance to common obesity and visceral adiposity to insulin resistance.

Trace thyroid hormone synthesis: iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter, oxidation and organification by thyroid peroxidase onto thyroglobulin tyrosines, coupling of MIT and DIT to T3 and T4, and release by thyroglobulin proteolysis.

Trace adrenal steroid synthesis from cholesterol (StAR transport, side-chain cleavage) through 17-alpha-hydroxylase, 21-hydroxylase, and 11-beta-hydroxylase to aldosterone, cortisol, and androgens, and predict which precursors accumulate when each enzyme is blocked.

Trace catecholamine synthesis from tyrosine (tyrosine hydroxylase as rate-limiting step, DOPA decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, PNMT) and breakdown by COMT and MAO to metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid, and relate these metabolites to pheochromocytoma testing.

Describe processing of preproinsulin to proinsulin and then insulin plus C-peptide, and use C-peptide to distinguish endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma, sulfonylurea ingestion) from exogenous insulin as the cause of hypoglycemia.
Describe synthesis of ADH and oxytocin in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, their axonal transport bound to neurophysins, and storage and release from the posterior pituitary.

Explain how renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 inactivates cortisol to cortisone to protect mineralocorticoid receptors, and predict hypertension with hypokalemia when it is inhibited by licorice (glycyrrhetinic acid).

Contrast loss-of-function mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin, with a second hit needed in tumor cells) with gain-of-function mutation of the RET proto-oncogene in MEN2, and explain the autosomal dominant inheritance of both syndromes.
Explain the autosomal recessive inheritance of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, with CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase) mutations as the most common cause.

Compare the genetics of type 1 diabetes (HLA-DR3 and DR4 association), type 2 diabetes (polygenic, with higher monozygotic twin concordance than type 1), and maturity-onset diabetes of the young (autosomal dominant glucokinase or HNF1A mutations).

Relate thyroid cancer types to their characteristic mutations: BRAF V600E and RET/PTC rearrangements in papillary carcinoma, RAS mutations and PAX8-PPARG fusion in follicular carcinoma, and RET mutations in medullary carcinoma.

Distinguish androgen insensitivity syndrome (X-linked androgen receptor defect, 46,XY, female external genitalia, testes, no uterus, high testosterone and LH) from 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (low DHT, ambiguous genitalia that virilize at puberty).

Distinguish primary hypogonadism (for example, Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY, with high LH and FSH) from secondary hypogonadism (for example, Kallmann syndrome, failed GnRH neuron migration with anosmia, with low LH and FSH).

Explain how steroid and thyroid hormones bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors at hormone response elements in DNA (the thyroid hormone receptor pairing with the retinoid X receptor), and relate this to their slower onset than peptide hormones.
Explain Graves disease as a type II hypersensitivity in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor, and predict transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis from transplacental IgG.

Describe the immune mechanisms of Hashimoto thyroiditis (T cell mediated follicular cell destruction, antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin), relate these antibodies to diagnosis, and relate chronic lymphoid stimulation to risk of thyroid B cell lymphoma.

Explain T cell mediated beta cell destruction (insulitis) in type 1 diabetes, the use of autoantibodies (GAD65, insulin, IA-2, ZnT8) as markers, and slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes in adults (type 1.5, LADA).

Contrast autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (AIRE mutation, autosomal recessive: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, Addison disease) with type 2 (Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes).

Explain how inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and how cortisol limits inflammation by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and NF-kB and reducing lymphocyte and eosinophil counts.

Explain why conjugating meningococcal capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier turns a T cell independent response into a T cell dependent response with class switching and memory, and relate vaccination to prevention of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Describe Neisseria meningitidis (gram-negative diplococcus, polysaccharide capsule, lipooligosaccharide endotoxin, respiratory droplet spread) and explain how endotoxin-driven sepsis and DIC cause adrenal hemorrhage in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Identify bacteria that cause acute suppurative thyroiditis (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae), and relate recurrent left-sided infection in children to a pyriform sinus fistula.
Relate subacute granulomatous thyroiditis to a preceding viral upper respiratory infection, with viruses such as coxsackievirus and mumps implicated.

Identify infectious causes of adrenalitis leading to Addison disease, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast, caseating granulomas), Histoplasma capsulatum, and cytomegalovirus in patients with AIDS.

Distinguish ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (pituitary adenoma, ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma) from ACTH-independent causes (adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, exogenous glucocorticoids) using plasma ACTH and high-dose dexamethasone suppression.

Relate cortisol excess to central obesity, moon facies, purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, and poor wound healing, and identify screening tests (24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression).

Explain primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome from adrenal adenoma, or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia) as hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin, and contrast it with secondary hyperaldosteronism with high renin.

Predict findings in 21-hydroxylase deficiency (salt wasting, hyperkalemia, raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone, virilization), 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency (virilization with hypertension), and 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency (hypertension, hypokalemia, absent sex steroids).

Explain primary hyperparathyroidism, most often from a single parathyroid adenoma, and interpret hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and raised PTH with stones, bone pain, abdominal symptoms, and osteitis fibrosa cystica (subperiosteal resorption, brown tumors).

Explain secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease (phosphate retention, low calcitriol) and vitamin D deficiency, interpret low or normal calcium with high PTH, and relate it to renal osteodystrophy and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.

Distinguish gigantism (GH excess before epiphyseal closure) from acromegaly (after closure), and relate acromegaly to coarse facial features, enlarged hands and feet, macroglossia, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease.
Interpret raised IGF-1 and failure of GH suppression after an oral glucose load as confirmation of GH excess, usually from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma.

Distinguish Graves disease (diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxedema, diffusely increased radioiodine uptake) from toxic multinodular goiter (patchy uptake, no eye or skin signs), both showing low TSH and high free T4.

Relate thyrotoxic findings (weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, bone loss) to raised metabolic rate and beta-adrenergic sensitivity, and identify thyroid storm as a life-threatening complication.

Explain the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (small cell lung carcinoma, CNS and pulmonary disease, drugs) and interpret euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium.
Distinguish familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation, low urine calcium, mildly raised PTH) from primary hyperparathyroidism.

Distinguish central precocious puberty (early GnRH activation, raised LH and FSH) from peripheral precocious puberty (low LH and FSH, for example from congenital adrenal hyperplasia, McCune-Albright syndrome, or sex steroid secreting tumors).

Distinguish central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency from head trauma, surgery, or tumors) from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 defects, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia), both causing polyuria with dilute urine and a tendency to hypernatremia when water intake is limited.
Interpret a water deprivation test with desmopressin, predicting urine concentration in central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and primary polydipsia.

Explain primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease; autoimmune adrenalitis, tuberculosis, metastases) and relate hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation from raised ACTH and POMC-derived MSH to low cortisol and aldosterone.

Identify causes of acute adrenocortical insufficiency (adrenal crisis), including stress in a patient with chronic insufficiency, rapid withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoids, and bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (anticoagulation, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), and relate it to shock.

Explain secondary adrenocortical insufficiency (pituitary disease, suppression by exogenous glucocorticoids) and predict why it lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia because ACTH is low and the renin-angiotensin system preserves aldosterone.

Identify causes of hypoparathyroidism (surgical removal, autoimmune, DiGeorge syndrome, hypomagnesemia) and relate hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and low PTH to tetany, perioral numbness, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and QT prolongation.

Distinguish pseudohypoparathyroidism (end-organ PTH resistance from GNAS mutation, high PTH, Albright hereditary osteodystrophy with short fourth and fifth metacarpals) from true hypoparathyroidism with low PTH.

Identify causes of hypopituitarism (nonfunctioning macroadenoma, Sheehan necrosis, pituitary apoplexy, surgery or radiation), and explain primary empty sella syndrome as arachnoid herniation through a defective diaphragma sellae flattening the pituitary.

Predict findings of hypothalamic lesions (craniopharyngioma, infiltrative disease, radiation), including deficiency of releasing hormones with low anterior pituitary output, diabetes insipidus, and hyperprolactinemia from interrupted dopamine delivery.

Explain how iodine deficiency lowers thyroid hormone, raises TSH, and causes diffuse then multinodular goiter, and relate hypothyroidism to cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia, myxedema, hyperlipidemia, and delayed reflex relaxation.

Interpret thyroid function tests in primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4), central hypothyroidism (low or normal TSH, low free T4), and TSH-secreting adenoma (high TSH, high free T4), and relate hypothyroid hyperprolactinemia to menstrual disturbance and infertility.

Identify causes of congenital hypothyroidism (thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, maternal iodine deficiency) and relate them to lethargy, prolonged jaundice, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and intellectual disability if untreated.
Interpret nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick) syndrome in severe illness, with low T3, raised reverse T3, and usually normal TSH from reduced peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.

Distinguish causes of short stature, including GH deficiency (low IGF-1, delayed bone age), GH receptor defects (Laron syndrome, high GH, low IGF-1), constitutional growth delay (delayed bone age), and familial short stature (normal bone age).

Explain the pathogenesis of Hashimoto thyroiditis and identify its histology (lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers, atrophic follicles, Hürthle cells) and painless goiter in a middle-aged woman.

Predict the course of Hashimoto thyroiditis from possible transient hyperthyroidism to permanent hypothyroidism, its association with other autoimmune diseases, and its increased risk of primary thyroid B cell lymphoma.

Identify granulomatous subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis by a painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, fever, raised ESR, and granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, and predict transient hyperthyroidism with low radioiodine uptake.
Predict the self-limited course of subacute thyroiditis from a thyrotoxic phase to a transient hypothyroid phase and usual recovery to normal thyroid function.

Distinguish painless (lymphocytic and postpartum) thyroiditis and Riedel thyroiditis (IgG4-related dense fibrosis producing a rock-hard thyroid fixed to adjacent structures) from Hashimoto and subacute thyroiditis.

Compare type 1 diabetes (autoimmune beta cell loss, absolute insulin deficiency, young onset, ketosis prone) with type 2 diabetes (insulin resistance with progressive beta cell dysfunction and islet amyloid, linked to obesity and family history).

Interpret diagnostic criteria for diabetes (fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL, 2-hour oral glucose tolerance value at least 200 mg/dL, HbA1c at least 6.5%, or random glucose at least 200 mg/dL with symptoms) and explain HbA1c as a three-month measure.

Contrast diabetic ketoacidosis (anion gap acidosis, ketones, Kussmaul breathing, raised serum potassium despite total body depletion) with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (very high glucose and osmolality, altered mental status, little ketosis).

Explain how nonenzymatic glycation (advanced glycation end products) and the sorbitol (polyol) pathway produce hyaline arteriolosclerosis, accelerated atherosclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, and cataracts in chronic hyperglycemia.

Predict chronic diabetic complications by organ: nephropathy (glomerular basement membrane thickening, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, albuminuria), retinopathy, autonomic neuropathy with gastroparesis, and peripheral vascular disease with foot ulcers.

Identify components of metabolic syndrome (abdominal obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, hypertension, raised fasting glucose), relate them to insulin resistance, and recognize acanthosis nigricans as a skin sign of insulin resistance.
Explain how a persistent thyroglossal duct forms a midline neck cyst near the hyoid bone that moves upward with swallowing and tongue protrusion, and identify infection as a complication.

Distinguish a midline thyroglossal duct cyst from a lateral branchial cleft cyst at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and explain why a normally located thyroid should be confirmed before removal, since the mass may be the only functioning thyroid tissue.

Explain Sheehan syndrome as ischemic necrosis of a pregnancy-enlarged anterior pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension, and explain why the posterior pituitary, with its direct arterial supply, is usually spared.
Predict the presentation of Sheehan syndrome (failure of lactation, amenorrhea, loss of axillary and pubic hair, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency) from loss of anterior pituitary hormones.

Explain pituitary apoplexy as sudden hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma, and relate severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia from cavernous sinus compression, and acute adrenal insufficiency to its mechanism.

Distinguish adrenal cortical adenoma (small, often nonfunctional or cortisol or aldosterone secreting) from adrenocortical carcinoma (large, invasive, often virilizing), and recognize that metastases are more common than primary adrenal cancer.

Identify neuroblastoma as an adrenal medulla tumor of young children with N-MYC amplification, Homer Wright rosettes, raised urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid, and possible opsoclonus-myoclonus.
Identify insulinoma as a beta cell tumor causing Whipple triad (hypoglycemic symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose) with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide, and relate it to MEN1.

Distinguish causes of hypoglycemia, including insulinoma (high insulin and C-peptide), surreptitious insulin use (high insulin, low C-peptide), sepsis, and liver failure (impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogen stores).

Identify other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors by their syndromes: glucagonoma (hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss) and somatostatinoma (diabetes, gallstones, steatorrhea, achlorhydria).

Distinguish parathyroid adenoma (single enlarged gland of chief cells, suppressed remaining glands), hyperplasia (multiple glands, as in MEN syndromes), and the rare carcinoma (marked hypercalcemia, invasion, metastasis).

Classify pituitary adenomas by size (microadenoma under 1 cm, macroadenoma) and hormone, and relate prolactinoma, the most common type, to galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility in women and decreased libido in men.
Predict mass effects of a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma: bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression, headache, hypopituitarism, and mild hyperprolactinemia from stalk compression.

Identify craniopharyngioma as a suprasellar tumor from Rathke pouch remnants, often calcified and cystic with oily fluid, causing headache, bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes insipidus, and growth failure in children.
Distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma by capsular or vascular invasion, and explain hematogenous spread of follicular carcinoma to bone and lung.

Identify papillary carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, by Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies, relate it to childhood radiation exposure, and explain lymphatic spread to cervical nodes with good prognosis.
Identify medullary carcinoma as a C cell tumor secreting calcitonin, with amyloid stroma derived from calcitonin, and relate it to RET mutations and MEN2.

Distinguish euthyroid (nontoxic) diffuse and multinodular goiter, with normal TSH and compressive symptoms such as dysphagia, from thyroid neoplasms, and relate a cold nodule on radioiodine scan to higher cancer risk.
Identify anaplastic thyroid carcinoma as a rapidly growing, locally invasive tumor of older adults with TP53 mutations and very poor prognosis.

Match the tumors of MEN1 (parathyroid, pituitary, pancreatic endocrine tumors such as gastrinoma), MEN2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia), and MEN2B (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus).

Identify pheochromocytoma as a chromaffin cell tumor causing episodic hypertension, headache, palpitations, and sweating, diagnosed by raised plasma or urine metanephrines, and associated with MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neurofibromatosis type 1.

Identify endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes: ACTH and ADH from small cell lung carcinoma, and hypercalcemia of malignancy from PTH-related peptide (squamous cell lung carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma) with suppressed PTH.

Identify acute infectious (suppurative) thyroiditis as a bacterial infection presenting with fever and a painful, tender, sometimes fluctuant thyroid with usually normal thyroid function, and identify abscess as a complication.

Explain Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome as bilateral adrenal hemorrhage during overwhelming sepsis, classically meningococcemia with DIC, and relate petechial rash, shock, and acute adrenal insufficiency to its mechanism.

Identify the foregut, midgut, and hindgut derivatives and their arteries (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric), and explain why visceral pain from each is referred to the epigastric, periumbilical, or suprapubic region.

Describe physiologic herniation of the midgut in week 6, its 270 degree counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery, and its return by week 10, and predict the results of malrotation and of failed return (omphalocele).
Explain how the tracheoesophageal septum divides the foregut into the esophagus and the respiratory diverticulum, and relate incomplete division to esophageal atresia and tracheoesophageal fistula.

Describe development of the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts from the hepatic diverticulum and of the pancreas from dorsal and ventral buds, and relate abnormal ventral bud migration to annular pancreas and failed duct fusion to pancreas divisum.
Explain how neural crest cells migrate to form the myenteric and submucosal plexuses, and relate failed migration (RET mutations) to the aganglionic distal segment of Hirschsprung disease.
Describe recanalization of the duodenal lumen and relate its failure to duodenal atresia, with bilious vomiting, the double bubble sign, and an association with Down syndrome.
Identify the four layers of the gastrointestinal wall (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa or adventitia) and locate the submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses within them.

Compare the epithelium of the esophagus (nonkeratinized stratified squamous), stomach and intestine (simple columnar), and anal canal (columnar above the pectinate line, stratified squamous below), and relate the gastroesophageal junction to Barrett metaplasia.

Identify gastric parietal cells (HCl, intrinsic factor), chief cells (pepsinogen), mucous neck cells, and antral G cells (gastrin), and predict which secretions fall when autoimmune gastritis destroys the body and fundus mucosa.
Distinguish the duodenum (Brunner glands in the submucosa), jejunum (tall plicae circulares), ileum (Peyer patches), and colon (crypts rich in goblet cells, no villi) on histologic sections.

Describe the hepatic lobule and acinus, including the portal triad, sinusoids, space of Disse, Kupffer cells, and stellate (Ito) cells, and explain why zone 3 is most vulnerable to ischemia and to acetaminophen injury.
Distinguish pancreatic acini with zymogen granules from islets of Langerhans, and compare serous and mucous salivary acini, identifying the parotid as a mainly serous gland.
Identify the parts of the stomach (cardia, fundus, body, antrum, pylorus) and the four parts of the duodenum, and locate the major duodenal papilla in the second part.

Classify abdominal organs as intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal, naming the retroperitoneal gut structures (duodenum parts 2 to 4, pancreas except the tail, ascending and descending colon, and part of the rectum).

Describe the liver lobes, bare area, and porta hepatis, and trace bile from the hepatic ducts to the common bile duct, which joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater under the sphincter of Oddi.
Distinguish the colon from the small intestine by taeniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices, and locate the base of the appendix at McBurney point where the taeniae converge.

Locate the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands and their ducts, including the parotid duct opening opposite the upper second molar, and explain why parotid disease can involve the facial nerve passing through the gland.

Unit name: The gut in the body cavities
Competency: Trace the esophagus from the pharynx through the superior and posterior mediastinum to the stomach, naming its three narrowings: the cricopharyngeus, the crossing of the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and the diaphragmatic hiatus at T10.

Unit name: The gut in the body cavities
Competency: Relate the innervation of the tongue (CN V3 and CN VII to the anterior two thirds, CN IX to the posterior third, CN XII motor except palatoglossus by CN X) to the deficit produced by a given nerve lesion.

Unit name: The gut in the body cavities
Competency: Describe the greater and lesser sacs, the greater and lesser omentum, and the omental (epiploic) foramen, and identify the hepatoduodenal ligament contents (portal vein, proper hepatic artery, common bile duct).

Unit name: The gut in the body cavities
Competency: Identify the structures carried by the falciform (ligamentum teres), gastrohepatic (gastric arteries), gastrosplenic (short gastric vessels), and splenorenal (splenic artery and vein, pancreatic tail) ligaments.

Unit name: The gut in the body cavities
Competency: Describe the boundaries of the inguinal canal and Hesselbach triangle, and distinguish indirect (lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, through the deep ring), direct (medial, through the triangle), and femoral (below the inguinal ligament) hernias.

Unit name: The gut in the body cavities
Competency: Locate the dependent peritoneal spaces where fluid, pus, or blood collects (hepatorenal pouch of Morison when supine, rectouterine or rectovesical pouch when upright, subphrenic spaces) and relate them to abscess formation.

Trace the branches of the celiac trunk (left gastric, splenic, common hepatic) to the stomach, liver, spleen, pancreas, and duodenum, and identify the gastroduodenal artery as the vessel eroded by a posterior duodenal ulcer.

Describe the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and the marginal artery, and predict ischemic colitis at the watershed zones (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid junction) after hypotension.
Trace portal blood from the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, which join behind the pancreatic neck, through the liver sinusoids and central veins to the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava.

Identify the portosystemic anastomoses (left gastric to esophageal veins draining to azygos, paraumbilical to abdominal wall veins, superior to middle and inferior rectal veins) and predict varices and caput medusae in portal hypertension.

Compare the anal canal above and below the pectinate line by epithelium, arterial supply, venous drainage (portal versus systemic), lymph drainage (internal iliac versus superficial inguinal), and pain sensation (visceral versus somatic).

Explain the dual blood supply of the liver (most flow from the portal vein, the rest from the hepatic artery) and why hepatic infarction is uncommon while the bile ducts depend on hepatic arterial flow.

Describe mastication by the muscles of mastication (CN V3), the voluntary oral and reflex pharyngeal and esophageal phases of swallowing coordinated by the medulla, and vagal nitric oxide and VIP relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and proximal stomach.

Explain how slow waves from the interstitial cells of Cajal set contraction frequency, how the myenteric plexus coordinates peristalsis (contraction above and relaxation below a bolus), and how motilin drives the fasting migrating motor complex.

Explain the cephalic, gastric, and intestinal phases of gastric acid secretion, including parietal cell stimulation by acetylcholine, gastrin, and histamine, inhibition by somatostatin, and the H+/K+ ATPase as the final step.
Relate gastrin, cholecystokinin, secretin, GIP, and motilin to their source cells (G, I, S, K, M) and stimuli, and predict the hormonal response to a meal that delivers acid and fat to the duodenum.

Explain carbohydrate, protein, and fat digestion by salivary and pancreatic amylase, brush border disaccharidases, enteropeptidase activation of trypsinogen, and pancreatic lipase acting with bile salts.

Describe the defecation reflex (rectal distension, reflex relaxation of the internal anal sphincter, voluntary control of the external sphincter by the pudendal nerve) and the gastrocolic reflex, and predict incontinence from loss of each element.

Explain how vomiting is triggered through the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema and the medullary vomiting center, and predict the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis of prolonged vomiting.

Explain monosaccharide absorption (SGLT1 sodium cotransport of glucose and galactose, GLUT5 uptake of fructose, GLUT2 basolateral exit) and why glucose plus sodium in oral rehydration solution increases water absorption.

Explain absorption of free amino acids by sodium-linked transporters and of dipeptides and tripeptides by H+ cotransport (PepT1), and relate the neutral amino acid transport defect of Hartnup disease to pellagra-like findings.

Trace fat absorption from micelles to re-esterification in enterocytes, packaging with apoB-48 into chylomicrons, and entry into lacteals, and predict steatorrhea, acanthocytes, and vitamin E deficiency in abetalipoproteinemia.
Identify where iron (duodenum), folate (jejunum), and vitamin B12 and bile acids (terminal ileum) are absorbed, and predict the deficiencies that follow duodenal disease or ileal resection.

Explain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids with active reabsorption in the terminal ileum, and predict steatorrhea and cholesterol gallstone risk when ileal disease or resection interrupts it.
