Compare secretory diarrhea (cholera toxin raising cAMP and opening CFTR chloride channels), osmotic diarrhea (unabsorbed lactose), and inflammatory diarrhea, and use the stool osmotic gap and response to fasting to distinguish them.

Identify the essential amino acids and essential fatty acids (linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid) required in the diet, and compare kwashiorkor (protein deficiency, edema from hypoalbuminemia, fatty liver) with marasmus (calorie deficiency, wasting without edema).

Explain how fat malabsorption (pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis, celiac disease) causes deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K, and predict night blindness, osteomalacia, hemolytic anemia with neuropathy, and a prolonged PT.

Trace vitamin B12 absorption (release by acid and pepsin, haptocorrin binding, pancreatic protease cleavage, intrinsic factor binding, ileal uptake) and distinguish B12 from folate deficiency by methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels.

Relate deficiencies of thiamine (Wernicke encephalopathy, beriberi), niacin (pellagra), pyridoxine (sideroblastic anemia, seizures), and vitamin C (scurvy from impaired collagen hydroxylation) to the cofactor role of each vitamin.

Explain endogenous energy production in the fed and fasting states, including hepatic glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis from alanine, lactate, and glycerol, and hepatic ketogenesis, and why the liver cannot use the ketones it makes.

Relate deficiencies of minerals absorbed in the gut to their findings: iron (microcytic anemia), zinc (poor wound healing, dysgeusia, acrodermatitis), and copper (anemia, neutropenia, myelopathy), including copper deficiency from excess zinc or gastric bypass.
Predict the findings of vitamin A toxicity (intracranial hypertension, liver injury, teratogenicity) and vitamin D toxicity (hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, kidney stones).

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Trace bilirubin from heme breakdown (heme oxygenase, biliverdin reductase) through albumin transport, hepatic conjugation by UGT1A1, canalicular excretion by MRP2, and conversion by gut bacteria to urobilinogen and stercobilin.

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Interpret conjugated and unconjugated serum bilirubin, urine bilirubin, and urine urobilinogen to distinguish hemolytic, hepatocellular, and obstructive jaundice.

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Explain phase I (cytochrome P450) and phase II (glucuronidation, sulfation, glutathione conjugation) biotransformation, and use acetaminophen overdose to show how glutathione depletion lets NAPQI cause zone 3 necrosis.

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Explain carbon tetrachloride hepatotoxicity as cytochrome P450 conversion to the trichloromethyl free radical, which causes lipid peroxidation, fatty change, and centrilobular necrosis.

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Explain the synthetic and metabolic functions of the liver (albumin, clotting factors, urea cycle disposal of ammonia), and predict hypoalbuminemia, a prolonged PT, and hyperammonemia in liver failure.

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Describe the protective functions of saliva (bicarbonate buffering, IgA, lysozyme, lactoferrin, enamel remineralization) and predict dental caries when salivary flow falls.

Unit name: Liver detoxification, bilirubin, and gland functions
Competency: Explain how the gallbladder concentrates bile by absorbing sodium and water and contracts under cholecystokinin, and relate stasis and concentration to gallstone formation.

Explain hereditary hemochromatosis (autosomal recessive HFE C282Y mutation, inappropriately low hepcidin, excess iron absorption) and predict cirrhosis, diabetes, skin bronzing, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, and hepatocellular carcinoma risk.

Explain Wilson disease (autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation, failed biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading) and relate it to low serum ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings, basal ganglia degeneration, and hepatitis or cirrhosis.

Explain how the PiZZ alpha-1 antitrypsin variant misfolds and is retained in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum as PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules causing cirrhosis, while low serum levels cause panacinar emphysema.
Compare the adenoma to carcinoma sequence (APC loss, KRAS activation, TP53 loss) with the mismatch repair pathway (MLH1, MSH2, microsatellite instability) of Lynch syndrome in colorectal cancer.

Distinguish familial adenomatous polyposis (autosomal dominant APC, hundreds of adenomas), Gardner and Turcot variants, MUTYH-associated polyposis (autosomal recessive), and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11, hamartomas, mucocutaneous pigmentation).
Relate CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis to meconium ileus, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and focal biliary cirrhosis.

Describe mucosal immunity in the gut, including antigen sampling by M cells over Peyer patches, secretory IgA transported by the polymeric Ig receptor, and oral tolerance, and relate selective IgA deficiency to recurrent mucosal infections.

Explain celiac disease immunopathogenesis: tissue transglutaminase deamidates gliadin, HLA-DQ2 or DQ8 presents it to CD4 T cells, and IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies appear.
Explain how NOD2 variants, impaired handling of commensal bacteria, and Th1 and Th17 responses produce transmural granulomatous inflammation in Crohn disease.

Match autoimmune gastrointestinal diseases to their autoantibodies: autoimmune gastritis (parietal cell and intrinsic factor), autoimmune hepatitis (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-LKM1), and primary biliary cholangitis (antimitochondrial).
Explain how chronic Helicobacter pylori antigen stimulation drives B cell proliferation in gastric MALT lymphoma, and why early lesions can regress when the organism is eradicated.

Explain that hepatocyte injury in hepatitis B is caused mainly by cytotoxic CD8 T cells rather than the virus itself, and relate HBsAg immune complexes to polyarteritis nodosa and membranous nephropathy.
Explain why hepatitis B vaccination with recombinant HBsAg produces anti-HBs without anti-HBc, so serology separates vaccine immunity from resolved infection.

Distinguish toxin-mediated causes of diarrhea and vomiting: preformed Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus toxins (onset within hours), cholera toxin and the ETEC heat-labile toxin (both raise cAMP), and Clostridioides difficile toxins A and B.

Compare invasive enteric bacteria by key features: Shigella (nonmotile, very low infectious dose), Salmonella (motile, H2S producing), and Campylobacter jejuni (comma-shaped, grows at 42 degrees C (107.6 degrees F), poultry).

Describe Yersinia enterocolitica (mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis), EHEC O157:H7 (Shiga toxin, bloody diarrhea, hemolytic uremic syndrome), and Listeria monocytogenes (deli meats and soft cheese, actin-based cell-to-cell spread).

Compare the viral causes of enteritis: rotavirus (segmented dsRNA, villus damage in infants), norovirus (ssRNA calicivirus, outbreaks), and the enteroviruses coxsackievirus and echovirus (ssRNA picornaviruses, fecal-oral).

Compare hepatitis viruses: HAV (picornavirus, fecal-oral), HBV (partially dsDNA hepadnavirus with reverse transcriptase), HCV (flavivirus, high antigenic variation), HDV (defective, requires HBsAg), and HEV (fecal-oral, severe in pregnancy).

Describe Helicobacter pylori as a curved, flagellated, microaerophilic gram-negative rod whose urease makes ammonia to buffer acid, and identify the urea breath test, stool antigen, and biopsy as ways to detect it.

Compare intestinal parasites: Giardia (cysts in water, fatty diarrhea), Entamoeba histolytica (flask-shaped ulcers, liver abscess), Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, and Cystoisospora (acid-fast oocysts), and Strongyloides (skin-penetrating larvae, autoinfection, hyperinfection with corticosteroids).

Distinguish mumps parotitis (paramyxovirus, often bilateral, raised serum amylase, with orchitis, pancreatitis, or aseptic meningitis) from acute bacterial parotitis (Staphylococcus aureus, dehydrated or postoperative patients, pus at the parotid duct).
Explain why salivary stones form most often in the submandibular gland (more viscous saliva, upward duct course), and predict painful swelling with meals and secondary sialadenitis.

Explain acute pancreatitis as premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsin and other enzymes, and identify its causes, led by gallstones and alcohol, plus hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, ERCP, mumps, trauma, and drugs such as thiazides.

Interpret the findings of acute pancreatitis: epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase above three times normal, fat necrosis with calcium soap formation and hypocalcemia, and Cullen and Grey Turner signs of retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
Predict complications of acute pancreatitis, including pseudocyst (lined by granulation tissue, not epithelium), necrosis with infection or abscess, ARDS, DIC, and hypovolemic shock.

Describe chronic pancreatitis (alcohol, cystic fibrosis, ductal obstruction, hereditary PRSS1 and SPINK1 mutations) with fibrosis and calcifications, and predict exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency) and diabetes.

Distinguish intrahepatic causes of cholestasis (drugs, pregnancy, total parenteral nutrition, primary biliary cholangitis) from extrahepatic obstruction, and interpret raised conjugated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and GGT, pruritus, pale stools, and xanthomas.

Compare primary biliary cholangitis (middle-aged women, antimitochondrial antibody, granulomatous destruction of small intrahepatic ducts) with primary sclerosing cholangitis (ulcerative colitis, onion-skin fibrosis, beaded ducts, cholangiocarcinoma risk).

Explain how activated hepatic stellate cells lay down collagen in the space of Disse to produce bridging fibrosis and regenerative nodules in cirrhosis, and identify its main causes (alcohol, chronic HBV and HCV, fatty liver disease, metabolic disease).

Predict the findings of cirrhosis from hepatocellular failure (jaundice, coagulopathy, hypoalbuminemia, hyperestrogenism with spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, and hepatic encephalopathy with asterixis) and from portal hypertension.

Explain hepatorenal syndrome (splanchnic vasodilation and renal vasoconstriction with histologically normal kidneys) and hepatopulmonary syndrome (intrapulmonary vascular dilation causing hypoxemia) as complications of cirrhosis.

Compare Gilbert syndrome (mildly reduced UGT1A1 activity, benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia during fasting, stress, or illness) with Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I (absent UGT1A1, kernicterus in infancy) and type II (partial deficiency, milder course).

Describe the progression of alcohol-related liver disease from steatosis to alcoholic hepatitis (hepatocyte ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophils) to cirrhosis, and interpret an AST to ALT ratio greater than 2.

Explain metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD, formerly nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) as a result of insulin resistance and obesity, and distinguish simple steatosis from steatohepatitis (MASH) that can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Distinguish autoimmune hepatitis (young women, hypergammaglobulinemia, interface hepatitis with plasma cells) from drug and toxin hepatitis, such as acetaminophen zone 3 necrosis and isoniazid hepatitis.

Classify causes of portal hypertension as prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis, schistosomiasis), or posthepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome, right heart failure), and predict ascites, splenomegaly, varices, and caput medusae.

Distinguish Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2 defect, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, black pigmented liver) from Rotor syndrome (similar but milder, liver not pigmented) as benign inherited causes of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

Explain acute calculous cholecystitis from persistent cystic duct obstruction with chemical then bacterial inflammation, interpret right upper quadrant pain, fever, Murphy sign, and leukocytosis, and contrast acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill patients.
Identify chronic cholecystitis with a calcified porcelain gallbladder as a risk for gallbladder adenocarcinoma.

Compare cholesterol stones (bile supersaturated with cholesterol, gallbladder stasis; risks include female sex, obesity, pregnancy, estrogen, rapid weight loss) with black pigment stones (hemolysis) and brown pigment stones (biliary infection).

Predict the consequence of a gallstone by its location: biliary colic, choledocholithiasis with obstructive jaundice, ascending cholangitis (fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain), gallstone pancreatitis, and gallstone ileus through a cholecystoenteric fistula.
Explain Mirizzi syndrome as a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compressing the common hepatic duct, producing obstructive jaundice.

Explain the causes of achlorhydria (autoimmune atrophic gastritis, chronic H. pylori pangastritis, gastrectomy) and predict hypergastrinemia with ECL cell hyperplasia and carcinoid risk, impaired iron and B12 absorption, and bacterial overgrowth.

Describe celiac disease findings: villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytes mainly in the distal duodenum and proximal jejunum, iron deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, and risk of enteropathy-associated T cell lymphoma.

Distinguish malabsorption from pancreatic enzyme deficiency (steatorrhea, low fecal elastase, normal D-xylose absorption) from mucosal disease (abnormal D-xylose absorption), and relate enteropeptidase deficiency to failed protease activation.

Explain how primary (adult-type) or secondary (after viral enteritis or celiac disease) lactase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhea, bloating, and flatulence after dairy, with a positive hydrogen breath test and normal villi in the primary form.

Predict the consequences of short bowel syndrome after extensive resection, including diarrhea, steatorrhea, B12 and bile acid loss after ileal resection, and calcium oxalate kidney stones from enteric hyperoxaluria.
Explain how bacterial overgrowth in a blind loop after gastric surgery deconjugates bile acids and consumes vitamin B12, causing steatorrhea and B12 deficiency with normal or raised folate.

Explain achalasia as loss of inhibitory (nitric oxide and VIP) neurons of the myenteric plexus, producing incomplete LES relaxation and aperistalsis, with dysphagia to solids and liquids, a bird-beak barium swallow, and Chagas disease as a secondary cause.

Distinguish adynamic (paralytic) ileus (after abdominal surgery, hypokalemia, peritonitis, opioids; absent bowel sounds, diffuse gas) from mechanical obstruction (adhesions, hernias, tumors, impaction; high-pitched bowel sounds, dilated loops proximal to a transition point).

Distinguish sliding from paraesophageal hiatal hernia, and explain how an incarcerated abdominal wall hernia becomes strangulated as venous congestion leads to arterial compromise and bowel infarction.

Compare intussusception (telescoping, usually ileocolic in young children, a lead point such as hypertrophied Peyer patches or Meckel diverticulum, currant jelly stool) with volvulus (twisting on the mesentery, sigmoid in older adults, midgut with malrotation in infants).

Distinguish causes of megacolon: Hirschsprung disease (absent ganglion cells in the rectum, delayed passage of meconium, empty rectal vault), Chagas disease (acquired loss of the plexus), and toxic megacolon complicating ulcerative colitis or C. difficile colitis.
Explain Zenker diverticulum as a false pharyngoesophageal diverticulum above the cricopharyngeus from cricopharyngeal dysfunction, causing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis.

Describe gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying from diabetic autonomic neuropathy, with early satiety and vomiting) and irritable bowel syndrome (recurrent pain linked to defecation and altered stool form without structural disease).

Explain appendicitis as luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) leading to distension, ischemia, and bacterial invasion, and trace pain from the periumbilical region (visceral) to McBurney point (parietal peritoneum) before perforation.
Describe Barrett esophagus as intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells replacing distal squamous epithelium after chronic reflux, and relate it to the dysplasia to adenocarcinoma sequence.

Explain how a low-fiber diet and high intraluminal pressure create false diverticula in the sigmoid colon where vasa recta penetrate the wall, and distinguish painless bleeding in diverticulosis from diverticulitis with left lower quadrant pain, fever, abscess, or fistula.

Identify noninfectious causes of enteritis and colitis, including radiation, NSAIDs, and microscopic colitis (collagenous with a thick subepithelial collagen band, lymphocytic with excess intraepithelial lymphocytes) causing chronic watery diarrhea with normal-looking mucosa.

Compare gastric and duodenal ulcers by mechanism (H. pylori, NSAID loss of prostaglandin protection, Zollinger-Ellison), pain timing with meals, and malignancy risk, and predict hemorrhage or perforation with free air under the diaphragm.

Explain acute erosive gastritis and stress ulcers, including Curling ulcer after severe burns (hypovolemia and mucosal ischemia) and Cushing ulcer after brain injury (vagal stimulation raising acid), and NSAID and alcohol injury.

Distinguish reflux esophagitis (basal cell hyperplasia, elongated papillae) from eosinophilic esophagitis (atopy, 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, rings and furrows, food impaction) and pill esophagitis (doxycycline, NSAIDs, potassium chloride).

Compare chronic H. pylori gastritis (antrum, intestinal metaplasia, risk of adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma) with autoimmune gastritis (body and fundus, parietal cell loss, achlorhydria, pernicious anemia).

Explain GERD from transient LES relaxation, low LES tone, and hiatal hernia (risks include obesity and pregnancy), and predict heartburn, chronic cough, hoarseness, and complications of stricture and Barrett esophagus.

Compare Crohn disease (mouth to anus, often terminal ileum, skip lesions, transmural inflammation, noncaseating granulomas, cobblestone mucosa) with ulcerative colitis (rectum extending proximally, continuous mucosal inflammation, crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps).

Predict complications of inflammatory bowel disease: fistulas, strictures, B12 and bile acid malabsorption, and oxalate stones in Crohn disease; toxic megacolon and primary sclerosing cholangitis in ulcerative colitis; colorectal cancer, erythema nodosum, uveitis, and arthritis in both.

Distinguish Mallory-Weiss syndrome (mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction with hematemesis after retching) from Boerhaave syndrome (transmural esophageal rupture with chest pain, pneumomediastinum, and subcutaneous emphysema).
Distinguish anal fissure (posterior midline tear, painful bright red bleeding) from anorectal abscess and fistula (Crohn disease association), proctitis, and rectal prolapse.

Describe esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula (the most common type), predicting polyhydramnios, drooling, choking and cyanosis with feeds, failure to pass a nasogastric tube, and air in the stomach, plus VACTERL associations.

Distinguish esophageal webs (upper esophagus; Plummer-Vinson syndrome with iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, and squamous cell carcinoma risk) from Schatzki rings (lower esophagus at the squamocolumnar junction, intermittent solid food dysphagia).

Describe Meckel diverticulum as a persistent vitelline duct forming a true diverticulum of the ileum, apply the rule of twos, and predict painless rectal bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa or obstruction from intussusception.

Explain infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, predicting nonbilious projectile vomiting at 2 to 6 weeks, a palpable olive-shaped mass, and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, with first-born males and macrolide exposure as risks.

Explain biliary atresia as progressive obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts, presenting in the first weeks of life with persistent conjugated jaundice, acholic stools, dark urine, and progression to cirrhosis.

Distinguish gastroschisis (defect usually right of the umbilicus, bowel not covered by peritoneum) from omphalocele (midline, covered by peritoneum and amnion, associated with trisomies and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome), and explain malrotation with Ladd bands.
Explain cleft lip as failed fusion of the maxillary and medial nasal processes and cleft palate as failed fusion of the palatine shelves, and predict feeding difficulty.

Explain ascites in cirrhosis from portal hypertension, hypoalbuminemia, and splanchnic vasodilation with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation and sodium retention, and interpret a serum-ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL or more as portal hypertension.

Distinguish spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (cirrhotic ascites, usually E. coli or Klebsiella, ascitic neutrophils of 250/mm3 or more) from secondary peritonitis (perforated viscus, polymicrobial, rigid abdomen).
Explain how fibrous adhesions form after abdominal surgery or peritonitis and predict small bowel obstruction as their main complication.

Explain esophageal varices as dilated submucosal veins fed by the left gastric vein draining to the azygos system in portal hypertension, and predict painless massive hematemesis as a major cause of death in cirrhosis.

Distinguish internal hemorrhoids (above the pectinate line, painless bright red bleeding, prolapse) from external hemorrhoids (below the line, painful when thrombosed), and identify straining, constipation, pregnancy, and low-fiber diet as risks.

Compare acute mesenteric ischemia (often an embolus from atrial fibrillation to the superior mesenteric artery, pain out of proportion to the exam, raised lactate) with chronic mesenteric ischemia (postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss) and ischemic colitis.

Describe angiodysplasia (dilated, tortuous submucosal vessels mostly in the cecum and right colon of older adults) as a cause of painless lower GI bleeding, and relate it to aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome) and end-stage kidney disease.
Explain necrotizing enterocolitis in premature infants as mucosal ischemia with bacterial invasion, predicting bloody stools, abdominal distension, and pneumatosis intestinalis on radiograph.

Compare esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (upper and middle third; alcohol, tobacco, achalasia, caustic injury, Plummer-Vinson) with adenocarcinoma (distal third; GERD, Barrett esophagus, obesity), and predict progressive dysphagia to solids then liquids with weight loss.

Distinguish intestinal-type gastric adenocarcinoma (H. pylori, nitrosamines, atrophic gastritis, gland formation) from diffuse type (signet ring cells, linitis plastica, CDH1 loss), and identify metastatic signs (Virchow node, Sister Mary Joseph nodule, Krukenberg tumor).

Identify gastric MALT lymphoma as an extranodal marginal zone B cell lymphoma driven by chronic H. pylori infection, and gastrointestinal stromal tumor as a KIT (CD117) mutant tumor of interstitial cells of Cajal, most often gastric.

Explain Zollinger-Ellison syndrome from a gastrin-secreting tumor of the duodenum or pancreas, predicting multiple or distal ulcers, diarrhea, steatorrhea from lipase inactivation by acid, a paradoxical gastrin rise after secretin, and MEN1 association.

Explain why carcinoid tumors of the small intestine cause carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, right-sided valve disease) mainly after liver metastasis, and identify raised urinary 5-HIAA as its marker.

Explain hepatocellular carcinoma risk factors (chronic HBV even without cirrhosis, HCV, alcohol, hemochromatosis, aflatoxin B1 with TP53 mutation) and findings (raised alpha-fetoprotein, hepatomegaly, hematogenous spread).

Identify metastases as the most common malignancy of the liver and peritoneum, and distinguish benign liver lesions: cavernous hemangioma (most common) and hepatocellular adenoma (oral contraceptive or anabolic steroid use, rupture risk).

Distinguish oral leukoplakia (white plaque that does not scrape off, may harbor dysplasia) from candidiasis (scrapes off) and hairy leukoplakia (EBV, lateral tongue, immunosuppression), and identify tobacco and alcohol as oral squamous cell carcinoma risks and HPV-16 as an oropharyngeal carcinoma risk.

Explain pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (KRAS mutation, smoking, chronic pancreatitis), predicting painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) in head tumors, migratory thrombophlebitis, weight loss, and raised CA 19-9.

Compare right-sided colon cancer (occult bleeding, iron deficiency anemia) with left-sided cancer (napkin-ring narrowing, change in bowel habit, obstruction), and identify risks (age, IBD, polyposis and Lynch syndromes) and CEA as a recurrence marker.

Classify colonic polyps as hyperplastic, adenomatous (tubular, tubulovillous, villous, with malignant risk rising with size and villous component), sessile serrated, or hamartomatous (juvenile, Peutz-Jeghers).

Identify pleomorphic adenoma as the most common salivary tumor (usually parotid, mixed epithelial and stromal tissue, recurs if incompletely excised), Warthin tumor (smokers, lymphoid stroma), and mucoepidermoid carcinoma as the most common salivary malignancy.

Describe cholangiocarcinoma (primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis) and gallbladder adenocarcinoma (gallstones), predicting painless obstructive jaundice, and identify anal squamous cell carcinoma below the pectinate line as HPV-related.

Explain pseudomembranous colitis: antibiotic disruption of colonic flora (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins), damage by C. difficile toxins A and B, yellow-white pseudomembranes, watery diarrhea, and toxic megacolon risk, diagnosed by stool toxin or toxin gene testing.

Distinguish causes of bloody enterocolitis (Shigella, Campylobacter, Salmonella, EHEC, Entamoeba histolytica) and predict their complications: hemolytic uremic syndrome after EHEC O157:H7, Guillain-Barre syndrome after Campylobacter, and reactive arthritis.

Distinguish infectious esophagitis in immunocompromised patients: Candida (white pseudomembranes, yeast and pseudohyphae), HSV-1 (punched-out ulcers, intranuclear inclusions), and CMV (linear ulcers, inclusions in endothelial and stromal cells).

Match acute watery gastroenteritis to its setting: rotavirus (unvaccinated infants), norovirus (cruise ship and institutional outbreaks), ETEC (traveler's diarrhea), Vibrio cholerae (contaminated water, rice-water stool), and Bacillus cereus (reheated rice).

Explain how plaque biofilm causes reversible gingivitis that can progress to periodontitis with loss of periodontal ligament and alveolar bone (Porphyromonas gingivalis), and relate acid from Streptococcus mutans to dental caries and tooth abscess.

Describe oral thrush as Candida albicans overgrowth (budding yeast and pseudohyphae, white plaques that scrape off) and predict it in infants, inhaled corticosteroid or antibiotic use, diabetes, and HIV with low CD4 counts.

Distinguish herpetic gingivostomatitis (primary HSV-1, fever with gum and lip vesicles), herpangina (coxsackie A, posterior pharyngeal vesicles), hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackie A16), and aphthous ulcers (Crohn disease, Behcet disease).

Interpret hepatitis B serology to identify acute infection (HBsAg, IgM anti-HBc), the window period (IgM anti-HBc alone), chronic infection (HBsAg over 6 months, IgG anti-HBc), resolved infection, and vaccination (anti-HBs alone).

Predict outcomes of viral hepatitis: chronic HBV in most infected neonates but few adults, chronic HCV in most adults, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma with HBV or HCV, and HCV-related mixed cryoglobulinemia.
Distinguish pyogenic liver abscess (biliary or portal spread, often E. coli or Klebsiella) from amebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica, anchovy paste fluid, travel history).

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Identify erythrocytes, neutrophils, bands, eosinophils, basophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, and platelets on a Wright-stained peripheral smear by cell size, nuclear shape, and granule color.

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Trace hematopoiesis from the hematopoietic stem cell through common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors to each mature blood cell lineage.

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Describe the sequence of hematopoietic sites in development (yolk sac, then liver and spleen, then bone marrow) and relate marrow fibrosis and ineffective erythropoiesis (beta thalassemia major) after birth to extramedullary hematopoiesis and splenomegaly.

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Describe erythroid maturation from proerythroblast through reticulocyte to mature erythrocyte, including nuclear condensation and extrusion, hemoglobin accumulation, and loss of residual ribosomal RNA, and explain what an elevated reticulocyte count indicates about marrow response.

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Describe granulocyte maturation from myeloblast through promyelocyte, myelocyte, metamyelocyte, and band to segmented neutrophil, and identify a left shift on a peripheral smear.

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Describe platelet formation by fragmentation of megakaryocyte cytoplasm and identify platelet granule contents: alpha granules (von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen) and dense granules (ADP, calcium, serotonin).

Unit name: Blood cell histology, origin, and maturation
Competency: Locate B cell and T cell zones in the lymph node (cortical follicles, paracortex, medullary cords and sinuses) and the spleen (white pulp, periarteriolar lymphoid sheath, marginal zone, red pulp cords and sinusoids).
Describe the composition of plasma (water, albumin, globulins, fibrinogen, electrolytes) and distinguish plasma from serum.
Explain the roles of albumin in plasma oncotic pressure and in transport of bilirubin, fatty acids, and calcium, and predict edema from hypoalbuminemia using Starling forces.

Describe red cell features that support gas transport (biconcave shape, no nucleus or mitochondria, carbonic anhydrase converting CO2 to bicarbonate, chloride shift) and explain their functional advantages.
Explain how erythropoietin from renal peritubular interstitial cells responds to tissue hypoxia, and predict erythropoietin levels in chronic kidney disease, high altitude, and polycythemia vera.

Interpret a complete blood count with hemoglobin, hematocrit, MCV, MCHC, RDW, and reticulocyte count to classify an anemia as microcytic, normocytic, or macrocytic and as underproduction or hemolytic.

Explain the functions of neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes, and relate neutrophilia, eosinophilia, and lymphocytosis to bacterial infection, parasitic or allergic disease, and viral infection.
Describe ABO and Rh antigens and naturally occurring IgM anti-A and anti-B antibodies, and predict compatible donors for red cell and plasma transfusion.
Describe the red cell life span of about 120 days and the removal of senescent red cells by macrophages of the spleen and liver.

Trace heme catabolism from heme to biliverdin (heme oxygenase) and unconjugated bilirubin (biliverdin reductase), albumin transport, hepatic conjugation by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, and excretion as urobilinogen, urobilin, and stercobilin.
Distinguish intravascular from extravascular hemolysis using haptoglobin, LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, hemoglobinuria, hemosiderinuria, and smear findings (schistocytes versus spherocytes).
Explain iron recycling and absorption: duodenal uptake of ferrous iron by DMT1, export through ferroportin, transferrin transport, ferritin storage, and hepcidin inhibition of ferroportin.

Relate the short circulating life of neutrophils (hours) and platelets (about 7 to 10 days) compared with red cells to explain why neutropenia and thrombocytopenia appear before anemia after sudden marrow suppression.
Identify the growth factors that drive each lineage: erythropoietin for red cells, G-CSF and GM-CSF for granulocytes, thrombopoietin for megakaryocytes, and IL-5 for eosinophils.

Describe primary hemostasis: vasoconstriction, von Willebrand factor bridging exposed collagen to platelet GpIb, platelet degranulation with ADP and thromboxane A2 release, and fibrinogen linking GpIIb/IIIa receptors during aggregation.

Trace secondary hemostasis through the tissue factor (extrinsic) and contact (intrinsic) pathways to the common pathway, thrombin generation, and fibrin cross-linking by factor XIIIa, and relate PT and PTT to each pathway.

Explain how antithrombin, thrombomodulin with proteins C and S, and tissue factor pathway inhibitor limit clotting, and how plasmin from tPA-activated plasminogen produces fibrin degradation products and D-dimer.
Interpret platelet count, bleeding time, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, and a mixing study to localize a bleeding disorder to platelets, a specific coagulation pathway, a factor inhibitor, or consumption.
Describe Virchow triad (stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability) and relate immobility, surgery, pregnancy, malignancy, and estrogen use to venous thrombosis risk.

Trace heme synthesis from glycine and succinyl-CoA through ALA synthase (rate limiting, pyridoxine dependent), ALA dehydratase, and ferrochelatase, locating mitochondrial and cytosolic steps and explaining heme feedback on ALA synthase.

Distinguish acute intermittent porphyria (porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency, abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms, high urine porphobilinogen) from porphyria cutanea tarda (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency, blistering photosensitivity, hepatitis C association).

Describe the globin chains of hemoglobin A, A2, and F, explain cooperative oxygen binding, and predict shifts of the oxygen dissociation curve with 2,3-BPG, H+, CO2, temperature, fetal hemoglobin, and carbon monoxide.

Explain how ferric iron in methemoglobin and carbon monoxide binding reduce oxygen delivery despite a normal PaO2, and identify congenital (cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency) and acquired (nitrites, dapsone, benzocaine) methemoglobinemia.

Explain why red cells depend on glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, and relate pyruvate kinase deficiency to ATP loss and G6PD deficiency to NADPH and reduced glutathione loss with oxidative hemolysis.

Explain the roles of vitamin B12 and folate in thymidine synthesis, methionine synthase, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and use methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels to distinguish B12 from folate deficiency.

Explain vitamin K dependent gamma-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S, and why these carboxylated residues need calcium to bind phosphatidylserine on activated platelet membranes.

Explain how a glutamate to valine substitution at position 6 of beta globin causes HbS polymerization when deoxygenated, and predict how fetal hemoglobin, dehydration, acidosis, and hypoxia change sickling.

Relate the number of deleted alpha globin genes (one to four) to silent carrier, alpha thalassemia trait, HbH disease, and Hb Barts hydrops fetalis, and contrast beta thalassemia caused by point mutations (often splice site or promoter).

Identify the inheritance of hemophilia A and B and G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive), sickle cell disease and thalassemias (autosomal recessive), and most hereditary spherocytosis and von Willebrand disease (autosomal dominant), and predict offspring risk.

Explain how t(9;22) forms the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene with constitutive tyrosine kinase activity in CML, and how the JAK2 V617F mutation drives growth factor independent proliferation in polycythemia vera.

Relate characteristic translocations to the genes they deregulate: t(8;14) MYC in Burkitt lymphoma, t(14;18) BCL2 (blocked apoptosis) in follicular lymphoma, t(11;14) cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma, and t(15;17) PML-RARA (blocked differentiation) in acute promyelocytic leukemia.
Explain how defective DNA crosslink repair in Fanconi anemia causes congenital marrow failure with short stature, thumb and radial anomalies, and increased risk of AML.
Explain how factor V Leiden (resistance to activated protein C) and the prothrombin G20210A mutation (increased prothrombin levels) raise venous thrombosis risk.

Distinguish warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgG, extravascular, spherocytes; SLE, CLL) from cold agglutinin disease (IgM with complement; Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV), and interpret a positive direct Coombs test.

Classify hematologic immune reactions by hypersensitivity type: acute hemolytic transfusion reaction, autoimmune hemolysis, and hemolytic disease of the newborn (type II), and cryoglobulinemia with immune complex vasculitis (type III).

Distinguish acute hemolytic, delayed hemolytic, febrile nonhemolytic, and anaphylactic (IgA deficiency) transfusion reactions, septic reactions from contaminated units, and TRALI by mechanism, timing, and key findings.

Explain how IgG antibodies against heparin and platelet factor 4 complexes activate platelets in heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, producing a falling platelet count with arterial and venous thrombosis.
Explain how antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2 glycoprotein I) cause arterial and venous thrombosis and pregnancy loss despite prolonging the PTT in vitro.

Explain how Epstein-Barr virus enters B cells through CD21, produces atypical CD8 T cell lymphocytosis in mononucleosis, and contributes to Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and lymphomas in immunosuppressed patients.

Explain why asplenia (surgical or sickle cell autosplenectomy) raises risk of sepsis from encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis) and why vaccination against them is protective.

Trace the Plasmodium life cycle from sporozoite inoculation by the female Anopheles mosquito through liver schizogony, the erythrocytic cycle, and gametocytes, and explain relapse from hypnozoites of P. vivax and P. ovale.

Explain the virulence of Plasmodium falciparum: invasion of red cells of all ages, high parasitemia, PfEMP1-mediated adherence of infected red cells to endothelium causing microvascular obstruction, and immune evasion by switching var genes that encode PfEMP1.
Explain how sickle cell trait, G6PD deficiency, and thalassemia trait reduce severe malaria, and why Duffy antigen negative red cells resist Plasmodium vivax invasion.
Describe Babesia microti transmission by Ixodes scapularis ticks and by transfusion, its intraerythrocytic ring forms and Maltese cross tetrads, and coinfection with Borrelia burgdorferi.

Describe the Schistosoma life cycle: freshwater snail intermediate host, cercarial skin penetration, adult worms in mesenteric (S. mansoni, S. japonicum) or vesical (S. haematobium) venules, and egg deposition.

Explain how parvovirus B19, a nonenveloped single-stranded DNA virus, infects erythroid progenitors through the P antigen, causing transient aplastic crisis in chronic hemolytic anemias and hydrops fetalis in fetal infection.

Identify causes of iron deficiency anemia (chronic gastrointestinal or menstrual blood loss, poor intake or absorption, pregnancy) and predict its profile: low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation, high RDW, and microcytic hypochromic cells.

Distinguish iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease (IL-6 driven hepcidin, high ferritin, low TIBC), thalassemia trait (normal iron studies, target cells), and sideroblastic anemia (high iron, ringed sideroblasts) using iron studies and smear.

Explain how lead inhibition of ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, alcohol, pyridoxine deficiency, and X-linked ALAS2 mutations cause sideroblastic anemia, and identify basophilic stippling and high zinc protoporphyrin in lead poisoning.

Explain how pernicious anemia (antibodies to parietal cells and intrinsic factor), ileal resection, and the fish tapeworm Dibothriocephalus (formerly Diphyllobothrium) latus cause B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord.

Identify causes of folate deficiency (poor intake, alcohol use, pregnancy, chronic hemolysis, methotrexate) and distinguish megaloblastic anemia from nonmegaloblastic macrocytosis due to liver disease, alcohol, and reticulocytosis.

Explain aplastic anemia as stem cell failure from autoimmune T cell injury, drugs, benzene, radiation, viral hepatitis, or Fanconi anemia, and identify pancytopenia with a hypocellular fatty marrow and no splenomegaly.

Distinguish polycythemia vera (JAK2 V617F, low erythropoietin, aquagenic pruritus, splenomegaly) from secondary polycythemia with appropriately high erythropoietin (hypoxia, altitude, smoking) or inappropriately high erythropoietin (renal cell or hepatocellular carcinoma), and from relative polycythemia.

Predict complications of polycythemia vera from hyperviscosity and thrombosis (stroke, Budd-Chiari syndrome, erythromelalgia), high cell turnover (gout), and progression to myelofibrosis or acute myeloid leukemia.
Predict hemoglobin, reticulocyte, and iron changes after acute blood loss (normal hemoglobin at first, fall after fluid shift, reticulocytosis in days) and after chronic blood loss (iron deficiency).

Classify neutropenia by mechanism (marrow failure, drug-induced agranulocytosis such as with propylthiouracil, immune destruction, cyclic neutropenia from ELANE mutation) and relate an absolute neutrophil count below 500/µL to severe bacterial and fungal infection risk.

Distinguish a leukemoid reaction (neutrophilia with left shift, toxic granulation, high leukocyte alkaline phosphatase) from chronic myeloid leukemia (basophilia, low leukocyte alkaline phosphatase, BCR-ABL1).

Predict complications of sickle cell disease from vaso-occlusion and hemolysis: dactylitis, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic autoinfarction, Salmonella osteomyelitis, renal papillary necrosis, priapism, pigment gallstones, and aplastic crisis.

Explain how beta thalassemia major causes ineffective erythropoiesis, extramedullary hematopoiesis (crew-cut skull, maxillary overgrowth), hepatosplenomegaly, and iron overload, and interpret electrophoresis showing high HbA2 in beta thalassemia minor.
Explain how G6PD deficiency causes episodic intravascular hemolysis after oxidant stress (infection, fava beans, sulfonamides, primaquine, dapsone), and identify Heinz bodies and bite cells on smear.

Explain how ankyrin, spectrin, or band 3 defects in hereditary spherocytosis cause membrane loss and splenic trapping, and predict spherocytes, high MCHC, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones, abnormal osmotic fragility or EMA binding, and a negative Coombs test.

Explain how maternal anti-D IgG formed after prior Rh-positive fetal exposure crosses the placenta to cause fetal hemolysis, anemia, and hydrops fetalis, and contrast milder ABO hemolytic disease in infants of group O mothers.

Interpret a positive direct Coombs test in the newborn and indirect Coombs test in the mother, and predict rising unconjugated bilirubin and kernicterus risk after birth when placental clearance ends.

Explain how an acquired PIGA mutation in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria removes GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59, causing complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, venous thrombosis, and cytopenias detected by flow cytometry.

Describe pyruvate kinase deficiency (autosomal recessive, ATP depletion, rigid red cells, extravascular hemolysis) and hereditary elliptocytosis (spectrin defects, elliptocytes, usually mild hemolysis).

Distinguish thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (ADAMTS13 deficiency, ultralarge von Willebrand multimers) from hemolytic uremic syndrome (Shiga toxin of E. coli O157:H7 injuring renal endothelium), noting schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and normal PT and PTT in both.
Explain how prosthetic heart valves and severe aortic stenosis cause mechanical intravascular hemolysis with schistocytes, and predict the iron deficiency that can follow chronic hemoglobinuria.

Identify causes of splenic rupture (blunt trauma, mononucleosis splenomegaly), infarct (sickle cell disease, emboli), and abscess (septic emboli from endocarditis), and predict post-splenectomy smear findings (Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, thrombocytosis).
Explain how hypersplenism from portal hypertension or infiltrative disease causes cytopenias by splenic sequestration, and distinguish it from marrow failure by marrow cellularity and splenomegaly.

Identify triggers of DIC (sepsis, trauma, placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism, acute promyelocytic leukemia, mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma) and predict thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, and schistocytes.

Relate microthrombi in DIC to ischemic injury of kidney, lung, brain, and adrenal glands, and consumption of platelets and clotting factors to simultaneous bleeding from venipuncture sites and mucosa.

Distinguish hemophilia A (factor VIII) from hemophilia B (factor IX) as X-linked deficiencies with hemarthroses and deep muscle bleeds, isolated prolonged PTT, and correction on mixing, unlike an acquired factor VIII inhibitor.

Explain how IgG autoantibodies against platelet GpIIb/IIIa cause splenic platelet destruction in ITP, and contrast acute childhood ITP after viral infection with chronic adult ITP, both showing isolated thrombocytopenia and increased marrow megakaryocytes.

Explain how von Willebrand factor deficiency impairs platelet adhesion and factor VIII stability, and predict mucosal bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, normal or prolonged PTT, and decreased ristocetin cofactor activity.

Identify causes of vitamin K deficiency (newborns not given prophylaxis, fat malabsorption, prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics, poor intake) and explain why the PT prolongs first, since factor VII has the shortest half-life.

Contrast the coagulation profile of liver failure (prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia, normal or high factor VIII) with that of vitamin K deficiency (prolonged PT, normal fibrinogen and platelets).

Distinguish Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb deficiency, large platelets, defective adhesion), Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, defective aggregation), and uremic platelet dysfunction by mechanism and platelet findings.

Explain how inherited antithrombin III, protein C, or protein S deficiency and hyperhomocysteinemia increase venous thrombosis risk, and identify features that suggest an inherited thrombophilia (young age, recurrent or unusual-site clots, family history).

Identify hematologic paraneoplastic syndromes: migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) with pancreatic and other adenocarcinomas, erythrocytosis from ectopic erythropoietin (renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma), and pure red cell aplasia with thymoma.

Describe acute lymphoblastic leukemia as a TdT-positive lymphoblast neoplasm, mainly of children, presenting with marrow failure and bone pain, with CNS and testicular spread and increased risk in Down syndrome.

Describe acute myeloid leukemia (usually at least 20% marrow blasts, myeloperoxidase-positive Auer rods, mainly adults), its risk factors (prior chemotherapy, radiation, benzene, myelodysplasia, Down syndrome), and the link between acute promyelocytic leukemia and DIC.

Describe chronic lymphocytic leukemia as a CD5-positive, CD23-positive mature B cell neoplasm of older adults with smudge cells, hypogammaglobulinemia, warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and Richter transformation to diffuse large B cell lymphoma.

Describe chronic myeloid leukemia (neutrophilia across all maturation stages, basophilia, splenomegaly), its confirmation by detecting t(9;22) BCR-ABL1, and progression from chronic phase to accelerated phase and blast crisis.

Identify hairy cell leukemia by mature B cells with hairlike projections, TRAP and CD11c positivity, BRAF V600E mutation, a dry tap from marrow fibrosis, and massive splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy.

Distinguish Hodgkin lymphoma (CD15 and CD30 positive Reed-Sternberg cells, contiguous nodal spread, bimodal age, EBV association, nodular sclerosis most common) from non-Hodgkin lymphoma (noncontiguous spread, frequent extranodal involvement).

Relate major non-Hodgkin lymphomas to their features: diffuse large B cell (most common, aggressive), follicular (t(14;18), indolent), Burkitt (t(8;14), starry sky, EBV), mantle cell (t(11;14), CD5 positive), and MALT lymphoma (Helicobacter pylori).
Describe T cell lymphomas: adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma (HTLV-1, hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions) and mycosis fungoides (skin-homing CD4 T cells, Pautrier microabscesses, Sezary cells in blood).

Explain how clonal plasma cells in multiple myeloma cause hypercalcemia and punched-out lytic lesions (osteoclast activation through RANKL), renal injury from light chain casts, anemia, rouleaux, infections, and an M spike on electrophoresis.

Distinguish multiple myeloma from MGUS (M protein below 3 g/dL, under 10% marrow plasma cells, no end-organ damage) and from Waldenström macroglobulinemia (IgM, hyperviscosity, no lytic lesions), and relate light chains to AL amyloidosis.

Describe myelodysplastic syndromes as clonal, ineffective hematopoiesis in older adults or after alkylating agents or radiation, with cytopenias, dysplastic cells (pseudo-Pelger-Huet neutrophils, ringed sideroblasts), and risk of progression to AML.

Describe primary myelofibrosis (JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation, megakaryocyte-driven marrow fibrosis, dry tap, teardrop cells, leukoerythroblastic smear) and massive splenomegaly from extramedullary hematopoiesis.

Describe Langerhans cell histiocytosis as a clonal proliferation of CD1a-positive, S100-positive Langerhans cells with Birbeck granules, presenting in children with lytic bone lesions (eosinophilic granuloma) or multisystem disease with diabetes insipidus.

Explain how rapid lysis of high-turnover tumors (Burkitt lymphoma, acute leukemias) during treatment causes tumor lysis syndrome, and predict hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia, and acute kidney injury.

Identify risk factors for severe babesiosis (asplenia, older age, immunosuppression) and predict fever, hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia after a tick bite in the northeastern or upper midwestern United States.

Relate the cyclic fevers of malaria to synchronized rupture of infected red cells (about 48 hours for P. vivax and P. ovale, 72 hours for P. malariae) and predict hemolytic anemia, splenomegaly, and thrombocytopenia.

Predict complications of Plasmodium falciparum malaria (cerebral malaria, severe anemia, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, hemoglobinuria, acute respiratory distress) and identify multiple ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes on a thin smear.

Explain how granulomatous reactions to trapped Schistosoma eggs cause presinusoidal portal hypertension with periportal pipestem fibrosis (S. mansoni) and hematuria, bladder fibrosis, and squamous cell carcinoma (S. haematobium), with eosinophilia.

Compare dengue, chikungunya, and Zika as Aedes-transmitted viruses: severe dengue with thrombocytopenia and plasma leakage after reinfection with another serotype, persistent arthralgia in chikungunya, and congenital microcephaly with Zika.
Describe Ebola and Marburg filoviruses: spread by contact with infected body fluids, fruit bats as the likely reservoir, and fever with vomiting, diarrhea, hemorrhage, DIC, and multiorgan failure.

Describe Yersinia pestis (rodent flea vector, bipolar staining, painful suppurative bubo, septicemic and pneumonic spread) and Bartonella henselae (cat scratch, regional lymphadenopathy with stellate necrotizing granulomas) as causes of lymphadenitis.

Describe acute lymphangitis from Streptococcus pyogenes (red streaks tracking toward regional nodes) and distinguish reactive lymphadenitis patterns (follicular hyperplasia, paracortical hyperplasia, sinus histiocytosis) from lymphoma.
Trace thymic development from third pharyngeal pouch endoderm (shared with the inferior parathyroids), with neural crest derived capsule and septa, and its descent into the anterior mediastinum.
Describe colonization of the thymic epithelial framework by bone marrow derived T cell precursors and the formation of cortex, medulla, and Hassall corpuscles during fetal life.

Relate failed third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development in 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome to absent thymic shadow, T cell deficiency, hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia or aplasia, and conotruncal heart defects.
Describe age-related thymic involution with replacement by adipose tissue, and explain why established peripheral T cell immunity persists after involution or adult thymectomy.

Locate the adult thymus in the anterior and superior mediastinum behind the manubrium, and distinguish thymoma from the other classic anterior mediastinal masses (teratoma, lymphoma, retrosternal thyroid).
Describe lymph node microanatomy: capsule and subcapsular sinus, cortical B cell follicles with germinal centers, paracortical T cells with high endothelial venules, and medullary cords and sinuses.

Predict which lymph node zone is depleted in DiGeorge syndrome (paracortex) and X-linked agammaglobulinemia (follicles and germinal centers), and which expands in reactive follicular versus paracortical hyperplasia.

Describe splenic histology: white pulp (periarteriolar lymphoid sheath of T cells, B cell follicles, marginal zone) and red pulp (cords of Billroth and venous sinusoids), and trace blood flow through them.
Distinguish thymic cortex (densely packed immature thymocytes, epithelial reticular cells, blood thymus barrier) from medulla (mature T cells, Hassall corpuscles) on a histologic section.
Describe mucosa associated lymphoid tissue, including tonsils and ileal Peyer patches with antigen-sampling M cells, and explain its role in generating IgA-secreting plasma cells.

Compare MHC class I (HLA-A, -B, -C; heavy chain with beta2-microglobulin; all nucleated cells; presents to CD8 T cells) with class II (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR; antigen-presenting cells; presents to CD4 T cells).
Trace antigen processing for class I (proteasome, TAP transport, loading in the endoplasmic reticulum) and class II (endosomal degradation, invariant chain, CLIP exchange by HLA-DM).
Describe the HLA locus on chromosome 6, codominant expression, polymorphism, and haplotype inheritance, and calculate the probability (25%) that a sibling is a full HLA match for transplantation.

Relate HLA alleles to disease: B27 (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive and psoriatic arthritis), DQ2 and DQ8 (celiac disease), DR3 and DR4 (type 1 diabetes), DR4 (rheumatoid arthritis), and DR2 (multiple sclerosis, Goodpasture syndrome).
Explain how NK cells kill cells that lose MHC class I expression (missing self), and why virus-infected and tumor cells that downregulate class I become NK targets.
Explain how preformed anti-HLA antibodies from prior transfusion, pregnancy, or transplant cause hyperacute rejection, and why crossmatching and HLA matching improve graft survival.

Trace lymph from the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdomen through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct to the left venous angle, and contrast the right lymphatic duct territory (right head, neck, upper limb, thorax).
Identify the regions drained by the palpable node groups (cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, superficial inguinal) and predict which group enlarges with an infection of a given site.

Predict first nodal spread of tumors: lateral breast to axillary and medial breast to parasternal nodes, testis to para-aortic but scrotum to superficial inguinal nodes, and anal canal above the pectinate line to internal iliac but below it to superficial inguinal nodes.
Relate an enlarged left supraclavicular (Virchow) node to abdominal or thoracic malignancy spreading along the thoracic duct.
Predict chylothorax after thoracic duct injury and describe the milky, triglyceride-rich pleural fluid containing chylomicrons and lymphocytes.

Describe immunoglobulin structure (two heavy and two light chains, Fab with hypervariable antigen-binding regions, Fc determining isotype functions such as complement fixation and Fc receptor binding).

Compare the isotypes: IgM (pentamer, first response, strongest complement activation), IgG (placental transfer, opsonization), secretory IgA (mucosal dimer), IgE (mast cells, helminths), and IgD (naive B cell receptor).

Explain T cell dependent B cell activation, including CD40L to CD40 signaling and cytokines driving isotype switching and affinity maturation in germinal centers, and contrast T independent responses to polysaccharide antigens.

Compare Th1 (IL-12 induced; IFN-gamma activates macrophages), Th2 (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13; IgE and eosinophils), Th17 (IL-17; neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi), and regulatory T cells (FOXP3; IL-10, TGF-beta).
Explain how CD8 cytotoxic T cells and NK cells kill target cells through perforin and granzymes and through Fas ligand binding Fas, both producing apoptosis.
Interpret primary versus secondary antibody response curves (lag phase, IgM then IgG, higher titer and affinity on re-exposure), and distinguish active from passive immunity such as maternal IgG.

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Describe pattern recognition: TLR4 with CD14 binding LPS, TLR5 binding flagellin, endosomal TLR3, 7, 8, and 9 binding nucleic acids, and the NLRP3 inflammasome activating caspase-1 to release IL-1beta in response to DAMPs.

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Trace leukocyte extravasation (selectin rolling, integrin adhesion to ICAM-1 induced by TNF and IL-1, PECAM-1 diapedesis, chemotaxis to C5a, LTB4, IL-8) and relate CD18 deficiency to leukocyte adhesion deficiency.

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Explain the acute phase response: IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha cause fever through hypothalamic PGE2, raise CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A, ferritin, and hepcidin, and lower albumin and transferrin.

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Explain opsonization by IgG and C3b and phagolysosome fusion, and relate LYST mutation in Chediak-Higashi syndrome to giant granules, partial albinism, neuropathy, and recurrent pyogenic infections.

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Describe the foreign body granuloma (macrophages, epithelioid cells, foreign body giant cells around sutures, talc, or splinters) and distinguish it from an immune granuloma driven by Th1 IFN-gamma.

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Explain how LPS signaling through TLR4 drives TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 release in sepsis, causing vasodilation, capillary leak, DIC, and organ dysfunction, and apply SIRS criteria (temperature above 38 °C (100.4 °F) or below 36 °C (96.8 °F), pulse, respirations, WBC).

Unit name: Cell and cytokine signaling in injury and infection
Competency: Explain how superantigens (S aureus TSST-1, S pyogenes pyrogenic exotoxins) bind MHC class II and TCR V-beta outside the peptide groove, causing polyclonal T cell activation and cytokine storm in toxic shock syndrome.

Compare activation of the classical (C1q binding IgM or IgG complexes), lectin (mannose-binding lectin on microbial sugars), and alternative (spontaneous C3 hydrolysis on microbial surfaces) pathways converging on C3 convertase.
Describe complement effector functions: C3b opsonization, C3a and C5a anaphylatoxins, C5a neutrophil chemotaxis, C5b-9 membrane attack complex lysis, and clearance of immune complexes.

Explain regulation by C1 esterase inhibitor, DAF (CD55), and CD59, and predict hereditary angioedema (bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria, low C4) and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PIGA mutation, intravascular hemolysis).

Predict the disease from each deficiency: C1q, C2, or C4 (SLE-like immune complex disease), C3 (severe pyogenic infections, immune complex glomerulonephritis), C5 to C9 (recurrent Neisseria), and MBL (childhood infections).
Interpret serum complement: low C3 and C4 in active SLE, low C3 with normal C4 in poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, and low C4 with normal C3 in hereditary angioedema.

Explain thymic T cell maturation: double negative to double positive thymocytes, positive selection on cortical epithelial MHC, and negative selection in the medulla by AIRE-driven expression of tissue antigens.
Explain splenic functions: removal of aged RBCs and inclusions, clearance of opsonized and encapsulated bacteria by marginal zone B cells and macrophages, IgM production, and platelet storage.

Predict findings after splenectomy or functional asplenia (sickle cell disease): Howell-Jolly bodies, target cells, thrombocytosis, and sepsis from S pneumoniae, H influenzae type b, and N meningitidis.
Explain naive lymphocyte homing into lymph nodes through high endothelial venules (L-selectin, CCR7), meeting antigen carried by dendritic cells in afferent lymph, and exit through efferent lymph.
Predict the effect of high cortisol (stress or Cushing syndrome) on the blood count and lymphoid organs: lymphopenia, eosinopenia, neutrophilia from demargination, and thymic atrophy.
Explain lymph formation from net capillary filtration by Starling forces, with about 2 to 3 L of lymph returned to the blood each day.

Describe lymph composition (interstitial fluid with filtered plasma protein, lymphocytes, and chylomicrons in intestinal chyle) and explain why lymph is the only route returning filtered protein to the blood.

Explain lymph propulsion by intrinsic lymphangion smooth muscle contraction, one-way valves, skeletal muscle pumping, and respiratory pressure changes, and why rising interstitial pressure increases lymph flow.

Predict lymphedema (protein-rich edema that becomes nonpitting with fibrosis) from axillary dissection or radiation, Wuchereria bancrofti filariasis, Milroy disease (FLT4), and Turner syndrome (cystic hygroma).

Trace the respiratory burst (NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway, NADPH oxidase to superoxide, superoxide dismutase to H2O2, myeloperoxidase to HOCl) and relate NADPH oxidase defects to chronic granulomatous disease.

Predict chronic granulomatous disease infections with catalase-positive organisms (S aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia, Nocardia) and interpret an abnormal dihydrorhodamine or nitroblue tetrazolium test.
Explain how adenosine deaminase deficiency causes dATP accumulation that inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and kills lymphocytes, producing autosomal recessive SCID.

Compare arachidonic acid products: COX-derived PGE2 (fever, pain, vasodilation) and thromboxane, and 5-lipoxygenase-derived LTB4 (neutrophil chemotaxis) and LTC4, LTD4, LTE4 (bronchoconstriction, vascular permeability).
Explain how granuloma macrophages in sarcoidosis express 1-alpha-hydroxylase, producing calcitriol and hypercalcemia, and how vitamin D induces macrophage cathelicidin.
Relate zinc deficiency (thymic atrophy, impaired T cell function, acrodermatitis enteropathica) and vitamin A deficiency (mucosal squamous metaplasia, more severe measles) to infection risk.
Explain why protein-energy malnutrition (marasmus, kwashiorkor) is the most common cause of acquired immunodeficiency worldwide, with thymic atrophy and impaired cell-mediated immunity.
Explain chylomicron assembly in enterocytes (triglyceride resynthesis, apoB-48, microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) and their entry into lacteals and thoracic duct lymph, bypassing the liver.
Trace chylomicron breakdown after entering the blood: apoC-II activation of endothelial lipoprotein lipase, fatty acid release to muscle and adipose tissue, and apoE-mediated hepatic remnant uptake.
Predict the findings of abetalipoproteinemia (MTP deficiency): absent chylomicrons and apoB lipoproteins, fat malabsorption, acanthocytes, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.
Explain why hepatic and intestinal lymph carry more protein than lymph from skeletal muscle, relating it to sinusoidal and fenestrated versus continuous capillary endothelium.
Explain V(D)J recombination by RAG1 and RAG2 and junctional diversity from TdT, and predict that RAG deficiency causes SCID with absent T and B cells but preserved NK cells.

Classify SCID genotypes by lymphocyte profile: X-linked IL2RG common gamma chain (T and NK absent, B present), ADA deficiency (all absent), and RAG deficiency, with low T cell receptor excision circles.

Relate X-linked WAS gene mutation in Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome to thrombocytopenia with small platelets, eczema, recurrent infections, low IgM with high IgA and IgE, and calculate risk for sons of carriers.
Explain how X-linked CD40 ligand deficiency blocks isotype switching, producing hyper-IgM syndrome with normal or high IgM, low IgG, IgA, and IgE, and Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium infections.
Relate AIRE mutation to autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency) and FOXP3 mutation to IPEX syndrome.

Explain how Fas-mediated apoptosis ends lymphocyte clonal expansion and removes self-reactive lymphocytes, and predict lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and autoimmune cytopenias in autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome from FAS mutation.

Compare innate immunity (germline pattern recognition receptors, rapid, no memory; neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, complement) with adaptive immunity (rearranged receptors, clonal expansion, memory).
Explain two-signal T cell activation (TCR binding peptide on MHC plus CD28 binding B7), anergy when costimulation is absent, and inhibition through CTLA-4 and PD-1.
Explain antitumor immunity by CD8 T cells recognizing tumor antigens on MHC class I and by NK cells, and tumor escape through loss of MHC class I and PD-L1 expression.

Compare live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, yellow fever; strong cellular and humoral immunity, avoided in immunodeficiency) with inactivated, subunit, toxoid, and protein-conjugated polysaccharide vaccines.

Explain mechanisms of autoimmunity: failed central or peripheral tolerance, HLA susceptibility, and molecular mimicry (group A strep M protein in rheumatic fever, Campylobacter jejuni in Guillain-Barre syndrome).
Compare the four hypersensitivity types by effector (IgE and mast cells; IgG or IgM against cell or matrix antigens; immune complexes; T cells) and time course, and classify a clinical reaction.
Describe parvovirus B19 (small nonenveloped ssDNA virus) tropism for erythroid progenitors through the P antigen, respiratory and transplacental spread, and why infection halts red cell production.

Describe Haemophilus influenzae type b: gram-negative coccobacillus, polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule as the key virulence factor, IgA protease, respiratory spread, and growth requiring factors X and V on chocolate agar.

Describe influenza virus (orthomyxovirus with segmented negative-sense RNA, hemagglutinin binding sialic acid, neuraminidase releasing virions) and distinguish antigenic drift (point mutations) from shift (reassortment causing pandemics).

Describe measles and mumps viruses (enveloped nonsegmented negative-sense RNA paramyxoviruses whose F protein forms syncytia, such as Warthin-Finkeldey cells in measles) and rubella virus (enveloped positive-sense RNA, formerly classed as a togavirus), all spread by respiratory droplets.

Describe the herpesviruses behind mononucleosis and roseola (enveloped dsDNA with lifelong latency): EBV entering B cells through CD21, and HHV-6 and HHV-7 infecting CD4 T cells, all spread by saliva.

Describe Streptococcus pyogenes (catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive gram-positive cocci in chains), M protein as antiphagocytic and mimicry antigen, and pyrogenic exotoxins as superantigens causing scarlet fever.
Trace the Toxoplasma gondii life cycle: sexual stage in the cat (definitive host), oocysts in cat feces, tissue cysts with bradyzoites in undercooked meat, and transplacental tachyzoites.

Explain common variable immunodeficiency (failed B cell differentiation into plasma cells with usually normal B cell counts), its frequent onset in adulthood, low IgG and IgA, sinopulmonary and Giardia infections, and autoimmune and lymphoma risk.

Identify DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion, TBX1) by cardiac defects (truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot), abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia with viral and fungal infections, cleft palate, and hypocalcemic tetany.

Describe selective IgA deficiency, the most common primary immunodeficiency: often asymptomatic, sinopulmonary and Giardia infections, celiac and autoimmune associations, anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products, and falsely negative IgA serologies.

Identify SCID in an infant with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, thrush, Pneumocystis pneumonia, and severe viral infections, with absent thymic shadow, and predict harm from live vaccines and nonirradiated transfusions.

Explain how BTK mutation in X-linked agammaglobulinemia blocks pre-B cell maturation, leaving absent B cells, very low immunoglobulins, scant tonsils, and infections after 6 months with encapsulated bacteria, enteroviruses, and Giardia.

Predict the defective arm from the infection pattern: B cell (encapsulated bacteria, enteroviruses), T cell (viruses, fungi, Pneumocystis), phagocyte (S aureus, Aspergillus), terminal complement (Neisseria), and choose the first test (immunoglobulin levels, flow cytometry, DHR, CH50).

Predict the infections caused by drug-induced immunodeficiency: glucocorticoids and calcineurin inhibitors (T cell suppression, Pneumocystis), TNF-alpha inhibitors (latent tuberculosis reactivation), rituximab (B cell depletion, hepatitis B reactivation), and chemotherapy neutropenia.

Describe HIV structure and entry: retrovirus with gag (p24 capsid), pol (reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease), and env (gp120 binding CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4, gp41 fusion), and why CCR5 delta32 homozygotes resist infection.

Trace the natural history of HIV: transmission routes, acute retroviral syndrome, clinical latency with ongoing lymphoid replication, CD4 decline, and AIDS defined by CD4 below 200 cells per mm3 or an AIDS-defining illness.

Interpret HIV testing: fourth generation antigen and antibody immunoassay followed by HIV-1 and HIV-2 differentiation, CD4 count for staging, viral load for replication, and why infants of infected mothers need nucleic acid testing rather than antibody tests.

Predict opportunistic infections by CD4 count: oral thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia earlier, Pneumocystis pneumonia below 200, Toxoplasma encephalitis below 100, and CMV retinitis and Mycobacterium avium complex below 50.

Relate noninfectious AIDS complications to their causes: Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), primary CNS lymphoma (EBV), HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing FSGS), neurocognitive disorder, peripheral neuropathy, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome.

Explain type I hypersensitivity: Th2 and IL-4 driven IgE sensitization, mast cell FcepsilonRI cross-linking on re-exposure, immediate histamine and tryptase release, and a late phase of leukotrienes and eosinophils.
Identify anaphylaxis from common triggers (foods such as peanut, insect stings, penicillin, latex) by urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension, and interpret an elevated serum tryptase.

Compare warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (IgG, extravascular splenic hemolysis, spherocytes; SLE, CLL) with cold agglutinin disease (IgM fixing complement; Mycoplasma pneumoniae, EBV; acrocyanosis), both with positive direct Coombs test.

Explain Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease; antibodies to the alpha3 chain of type IV collagen) causing hemoptysis and rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG on immunofluorescence.

Explain myasthenia gravis as noncytotoxic type II hypersensitivity (antibodies to the acetylcholine receptor or MuSK), with fatigable ptosis, diplopia, and proximal weakness, and its association with thymic hyperplasia and thymoma.

Explain SLE pathogenesis (impaired clearance of apoptotic nuclear material, immune complexes) and interpret ANA (sensitive), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific), anti-histone (drug-induced), and low C3 and C4 during flares.

Identify SLE manifestations in a young woman (malar rash, photosensitivity, nonerosive arthritis, serositis, cytopenias, lupus nephritis with wire loops, Libman-Sacks endocarditis) and antiphospholipid syndrome thrombosis and pregnancy loss.

Describe polyarteritis nodosa: immune complex medium-vessel vasculitis linked to hepatitis B, ANCA-negative, sparing the lungs, with transmural fibrinoid necrosis at different stages and renal and mesenteric microaneurysms.

Explain poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 1 to 4 weeks after group A strep pharyngitis or skin infection: nephritic syndrome, low C3, elevated ASO or anti-DNase B, subepithelial humps, and granular immunofluorescence.

Describe rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis (HLA-DR4, citrullinated peptide autoimmunity, synovial pannus) and findings: symmetric MCP, PIP, and wrist erosions sparing DIP joints, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, nodules, and Felty syndrome.

Explain type IV granulomatous inflammation (Th1 IFN-gamma activating macrophages, TNF maintaining granulomas), distinguishing caseating tuberculosis granulomas from noncaseating ones, and interpret a tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours.

Identify sarcoidosis by noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, elevated ACE, hypercalcemia, uveitis, and erythema nodosum, and recognize Lofgren syndrome (erythema nodosum, hilar adenopathy, arthritis).

Compare hyperacute (preformed antibody, minutes), acute (T cell or antibody mediated, weeks to months), and chronic (graft arteriosclerosis, bronchiolitis obliterans, months to years) rejection, and distinguish graft-versus-host disease (skin, liver, gut).

Explain serum sickness (fever, urticaria, arthralgia, proteinuria, low complement about 1 to 2 weeks after foreign protein exposure) and the local Arthus reaction as systemic and local type III reactions.

Classify drug hypersensitivity examples by mechanism: penicillin anaphylaxis (type I), penicillin or methyldopa hemolytic anemia (type II), serum sickness from chimeric antibodies (type III), and contact dermatitis from topical neomycin (type IV).

Explain systemic sclerosis pathogenesis (endothelial injury, autoimmunity, TGF-beta driven fibroblast collagen deposition) causing skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, and interstitial lung disease.

Distinguish diffuse systemic sclerosis (anti-Scl-70, early visceral disease, scleroderma renal crisis) from limited CREST disease (anticentromere; calcinosis, Raynaud, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia; pulmonary hypertension).

Explain acute rheumatic fever as type II hypersensitivity from M protein mimicry of cardiac proteins 2 to 4 weeks after untreated group A strep pharyngitis, with Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells in pancarditis.
Apply the Jones major criteria (migratory polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea) with evidence of strep infection, and predict chronic mitral stenosis.

Explain Sjogren syndrome (lymphocytic destruction of salivary and lacrimal glands) causing dry mouth and keratoconjunctivitis sicca, with anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB), RA association, and marginal zone lymphoma risk.
Predict congenital heart block and neonatal lupus in infants of mothers with anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies from Sjogren syndrome or SLE, through transplacental IgG.
Identify mixed connective tissue disease by overlapping features of SLE, systemic sclerosis, and polymyositis with high-titer anti-U1 RNP antibodies.

Describe amyloid as misfolded proteins in beta-pleated sheets deposited extracellularly, showing apple-green birefringence with Congo red under polarized light, and diagnosed by abdominal fat pad or organ biopsy.

Explain primary (AL) amyloidosis from monoclonal plasma cell light chains (a plasma cell dyscrasia, sometimes with multiple myeloma) and predict restrictive cardiomyopathy, nephrotic syndrome, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, and carpal tunnel neuropathy.

Explain secondary (AA) amyloidosis from serum amyloid A in chronic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic infections, familial Mediterranean fever) and predict renal involvement with nephrotic syndrome.

Match other amyloid proteins to their settings: beta2-microglobulin (long-term dialysis), transthyretin (wild-type age-related cardiac and hereditary), A-beta (Alzheimer disease), calcitonin (medullary thyroid carcinoma), and amylin (type 2 diabetes islets).

Identify erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek then lacy reticular rash in children, arthropathy in adults) and predict parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis in hemolytic anemias and hydrops fetalis in pregnancy.

Identify invasive Haemophilus influenzae type b disease in unvaccinated young children (epiglottitis with drooling and stridor, meningitis, bacteremia, pneumonia), and contrast nontypeable strains causing otitis media and sinusitis.

Identify influenza by abrupt fever, myalgia, headache, and cough, and predict complications: primary viral pneumonia, secondary bacterial pneumonia (S aureus, S pneumoniae), and Reye syndrome with aspirin use in children.

Identify measles by cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a rash spreading from the head downward, and predict pneumonia, encephalitis, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, and worse outcomes with vitamin A deficiency.

Identify infectious mononucleosis in an adolescent (fever, pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly) by atypical CD8 T lymphocytes and heterophile antibodies, and predict rash after amoxicillin.

Predict complications of EBV infection: splenic rupture, hepatitis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and associated malignancies (Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, lymphoma in immunosuppression).
Identify mumps by parotitis, and predict orchitis in postpubertal males, aseptic meningitis, and pancreatitis, with elevated serum amylase.
Identify roseola infantum (HHV-6, less often HHV-7) in a child under 2 years: several days of high fever, then a truncal rash as the fever breaks, with risk of febrile seizures.

Identify rubella (enveloped positive-sense RNA virus) by mild face-to-trunk rash, postauricular lymphadenopathy, and adult arthralgia, and predict congenital rubella (cataracts, sensorineural deafness, PDA, blueberry muffin rash) after first trimester infection.
