Identify scarlet fever after strep pharyngitis (sandpaper rash, circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, Pastia lines, later desquamation) and predict rheumatic fever and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Predict toxoplasmosis presentations: mono-like lymphadenopathy in healthy hosts, congenital chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications, and multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS with CD4 below 100.
Distinguish the childhood exanthems by rash pattern and timing relative to fever: measles, rubella, erythema infectiosum, roseola, and scarlet fever.

Identify CMV infection: heterophile-negative mononucleosis, owl's eye inclusions, congenital infection with periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, and retinitis, colitis, or pneumonitis in transplant and AIDS patients.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Identify the epidermal layers from stratum basale to stratum corneum and describe how keratinocytes change in each (keratins 5 and 14 to 1 and 10, keratohyalin granules, lamellar bodies, loss of nuclei), noting that stratum lucidum appears only in thick skin.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Identify melanocytes (neural crest origin, melanin transfer to keratinocytes), Langerhans cells (bone marrow origin, Birbeck granules, CD1a, antigen presentation), and Merkel cells (basal layer touch receptors) by epidermal location and function.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Compare desmosomes (desmogleins), hemidesmosomes (BP180 or collagen XVII, BP230, integrin alpha6 beta4), and adherens junctions (E-cadherin), and predict the blistering disease that results when desmosomal or hemidesmosomal proteins are targeted by autoantibodies or mutation.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Describe the dermal-epidermal junction (lamina lucida with laminin 332 and collagen XVII anchoring filaments, lamina densa with type IV collagen, type VII collagen anchoring fibrils) and predict the level of the split when each component fails.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Compare the papillary dermis, reticular dermis, and hypodermis by connective tissue density, vessels, and sensory receptors (Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae, Pacinian corpuscles in deep dermis and subcutis, free nerve endings).

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Distinguish eccrine, apocrine, and sebaceous glands by location, secretion, and control (eccrine glands by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, apocrine glands opening into axillary and anogenital hair follicles, sebaceous glands holocrine and androgen driven), and relate hyperhidrosis to eccrine glands and acne to sebaceous glands.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Describe the hair follicle (bulb, dermal papilla, bulge stem cells, arrector pili) and nail unit (matrix, plate, bed, folds), and relate anagen, catagen, and telogen to telogen effluvium and the lateral nail fold to an ingrown nail.

Unit name: Skin layers and the dermal-epidermal junction
Competency: Define acanthosis, hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, spongiosis, acantholysis, and dyskeratosis, and match each to an example disease such as psoriasis, eczema, or pemphigus.

Distinguish derivatives of surface ectoderm (epidermis, hair, nails, cutaneous and mammary glands, lens, anterior pituitary, tooth enamel) from those of neuroectoderm (central nervous system, retina, posterior pituitary) and neural crest.

Identify neural crest derivatives relevant to skin and nerves (melanocytes, Schwann cells, dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, adrenal medulla, odontoblasts), and explain why facial dermis arises from neural crest while dermis of the back arises from somite dermatomes.

Describe fetal skin development, including the periderm, epidermal stratification, melanoblast migration from the neural crest, hair bud and dermal papilla formation, lanugo, and vernix caseosa as a protective coat of sebum and shed cells.

Explain why melanocytes arrested in the dermis during migration produce dermal melanocytosis (Mongolian spots), and distinguish it from congenital melanocytic nevi, infantile hemangiomas, and port-wine stains in newborns.
Explain why failed melanoblast migration in piebaldism produces congenital white patches lacking melanocytes, whereas albinism shows normal melanocyte numbers with reduced melanin synthesis.

Describe the plasma membrane components (phospholipid bilayer, cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins, glycocalyx) and explain how cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity and how unsaturated fatty acids increase it.

Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, primary active transport, secondary active transport, and endocytosis by energy source, saturability, and direction, using the Na+/K+-ATPase, GLUT transporters, and SGLT1 as examples.
Predict how inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) changes intracellular sodium, cell volume, and membrane potential, and relate this to cellular swelling in hypoxic cell injury.
Explain osmosis, distinguish osmolarity from tonicity, and predict cell volume in isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic solutions, including why urea is an ineffective osmole.

Calculate an ion's equilibrium potential with the Nernst equation, and explain how potassium leak channels, the Goldman equation, and the Gibbs-Donnan effect of impermeant intracellular anions establish the resting membrane potential.

Predict how hyperkalemia depolarizes and hypokalemia hyperpolarizes the resting membrane potential, and explain why sustained depolarization inactivates voltage-gated sodium channels and lowers nerve and muscle excitability.
Explain how CFTR mutation blocks chloride reabsorption in the eccrine sweat duct, raising sweat chloride to 60 mmol/L or higher, while it blocks chloride secretion in airway epithelium.

Explain how the hypothalamus integrates core and skin thermoreceptor input around a set point, with the anterior (preoptic) hypothalamus driving heat loss and the posterior hypothalamus driving heat conservation and production.

Compare heat loss by radiation, conduction, convection, and evaporation, and predict why sweat evaporation becomes the only route when ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature and why high humidity impairs cooling.

Explain heat conservation and production by cutaneous vasoconstriction, piloerection, shivering, thyroid hormone, and nonshivering thermogenesis through UCP1 (thermogenin) in brown fat, and why neonates depend on brown fat.
Explain how IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha induce hypothalamic PGE2 to raise the set point in fever, and distinguish fever from hyperthermia, in which the set point is unchanged.

Distinguish heat exhaustion from heat stroke (core temperature above 40 °C (104 °F) with central nervous system dysfunction), compare classic and exertional heat stroke, and predict rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and DIC.

Explain how an RYR1 mutation causes malignant hyperthermia after volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine through uncontrolled sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release, producing muscle rigidity, hypercarbia, and rising core temperature.

Describe hypothermia (core below 35 °C (95 °F)), including loss of shivering when severe, bradycardia, Osborn (J) waves, and arrhythmias, and distinguish frostbite (ice crystals, endothelial injury, thrombosis) from perniosis (nonfreezing damp cold).

Trace collagen synthesis (prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation needing vitamin C and Fe2+, glycosylation, triple helix formation, procollagen peptidase cleavage, lysyl oxidase cross-linking needing copper) and predict the connective tissue defect when each step fails.

Relate vitamin C deficiency to scurvy findings (perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor wound healing) and defective copper transport in Menkes disease to brittle kinky hair and connective tissue weakness.
Explain the photosensitive dermatitis of niacin deficiency (pellagra) and its causes, including corn-based diets, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome, and isoniazid-induced vitamin B6 deficiency.

Distinguish skin findings of deficiency of vitamin A (follicular hyperkeratosis, xerosis), zinc (acrodermatitis enteropathica with periorificial and acral dermatitis, alopecia, poor healing), biotin (dermatitis, alopecia), riboflavin (angular cheilitis), and essential fatty acids (scaly dermatitis).

Trace vitamin D synthesis from 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis by UVB to cholecalciferol, then 25-hydroxylation in the liver and 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the kidney, and predict how dark skin, high latitude, and sunscreen reduce it.

Describe the stratum corneum lipid barrier (ceramides, cholesterol, free fatty acids from lamellar bodies), sebum composition (triglycerides, wax esters, squalene), and dermal glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid and dermatan sulfate.

Relate xanthoma type to lipid disorder: eruptive xanthomas with severe hypertriglyceridemia (lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency), tendon xanthomas and xanthelasma with familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor), and palmar xanthomas with dysbetalipoproteinemia (apoE2).

Explain how uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency in porphyria cutanea tarda causes blistering, fragility, and hypertrichosis on sun-exposed skin, and identify triggers such as alcohol, hepatitis C, iron overload, and estrogen.

Describe how superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radical form (mitochondrial electron leak, NADPH oxidase, UV and ionizing radiation, Fenton reaction with Fe2+) and how they damage membrane lipids, proteins, and DNA.

Explain how superoxide dismutase (Cu/Zn cytosolic, Mn mitochondrial), catalase, and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase detoxify reactive oxygen species, and why glutathione regeneration needs NADPH from G6PD in the pentose phosphate pathway.

Explain how non-vitamin antioxidants protect skin, including reduced glutathione, ubiquinol (coenzyme Q10), dietary carotenoids such as lycopene, and melanin, and why eumelanin is more photoprotective than pheomelanin.

Compare UVB injury (direct DNA damage forming cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, sunburn) with UVA injury (deeper penetration, oxidative DNA damage), and explain photoaging through matrix metalloproteinase breakdown of collagen and solar elastosis.

Explain how the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst and myeloperoxidase kill microbes, and predict recurrent skin abscesses and granulomas with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus in chronic granulomatous disease.
Explain how cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases, Rb, and p53 control the G1 to S checkpoint, and how UV-signature C to T mutations in TP53 drive actinic keratosis and squamous cell carcinoma.

Explain how defective nucleotide excision repair in xeroderma pigmentosum (autosomal recessive) causes extreme photosensitivity, early freckling, and basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma in childhood.

Relate driver mutations to skin tumors: PTCH1 loss activating hedgehog signaling in basal cell carcinoma and Gorlin syndrome, BRAF V600E or NRAS in nevi and melanoma, and germline CDKN2A (p16) in familial melanoma.

Interpret pedigrees of skin disorders with autosomal dominant (NF1, tuberous sclerosis, epidermolysis bullosa simplex), autosomal recessive (oculocutaneous albinism, xeroderma pigmentosum), and X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis) inheritance, and calculate recurrence risk for offspring.

Explain the gene products in NF1 (neurofibromin, a Ras GTPase-activating protein on chromosome 17) and tuberous sclerosis (hamartin and tuberin, which inhibit mTOR), and identify café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, ash-leaf macules, and facial angiofibromas.

Explain how loss-of-function filaggrin (FLG) mutations impair the epidermal barrier in ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis, and how steroid sulfatase deficiency causes X-linked ichthyosis in males.

Explain how MSH binding the MC1R receptor raises cAMP and MITF-driven tyrosinase expression to favor eumelanin, and why MC1R loss-of-function variants cause red hair, fair skin, and higher melanoma risk.

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Distinguish hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, and metaplasia by mechanism and example (epidermal hyperplasia in a callus, squamous metaplasia of bronchi in smokers, columnar metaplasia in Barrett esophagus), and explain how metaplasia and pathologic hyperplasia can progress to dysplasia.

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Explain how ATP depletion, mitochondrial damage, calcium influx, oxidative stress, and membrane damage injure cells, and distinguish reversible changes (swelling, fatty change, blebbing, ribosome detachment) from irreversible ones (membrane rupture, mitochondrial densities, pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis).

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Classify necrosis as coagulative, liquefactive, caseous, fat, fibrinoid, or gangrenous, and predict the type from its setting (myocardial infarct, brain infarct or abscess, tuberculosis, acute pancreatitis, vasculitis, limb ischemia).

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Compare intrinsic (BCL-2 family, cytochrome c, caspase-9) and extrinsic (Fas ligand, TNF, caspase-8) apoptosis and perforin-granzyme killing by cytotoxic T cells, and distinguish apoptosis (shrinkage, apoptotic bodies, no inflammation) from necrosis.

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Distinguish endogenous pigments (lipofuscin from lipid peroxidation, hemosiderin staining with Prussian blue, melanin, bilirubin) from exogenous pigments (inhaled carbon in anthracosis, tattoo ink held in dermal macrophages), and relate each to its source.

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Distinguish dystrophic calcification (necrotic tissue, normal serum calcium) from metastatic calcification (hypercalcemia, normal tissues), and identify infiltrates of fat (steatosis), cholesterol (foam cells, xanthomas), and amyloid (Congo red with apple-green birefringence).

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Distinguish benign from malignant neoplasms by differentiation, anaplasia (pleomorphism, high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, atypical mitoses), invasion, and metastasis, apply tumor naming rules, and distinguish dysplasia, carcinoma in situ, grade, and stage.

Unit name: Cell adaptation, injury, pigmentation, and neoplasia
Competency: Explain the hallmarks of cancer, including oncogene growth signaling (BRAF in melanoma), two-hit loss of tumor suppressors (RB, TP53), evasion of apoptosis, telomerase activity, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, invasion, Warburg metabolism, and immune evasion.

Identify normal skin flora (Staphylococcus epidermidis, Cutibacterium acnes, Corynebacterium, Malassezia, nasal Staphylococcus aureus carriage) and explain how flora, acidic pH, sebum fatty acids, desquamation, and antimicrobial peptides resist pathogen colonization.

Trace the stages of a skin infection (entry through a breach, adherence, colonization, invasion, spread, tissue damage) and relate the depth reached to impetigo, folliculitis, erysipelas, cellulitis, abscess, and necrotizing fasciitis.

Distinguish skin disease from direct invasion versus toxins, explaining how exfoliative toxins cleave desmoglein 1 in staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and how superantigens (TSST-1, streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins) cause diffuse rash and shock.

Explain how diabetes, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, tinea pedis fissures, injection drug use, neutropenia, and T cell deficiency predispose to skin infection, and predict the likely organism from the host context.

Sequence wound healing: hemostasis, inflammation (neutrophils, then macrophages by day 3), proliferation (granulation tissue, VEGF-driven angiogenesis, type III collagen), and remodeling (type I collagen, zinc-dependent metalloproteinases), noting scars regain only about 70 to 80 percent of normal strength.

Compare healing by primary and secondary intention (more granulation tissue, myofibroblast contraction), and explain how infection, diabetes, ischemia, glucocorticoids, malnutrition, vitamin C or zinc deficiency, and foreign bodies delay healing.

Distinguish hypertrophic scars (parallel type III collagen, confined to the wound, may regress) from keloids (disorganized type I and III collagen beyond wound borders, earlobes, darker skin), and identify exuberant granulation tissue, dehiscence, and contracture.

Classify burns as superficial, superficial partial-thickness, deep partial-thickness, or full-thickness by blisters, blanching, and sensation, estimate burned area by the rule of nines, and predict hypovolemia, Pseudomonas sepsis, hypermetabolism, inhalation injury, and contracture.

Explain why electrical injury causes small entry and exit skin wounds with extensive deep muscle and nerve necrosis, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuric kidney injury, and arrhythmias, and identify Lichtenberg figures and cardiac arrest after lightning strike.

Explain how ionizing radiation damages DNA directly and through free radicals, and distinguish acute radiation dermatitis (erythema, desquamation) from chronic changes (atrophy, telangiectasia, fibrosis, obliterative endarteritis) and later skin cancers or angiosarcoma.

Explain how sustained pressure and shear over bony prominences cause ischemic decubitus ulcers, stage them from nonblanching erythema to exposed bone, and explain how an auricular hematoma separating perichondrium from cartilage leads to cauliflower ear.
Explain how brown recluse spider venom (sphingomyelinase D) causes dermonecrosis with a central necrotic ulcer and, rarely, systemic hemolysis.

Explain how keratinocytes (Toll-like receptors, IL-1, TNF, defensins, cathelicidin), mast cells, and Langerhans cells provide innate defense, and trace Langerhans cell antigen capture and migration to regional lymph nodes to prime naive T cells.

Trace acute inflammation from vasodilation and venular leak (histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins) through rolling (selectins), firm adhesion (integrins binding ICAM-1), transmigration (PECAM-1), and chemotaxis (C5a, LTB4, IL-8), and predict findings in leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1.

Explain how acute inflammation resolves, forms an abscess, or becomes chronic, and how Th1 cells and IFN-gamma activate macrophages to form granulomas, distinguishing caseating (tuberculosis) from noncaseating (sarcoidosis) granulomas.

Classify skin reactions by hypersensitivity type: type I (urticaria, angioedema), type II (pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid), type III (Arthus reaction, leukocytoclastic vasculitis), and type IV (allergic contact dermatitis, tuberculin test), and predict the timing and mediators of each.

Relate autoimmune skin findings to disease: malar and discoid lesions with interface dermatitis and junctional immune deposits in lupus, Gottron papules and heliotrope rash in dermatomyositis, and sclerodactyly with anticentromere or anti-Scl-70 antibodies in systemic sclerosis.

Explain how CD8 T cells and NK cells eliminate tumor cells, how tumors escape by losing MHC class I or expressing PD-L1, and why organ transplant recipients develop many cutaneous squamous cell carcinomas.

Explain how the recombinant HPV L1 virus-like particle vaccine induces neutralizing antibody, how live attenuated varicella vaccine induces both antibody and cell-mediated immunity, and why an Arthus (type III) local reaction can follow a toxoid booster.

Identify Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive) and explain its virulence factors (protein A, Panton-Valentine leukocidin, exfoliative toxins, TSST-1) and how mecA-encoded PBP2a makes MRSA resistant to beta-lactams.

Identify Streptococcus pyogenes (beta-hemolytic, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive), explain M protein, hyaluronic acid capsule, streptolysin O, streptokinase, and pyrogenic exotoxins, and explain why skin infection can cause glomerulonephritis but not rheumatic fever.

Explain how dermatophytes (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) use keratinases to live in stratum corneum, hair, and nails, identify septate hyphae on KOH prep, and contrast Malassezia (spaghetti and meatballs, hypopigmented or hyperpigmented tinea versicolor).

Identify Candida albicans as a dimorphic commensal forming budding yeast and pseudohyphae (germ tube positive), and explain how moisture, diabetes, antibiotics, glucocorticoids, and T cell or neutrophil defects allow mucocutaneous or invasive disease.

Compare human papillomavirus (nonenveloped circular dsDNA, infects basal keratinocytes, koilocytes, E6 degrading p53 and E7 inactivating Rb in high-risk types) with molluscum contagiosum poxvirus (enveloped dsDNA replicating in cytoplasm, molluscum bodies) in structure, replication, and transmission.

Explain how HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella zoster virus (enveloped dsDNA) infect epithelium, establish latency in sensory ganglia, and reactivate as herpes labialis, genital herpes, or dermatomal zoster, and identify multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear.

Explain how Cutibacterium acnes (gram-positive anaerobic rod) lipases release free fatty acids and activate TLR2 in acne, and how Pseudomonas aeruginosa (gram-negative, oxidase positive) causes hot tub folliculitis.

Identify vectors of skin-presenting infections: Ixodes ticks (Borrelia burgdorferi, erythema migrans), Dermacentor ticks (Rickettsia rickettsii, rash starting at wrists and ankles and spreading to the trunk, palms, and soles), sandflies (Leishmania), and dog and cat hookworm larvae in sand or soil (cutaneous larva migrans).

Explain how activating BRAF or NRAS mutations followed by oncogene-induced senescence produce nevocellular nevi, and classify junctional, compound, and intradermal nevi by nest location, relating this to patient age and to maturation of cells with depth.
Distinguish a benign nevus (small, symmetric, uniform color, stable) from melanoma using ABCDE criteria, and identify large congenital melanocytic nevi as carrying increased melanoma risk.

Explain vitiligo as CD8 T cell destruction of melanocytes, identify sharply demarcated depigmented macules accentuated by Wood lamp, Koebner phenomenon, and absent melanocytes on biopsy, and relate it to autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes.

Distinguish vitiligo (melanocytes absent) from albinism (melanocytes present, melanin reduced), tinea versicolor, and postinflammatory hypopigmentation using distribution, Wood lamp, and KOH findings.

Distinguish ephelides (normal melanocyte number with more melanin, darken in sun) from lentigo simplex and solar lentigines (increased basal melanocytes) and from melasma linked to pregnancy and estrogen.
Explain how high ACTH in primary adrenal insufficiency causes diffuse hyperpigmentation through POMC-derived MSH acting on melanocortin receptors, and why secondary adrenal insufficiency does not.

Explain atopic dermatitis as filaggrin-related barrier failure plus Th2 inflammation (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31 itch), and identify infant facial and extensor versus older flexural distribution, lichenification, the atopic triad, and Staphylococcus aureus and eczema herpeticum complications.

Distinguish allergic contact dermatitis (type IV, hapten sensitization via Langerhans cells, nickel or urushiol from poison ivy and oak, eruption 48 to 72 hours after re-exposure, positive patch test) from irritant contact dermatitis (direct damage, no sensitization).
Predict the distribution of contact dermatitis from the exposure (earlobes or wrist from nickel, linear vesicles from plants, hands from wet work) and identify spongiosis as its histologic hallmark.

Explain erythema multiforme as a cytotoxic T cell reaction most often triggered by HSV (also Mycoplasma pneumoniae), and identify acral target lesions with dusky centers, limited mucosal involvement, and interface dermatitis with keratinocyte necrosis.

Explain urticaria as mast cell degranulation (IgE-mediated, physical, or direct) causing superficial dermal edema with wheals lasting under 24 hours, and distinguish angioedema, chronic urticaria (over 6 weeks), and bradykinin-mediated C1 inhibitor deficiency without hives.

Distinguish Stevens-Johnson syndrome (under 10 percent body surface) from toxic epidermal necrolysis (over 30 percent) by extent of full-thickness epidermal necrosis, and identify mucosal involvement, positive Nikolsky sign, and drug triggers (sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol).
Identify pityriasis rosea by a herald patch followed by oval scaly patches along skin cleavage lines in a Christmas tree pattern on the trunk, resolving on its own within weeks.

Explain seborrheic dermatitis as an inflammatory response to Malassezia in sebaceous areas (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds), identify greasy yellow scale and infant cradle cap, and relate severe disease to HIV and Parkinson disease.

Identify recurrent aphthous ulcers as painful shallow ulcers with a yellow-gray base and red halo on nonkeratinized oral mucosa, and relate them to Behçet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and celiac disease.

Identify rosacea by central facial flushing, persistent erythema, telangiectasias, and papules and pustules without comedones, identify triggers (heat, sunlight, alcohol, spicy food), and predict rhinophyma and ocular rosacea as complications.
Distinguish rosacea from acne vulgaris (comedones, adolescents), seborrheic dermatitis (greasy scale), and the malar rash of lupus, which spares the nasolabial folds.

Identify lichen planus by pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules with Wickham striae and reticular oral lesions, explain its band-like T cell infiltrate with sawtooth rete ridges and Civatte bodies, and relate it to hepatitis C.

Explain psoriasis as IL-23 and Th17 (IL-17) driven keratinocyte hyperproliferation with TNF and HLA-Cw6 risk, and identify silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces and scalp, Koebner phenomenon, nail pitting, and psoriatic arthritis.

Interpret psoriasis histology (acanthosis with regularly elongated rete ridges, parakeratosis, reduced stratum granulosum, thinned suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries, Munro microabscesses) and relate the thin suprapapillary plates to the Auspitz sign.

Identify pyoderma gangrenosum as a neutrophilic dermatosis forming painful ulcers with violaceous undermined borders that worsen after trauma (pathergy), and relate it to inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, and hematologic malignancy.

Explain hidradenitis suppurativa as chronic follicular occlusion in axillary, inguinal, and perineal skin that produces painful nodules, abscesses, sinus tracts, and scarring, and identify obesity and smoking as risk factors.

Distinguish nonscarring alopecias (alopecia areata from autoimmune attack on anagen follicles with exclamation point hairs, androgenetic alopecia from DHT-driven follicle miniaturization, telogen effluvium) from scarring alopecias that destroy follicles.

Compare the main types of epidermolysis bullosa by defective protein and split level: simplex (keratins 5 and 14, basal keratinocytes), junctional (laminin 332 or collagen XVII, lamina lucida), and dystrophic (type VII collagen, below the lamina densa).

Predict the clinical course of epidermolysis bullosa, including blisters from minor friction beginning at birth, mucosal and nail involvement, and, in recessive dystrophic disease, scarring, fused digits, and aggressive squamous cell carcinoma.

Explain bullous pemphigoid as IgG against hemidesmosomal BP180 and BP230 with complement and eosinophils, and identify tense subepidermal bullae in older adults, infrequent oral lesions, negative Nikolsky sign, and linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane.

Explain pemphigus vulgaris as IgG against desmoglein 3 (often also 1) causing suprabasal acantholysis with a tombstone basal layer, and identify flaccid bullae, early painful oral erosions, positive Nikolsky sign, and net-like intercellular IgG on immunofluorescence.

Distinguish pemphigus vulgaris, pemphigus foliaceus (desmoglein 1, subcorneal split, no mucosal lesions), and bullous pemphigoid by target antigen, split level, Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement, and immunofluorescence pattern.

Explain dermatitis herpetiformis as IgA against epidermal transglutaminase linked to celiac disease, and identify grouped pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces, neutrophilic microabscesses at dermal papillary tips, and granular IgA deposits.

Explain oculocutaneous albinism as autosomal recessive loss of tyrosinase or other melanosome proteins with normal melanocyte numbers, and predict photosensitivity, skin cancer risk, and visual problems such as nystagmus and reduced acuity.
Distinguish oculocutaneous albinism from X-linked ocular albinism and from the partial albinism of Chediak-Higashi syndrome (LYST defect, giant granules, recurrent pyogenic infections, neuropathy).

Explain how defects in collagen synthesis or processing cause Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, linking the classic type to type V collagen (COL5A1), the vascular type to type III collagen (COL3A1), and the kyphoscoliotic type to lysyl hydroxylase.

Identify skin features of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hyperextensible, soft, fragile skin, easy bruising, wide atrophic cigarette-paper scars) with joint hypermobility, and predict arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture and berry aneurysms in the vascular type.

Distinguish Ehlers-Danlos syndrome from Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1, tall stature, lens subluxation, aortic root dilation) and osteogenesis imperfecta (type I collagen, fractures, blue sclerae) by defective protein and findings.

Explain actinic keratosis as UV-induced keratinocyte dysplasia, identify rough sandpaper-like scaly papules on sun-exposed skin of older fair-skinned adults, lower epidermal atypia with parakeratosis and solar elastosis, and predict progression of some lesions to squamous cell carcinoma.

Identify dysplastic nevi as larger than common nevi with irregular borders and variable pigment, with cytologic and architectural atypia on biopsy, and explain why multiple dysplastic nevi and familial CDKN2A mutation mark high melanoma risk.

Identify seborrheic keratosis as a benign epidermal proliferation of older adults with a stuck-on waxy appearance, basaloid cells, horn cysts, and FGFR3 activating mutations, and interpret sudden eruption of many lesions as the Leser-Trélat sign.

Relate mucocutaneous paraneoplastic signs to cancers: acanthosis nigricans and Leser-Trélat sign with gastric adenocarcinoma, dermatomyositis with ovarian, lung, and GI cancers, and paraneoplastic pemphigus with lymphoma, noting acanthosis nigricans more often reflects insulin resistance.

Distinguish an epidermal inclusion cyst (stratified squamous lining with granular layer, laminated keratin, foreign body reaction on rupture) from a trichilemmal (pilar) cyst of the scalp, and identify lipoma as a soft, mobile, benign adipocyte tumor.

Distinguish infantile hemangioma (appears in the first weeks, proliferates, then involutes), cherry hemangioma of older adults, pyogenic granuloma (rapid, friable, bleeds, often in pregnancy), and port-wine stain (persistent capillary malformation, Sturge-Weber association).

Distinguish oral leukoplakia (white plaque that cannot be scraped off, linked to tobacco and alcohol, may show dysplasia and progress to squamous cell carcinoma) from oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV, lateral tongue, HIV) and thrush (scrapes off).

Explain basal cell carcinoma as the most common skin cancer, driven by UV and hedgehog activation, identify pearly papules with telangiectasias, rolled borders, or ulceration and basaloid nests with peripheral palisading, and predict local invasion with rare metastasis.

Identify risk factors for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cumulative UV, actinic keratosis, transplant immunosuppression, arsenic, HPV, xeroderma pigmentosum, chronic scars or ulcers giving Marjolin ulcer) and explain why it favors the lower lip and sun-exposed skin.

Identify squamous cell carcinoma as a scaly, crusted, or ulcerated nodule with keratin pearls and intercellular bridges, distinguish it from squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease) and keratoacanthoma, and predict higher metastatic risk than basal cell carcinoma.

Explain melanoma risk factors (intense intermittent UV, fair skin, many or dysplastic nevi, family history, CDKN2A, xeroderma pigmentosum) and distinguish superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, acral lentiginous, and mucosal (including genital) subtypes by site and behavior.

Explain why entry into the vertical growth phase allows melanoma to metastasize, identify Breslow thickness as the key prognostic factor for localized melanoma, and identify S-100, HMB-45, and Melan-A as melanocytic immunostains.

Describe mycosis fungoides as a cutaneous CD4 T cell lymphoma progressing through patch, plaque, and tumor stages with Pautrier microabscesses of cerebriform cells, and identify Sézary syndrome by erythroderma with circulating Sézary cells.

Explain the four steps of acne vulgaris (follicular hyperkeratinization, androgen-driven sebum, Cutibacterium acnes growth, inflammation), distinguish comedones from inflammatory papules, pustules, and nodules, and identify hyperandrogenism (polycystic ovary syndrome) and glucocorticoids as aggravating causes.

Identify cutaneous candidiasis by beefy red intertriginous plaques with satellite pustules, distinguish candidal diaper dermatitis (involves folds) from irritant diaper dermatitis (spares folds), and relate thrush and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis to host risk factors.

Distinguish erysipelas (upper dermis and superficial lymphatics, raised sharply demarcated erythema, usually Streptococcus pyogenes) from cellulitis (deep dermis and subcutaneous fat, ill-defined borders, Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus) and relate each to its portal of entry.

Predict complications of cellulitis, including abscess, lymphangitis, bacteremia, and necrotizing fasciitis, suspected when pain is out of proportion to findings, with crepitus and rapid spread along fascial planes.

Explain erythema nodosum as a septal panniculitis without vasculitis, identify tender red nodules on the anterior shins that heal without scarring, and relate it to streptococcal infection, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, inflammatory bowel disease, and pregnancy.

Distinguish folliculitis, furuncles, and carbuncles by depth and extent of follicular infection, mostly by Staphylococcus aureus, and identify hot tub folliculitis from Pseudomonas aeruginosa and cutaneous or pilonidal abscess as related suppurative lesions.

Distinguish nonbullous impetigo (honey-colored crusts, Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes) from bullous impetigo (staphylococcal exfoliative toxin splitting the granular layer) in children, and predict poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis as a complication.

Explain how MRSA carries mecA on SCCmec, distinguish community-acquired MRSA (Panton-Valentine leukocidin, recurrent abscesses and furuncles in athletes, crowded settings, and injection drug use) from hospital-acquired MRSA, and identify nasal colonization as a reservoir.

Identify molluscum contagiosum by firm, flesh-colored, dome-shaped papules with central umbilication, spread by skin contact, autoinoculation, and sexual contact, with a self-limited course in children and extensive lesions in HIV.

Classify tinea by site (capitis with kerion and alopecia, corporis with annular scaly border and central clearing, cruris, pedis, barbae, unguium or onychomycosis), and distinguish tinea versicolor as a Malassezia infection, not a dermatophytosis.

Distinguish common, plantar, flat, and anogenital warts (condyloma acuminatum from HPV 6 and 11), identify papillomatosis, hyperkeratosis, and koilocytes on histology, and predict extensive warts with T cell immunodeficiency.

Rank bloodborne pathogen transmission risk after a needle stick (hepatitis B highest, then hepatitis C, then HIV), and explain how a hollow-bore needle, deep injury, and high source viral load raise risk.

Predict the wound infection organism from context: Pasteurella multocida (cat or dog bite), Capnocytophaga canimorsus (dog bite with asplenia), Eikenella corrodens (human bite), Vibrio vulnificus and Mycobacterium marinum (water exposure), and Sporothrix schenckii (rose thorn).

Explain how Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin (lecithinase) causes gas gangrene with crepitus and myonecrosis, and how Clostridium tetani in a puncture wound releases tetanospasmin that blocks GABA and glycine release, causing spastic paralysis.

Identify herpes simplex skin infections (herpes labialis, genital herpes, herpetic whitlow, eczema herpeticum) and herpes zoster (painful dermatomal vesicles, Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and ear vesicles), and predict postherpetic neuralgia.

Distinguish viral exanthems: measles (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, rash spreading down from the head), rubella (postauricular nodes, milder rash), roseola (HHV-6, high fever then rash), and erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19, slapped cheek, lacy rash).

Distinguish varicella (crops of vesicles in different stages starting on the trunk), hand-foot-and-mouth disease and herpangina (coxsackievirus A), and scarlet fever (sandpaper rash, strawberry tongue, circumoral pallor, desquamation from streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin).

Distinguish staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (young children, toxin cleaves desmoglein 1 in the granular layer, mucosa spared) from toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug-triggered full-thickness epidermal necrosis with mucosal involvement) by split level and cause.

Compare tuberculoid leprosy (Th1, few bacilli, few hypopigmented anesthetic plaques) with lepromatous leprosy (Th2, many bacilli, diffuse nodules, leonine facies), and explain why Mycobacterium leprae favors cool skin and peripheral nerves and cannot be cultured in vitro.

Explain how Bacillus anthracis edema factor (adenylate cyclase), lethal factor, protective antigen, and polypeptide capsule produce cutaneous anthrax, a painless papule that becomes a black eschar surrounded by edema.

Identify scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei burrows in web spaces, wrists, and genitals, nocturnal itch, crusted scabies with immunosuppression), head and pubic lice, body lice as vectors of Rickettsia prowazekii and Bartonella quintana, and bedbug bites in linear clusters.

Trace the fate of somites from paraxial mesoderm into sclerotome (vertebrae, ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle), and dermatome (dermis), and relate epaxial muscles to dorsal rami and hypaxial muscles to ventral rami.
Explain resegmentation, in which each vertebral body forms from the caudal half of one sclerotome and the cranial half of the next, and identify the notochord remnant as the nucleus pulposus.

Relate limb patterning signals to limb defects: FGF from the apical ectodermal ridge (proximal to distal outgrowth), sonic hedgehog from the zone of polarizing activity (anterior to posterior patterning; ectopic expression causes polydactyly), HOX genes (segment identity), and thalidomide (phocomelia).

Explain why the upper limb rotates laterally and the lower limb rotates medially during development, and use this to predict the position of flexor and extensor compartments and the spiral dermatome pattern of the leg.

Compare intramembranous ossification (flat bones of the skull vault, most of the clavicle) with endochondral ossification (hyaline cartilage model, primary center in the diaphysis, secondary centers in the epiphyses), and describe how joints form from interzone mesenchyme by cavitation.

Match pharyngeal arch muscles to their nerves: first arch (muscles of mastication, CN V3), second arch (muscles of facial expression, CN VII), third arch (stylopharyngeus, CN IX), fourth and sixth arches (pharynx and larynx, CN X).
Identify the A band, I band, H zone, M line, and Z line of the sarcomere, and predict which bands shorten during contraction (I band and H zone) and which stays constant (A band).

Distinguish skeletal muscle (multinucleate, peripheral nuclei, triads), cardiac muscle (branched, central nuclei, intercalated discs with gap junctions and desmosomes, dyads), and smooth muscle (fusiform, central nucleus, dense bodies, no striations) on histology.

Describe compact bone (osteons with central Haversian canals, Volkmann canals, concentric lamellae, osteocytes in lacunae linked by canaliculi) and spongy bone (trabeculae surrounding marrow), and distinguish woven from lamellar bone.

Compare osteoblasts (mesenchymal origin, secrete type I collagen osteoid and alkaline phosphatase), osteocytes (mechanosensing, FGF23 secretion), and osteoclasts (monocyte and macrophage lineage, multinucleated, ruffled border, acid and cathepsin K in Howship lacunae).

Describe the epiphyseal growth plate zones (reserve, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcification, ossification) and predict how defects in chondrocyte proliferation (achondroplasia) or mineralization (rickets) alter the plate.

Distinguish fibrous joints (sutures, syndesmoses, gomphoses), cartilaginous joints (hyaline synchondroses, fibrocartilage symphyses such as the pubic symphysis and intervertebral disc), and synovial joints (avascular articular hyaline cartilage, synoviocytes producing hyaluronan and lubricin).

Identify regional vertebral features: cervical transverse foramina and bifid spines, the atlas (no body) and axis (dens), thoracic costal facets, and large lumbar bodies, and explain how each relates to regional function.

Distinguish the normal cervical and lumbar lordosis and thoracic kyphosis from scoliosis (lateral curvature with vertebral rotation) and excessive kyphosis, and predict how severe thoracic scoliosis restricts lung expansion.

Locate the major skull foramina and their contents (superior orbital fissure, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, internal acoustic meatus, jugular foramen, foramen magnum), and explain why a pterion fracture can tear the middle meningeal artery.

Describe the clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, and carpal bones, and predict the nerve at risk with fractures of the humeral surgical neck (axillary), radial groove (radial), and medial epicondyle (ulnar).

Describe the hip bone (ilium, ischium, pubis fused at the acetabulum), femur, tibia, fibula, and foot arches, relate a collapsed medial longitudinal arch to flat foot (pes planus), and predict common fibular nerve injury with a fibular neck fracture.

Classify joints by function (synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, diarthrosis) and synovial joints by type (hinge, pivot, ball and socket, saddle, condyloid, plane), giving an example of each such as the atlantoaxial pivot and first carpometacarpal saddle.

Apply Hilton law (nerves to muscles acting on a joint also supply the joint) to explain articular proprioception and nociception, and why hip disease can present as knee pain through the obturator and femoral nerves.
Explain why the glenohumeral joint depends on the rotator cuff for stability, and predict axillary nerve injury and loss of deltoid abduction after anterior shoulder dislocation.

Relate knee ligaments and menisci to clinical tests: anterior drawer and Lachman (ACL), posterior drawer (PCL), valgus stress (MCL), varus stress (LCL), and explain why the medial meniscus, attached to the MCL, is injured more often.

Describe the temporomandibular joint (synovial joint with an articular disc, hinge and gliding movement, innervated by auriculotemporal and masseteric branches of CN V3) and relate disc displacement to clicking and jaw pain.

Describe the rotator cuff muscles: supraspinatus (initial abduction, suprascapular nerve), infraspinatus (lateral rotation, suprascapular nerve), teres minor (lateral rotation, axillary nerve), subscapularis (medial rotation, subscapular nerves), and identify supraspinatus as most often injured.

Predict upper limb deficits from nerve injury: musculocutaneous (weak elbow flexion), radial (wrist drop), median (loss of thenar opposition, ape hand), ulnar (claw hand, weak finger abduction), and long thoracic (winged scapula from serratus anterior paralysis).

Predict lower limb deficits from nerve injury: femoral (weak knee extension), obturator (weak adduction), superior gluteal (Trendelenburg sign with pelvic drop on the opposite side), common fibular (foot drop, weak eversion), and tibial (weak plantarflexion and inversion).

Describe the action and innervation of head and neck muscles: muscles of mastication (CN V3), muscles of facial expression (CN VII), tongue muscles (CN XII, except palatoglossus by CN X), and sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (CN XI).

Describe trunk muscles: erector spinae (extension, dorsal rami), diaphragm (inspiration, phrenic nerve C3 to C5), anterior abdominal wall layers (thoracoabdominal and subcostal nerves), and levator ani (pelvic floor support).

Trace musculoskeletal connective tissue origins: limb bones, cartilage, and tendons from lateral plate (somatic) mesoderm, axial skeleton from sclerotome, and craniofacial bone and cartilage largely from neural crest mesenchyme.

Match collagen types to tissues: type I (bone, tendon, ligament, fibrocartilage), type II (hyaline cartilage, nucleus pulposus), type III (reticular fibers, vessels, granulation tissue), and type IV (basement membrane).

Sequence collagen synthesis (Gly-X-Y chains, proline and lysine hydroxylation requiring vitamin C, triple helix formation, propeptide cleavage, lysyl oxidase cross-linking requiring copper) and predict the defect at each step in scurvy, osteogenesis imperfecta, and Menkes disease.
Explain how articular cartilage resists compression (aggrecan with chondroitin and keratan sulfate on hyaluronan binding water) and why avascular cartilage and poorly vascular tendons heal slowly.
Describe elastic fibers (elastin cores on fibrillin-1 microfibrils) in elastic ligaments such as the ligamentum flavum, and explain how fibrillin-1 normally sequesters TGF-beta.

Trace skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling from T-tubule depolarization through the dihydropyridine receptor and its mechanical link to ryanodine receptor 1, calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium binding to troponin C, and calcium reuptake by SERCA.
Sequence the cross-bridge cycle (ATP binding releases myosin from actin, hydrolysis cocks the head, phosphate release drives the power stroke) and explain rigor mortis as the loss of ATP.
Explain how skeletal muscle force is graded by motor unit recruitment (size principle) and summation to tetanus, and interpret length-tension and force-velocity relationships.

Explain calcium-induced calcium release through L-type channels and ryanodine receptor 2 in cardiac muscle, why its long refractory period prevents tetany, and how sympathetic stimulation increases contractility via phospholamban phosphorylation.

Explain smooth muscle contraction through calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase, relaxation by myosin light chain phosphatase, the latch state, and nitric oxide induced relaxation through cGMP.

Compare type I fibers (slow, oxidative, red, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, fatigue resistant) with type II fibers (fast, glycolytic, fatigable), and predict adaptations to endurance training (greater oxidative capacity) and resistance training (type II fiber hypertrophy).

Trace vitamin D activation from 7-dehydrocholesterol in UVB-exposed skin through hepatic 25-hydroxylation and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, and explain why serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D reflects vitamin D status.

Explain how PTH (bone resorption via osteoblast RANKL, distal tubule calcium reabsorption, phosphaturia, 1-alpha-hydroxylase activation), calcitriol, calcitonin, and osteocyte FGF23 regulate serum calcium and phosphate, and how osteoprotegerin limits osteoclast activation.

Compare muscle fuel use across exercise duration (phosphocreatine via creatine kinase, anaerobic glycolysis to lactate, oxidative metabolism of glucose and fatty acids) and explain the Cori cycle and creatinine as a marker of muscle mass.

Explain McArdle disease (autosomal recessive muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency) and predict exercise intolerance, cramps, myoglobinuria, failure of blood lactate to rise with exercise, and the second wind phenomenon.

Relate carnitine shuttle defects such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase II deficiency to muscle weakness and exertional rhabdomyolysis during prolonged exercise or fasting, when muscle depends on fatty acid oxidation.

Explain mineral and cofactor roles in bone and muscle: magnesium for PTH secretion, copper for lysyl oxidase cross-linking, vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation of osteocalcin, and calcium hydroxyapatite as the bone mineral.

Relate transcription factors to skeletal development: RUNX2 for osteoblast differentiation (haploinsufficiency causes cleidocranial dysplasia with absent clavicles and delayed suture closure), SOX9 for chondrocyte differentiation, and HOX genes for segment identity.
Explain how FGFR3 gain-of-function mutations inhibit chondrocyte proliferation in achondroplasia, and why most cases are new autosomal dominant mutations associated with advanced paternal age.

Explain the dominant-negative effect of glycine substitutions in COL1A1 or COL1A2 in severe osteogenesis imperfecta, compared with null alleles that halve normal collagen output and cause the milder type I form.

Apply the reading frame rule to dystrophin: frameshift deletions abolish dystrophin (Duchenne), while in-frame deletions produce a truncated, partly functional protein (Becker), and explain why the very large DMD gene has a high new mutation rate.

Explain myotonic dystrophy type 1 as an autosomal dominant CTG repeat expansion in DMPK showing anticipation, and predict myotonia, distal weakness, cataracts, frontal balding, testicular atrophy, and cardiac conduction defects.
Explain maternal inheritance and heteroplasmy in mitochondrial myopathies, and identify ragged red fibers on Gomori trichrome stain in disorders such as MERRF and MELAS.

Relate cell cycle and oncogene defects to bone and soft tissue sarcomas: RB1 loss (osteosarcoma after hereditary retinoblastoma), TP53 loss in Li-Fraumeni syndrome, and the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion transcription factor from t(11;22) in Ewing sarcoma.

Trace neuromuscular transmission (calcium entry, SNARE-mediated acetylcholine release, nicotinic receptor end plate potential, acetylcholinesterase) and localize the defect in myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton syndrome, and botulism.

Distinguish myasthenia gravis (anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, weakness that worsens with use, ptosis and diplopia) from Lambert-Eaton syndrome (anti-presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, strength improving with repeated effort, small cell lung cancer).

Compare muscle spindles (Ia afferents, stretch reflex, gamma motor neuron tuning) with Golgi tendon organs (Ib afferents, tension sensing), and match reflexes to roots: biceps C5 to C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1.

Distinguish neurogenic weakness (fasciculations, grouped atrophy, fiber type grouping, as in spinal muscular atrophy from SMN1 deletion) from myopathic weakness (proximal weakness, elevated CK), and identify type II fiber atrophy from disuse or corticosteroids.

Explain why hypocalcemia increases nerve and muscle excitability (lower sodium channel threshold), producing tetany with Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and why hypokalemia and hyperkalemia both cause muscle weakness.

Explain rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis: HLA-DR4 associated autoimmunity to citrullinated peptides, CD4 T cell and cytokine (TNF, IL-1, IL-6) driven synovitis, and pannus with RANKL-driven osteoclasts eroding cartilage and bone.

Distinguish rheumatoid arthritis (symmetric MCP and PIP synovitis sparing the DIP, morning stiffness over 1 hour, ulnar deviation, swan neck deformity, nodules, anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor) from osteoarthritis, and identify Felty syndrome (RA, splenomegaly, neutropenia).

Match autoantibodies to rheumatic diseases: anti-CCP (rheumatoid arthritis), anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (SLE), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse systemic sclerosis), anticentromere (limited systemic sclerosis), anti-U1 RNP (mixed connective tissue disease), anti-Jo-1 (myositis), anti-SSA and anti-SSB (Sjogren syndrome).

Describe musculoskeletal features of SLE (nonerosive arthritis), systemic sclerosis (sclerodactyly, calcinosis, flexion contractures, Raynaud phenomenon), and mixed connective tissue disease (overlapping SLE, scleroderma, and myositis features with anti-U1 RNP).

Classify hypersensitivity in musculoskeletal disease: type II in rheumatic fever polyarthritis (molecular mimicry) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies against small cell lung cancer cross-reacting with presynaptic calcium channels), type III in SLE arthritis, and type IV in polymyositis.

Explain innate immune activation in joints: urate crystals activating the NLRP3 inflammasome to release IL-1 beta in gout, and neutrophil proteases destroying articular cartilage within days in septic arthritis.

Describe postinfectious and postvaccine arthritis: HLA-B27 associated reactive arthritis after enteric or chlamydial infection, symmetric small joint arthritis after parvovirus B19 or rubella infection, and transient arthralgia in adult women after rubella vaccination.

Describe Staphylococcus aureus (gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive) and explain how protein A, collagen and fibronectin adhesins, and biofilm on hardware make it the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis.

Describe Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococci; pili with antigenic variation, IgA protease) and the disseminated gonococcal infection pattern of tenosynovitis, pustular dermatitis, and migratory polyarthralgia or purulent monoarthritis in sexually active young adults.

Match osteomyelitis organisms to settings: Salmonella (sickle cell disease), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (injection drug use, puncture through a shoe sole), Pasteurella multocida (cat and dog bites), Staphylococcus epidermidis (prosthetic material), and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (vertebrae).

Describe Clostridium perfringens (gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming rod) and explain how alpha toxin (phospholipase C, lecithinase) destroys cell membranes, producing myonecrosis, gas, and hemolysis in contaminated deep wounds.

Describe Streptococcus pyogenes (beta-hemolytic gram-positive cocci in chains) and explain how M protein resists phagocytosis while hyaluronidase, streptokinase, and superantigen pyrogenic exotoxins promote spread along fascia and toxic shock.

Describe Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete) and its transmission cycle, in which Ixodes larvae acquire it from white-footed mice and nymphs transmit it after about 36 hours or more of attachment, and the late Lyme arthritis of large joints, especially the knee.

Explain how Mycobacterium tuberculosis spreads hematogenously to vertebral bodies (Pott disease), forming caseating granulomas that collapse adjacent vertebrae and disc space, producing gibbus deformity and psoas abscess.
Explain how vitamin D deficiency or phosphate loss causes defective mineralization of osteoid, producing rickets before growth plate closure and osteomalacia after it.
Identify risk factors for vitamin D deficiency: limited sun exposure, darker skin, unsupplemented exclusive breastfeeding, fat malabsorption, liver or kidney disease, and anticonvulsant use.

Describe osteomalacia findings: diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, Looser zones (pseudofractures), and labs showing low or normal calcium, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, high PTH, and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D.

Describe rickets findings: rachitic rosary, craniotabes, frontal bossing, bowed legs (genu varum), widened and cupped metaphyses on radiograph, and distinguish X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets caused by FGF23 excess.
Explain how vitamin C deficiency impairs prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation, producing unstable collagen triple helices, fragile vessels, and poor wound healing.

Describe scurvy findings and risks: perifollicular hemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums, poor wound healing, hemarthrosis, and painful subperiosteal hemorrhage in children, in people with diets lacking fruit and vegetables or with alcohol use disorder.

Explain ankylosing spondylitis as an HLA-B27 associated seronegative spondyloarthropathy with enthesitis and sacroiliitis, and predict inflammatory back pain in young men that improves with exercise, reduced chest expansion, and bamboo spine from syndesmophytes.
Identify extra-articular complications of ankylosing spondylitis: anterior uveitis, aortitis with aortic regurgitation, restrictive lung disease, and vertebral fractures in a fused spine.

Describe bursitis by site and cause, including prepatellar bursitis from kneeling, olecranon bursitis, subacromial and trochanteric bursitis from overuse, and septic bursitis from Staphylococcus aureus.

Explain fibromyalgia as a disorder of central pain sensitization, and identify widespread pain for at least 3 months with fatigue and unrefreshing sleep, most often in women, with normal inflammatory markers and CK.

Explain hyperuricemia in gout from urate underexcretion (most cases, thiazides, kidney disease) or overproduction (Lesch-Nyhan HGPRT deficiency, tumor lysis, glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency), with xanthine oxidase converting hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid.

Identify gout findings: acute monoarthritis of the first MTP joint (podagra) triggered by alcohol or purine-rich meals, needle-shaped negatively birefringent urate crystals, tophi, punched-out erosions, and uric acid kidney stones.

Distinguish dermatomyositis (complement-mediated capillary injury, perifascicular atrophy, heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, association with internal cancer) from polymyositis (endomysial CD8 T cells), both with proximal weakness, high CK, and possible anti-Jo-1 interstitial lung disease.

Interpret muscle biopsy and laboratory findings to separate inflammatory myositis (high CK, inflammatory infiltrates, myofiber necrosis) from polymyalgia rheumatica (normal CK and strength) and steroid myopathy.

Describe polymyalgia rheumatica in adults over 50: pain and stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles, elevated ESR, normal CK, and its association with giant cell (temporal) arteritis and risk of vision loss.

Explain reactive arthritis as an HLA-B27 associated sterile arthritis following Chlamydia trachomatis or enteric infection (Shigella, Salmonella, Yersinia, Campylobacter), presenting with arthritis, conjunctivitis, and urethritis, plus enthesitis and keratoderma blennorrhagicum.

Explain tendinopathy as overuse-induced collagen disorganization with limited inflammation (tendinosis), and identify lateral epicondylitis (extensor carpi radialis brevis origin), medial epicondylitis, and supraspinatus impingement with a painful arc.

Describe de Quervain tenosynovitis (abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, positive Finkelstein test), plantar fasciitis, and Achilles tendinopathy with rupture risk increased by fluoroquinolones.
Distinguish psoriatic arthritis (DIP involvement, dactylitis, nail pitting, pencil-in-cup deformity, axial disease linked to HLA-B27) from rheumatoid arthritis.

Describe juvenile idiopathic arthritis (arthritis before age 16 lasting at least 6 weeks), including the oligoarticular ANA-positive form with silent anterior uveitis and the systemic form with daily spiking fever and salmon-colored rash.

Distinguish pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate deposition, rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals, chondrocalcinosis, knee and wrist, linked to hyperparathyroidism and hemochromatosis) from gout.

Describe adhesive capsulitis (capsular inflammation and fibrosis with loss of both active and passive shoulder motion, associated with diabetes) and ganglion cysts (myxoid degeneration near a joint capsule or tendon sheath, often the dorsal wrist, lacking a true lining).
Explain osteopetrosis as failure of osteoclast bone resorption (for example carbonic anhydrase II deficiency with renal tubular acidosis, or CLCN7 mutations), producing dense but brittle bone.

Predict osteopetrosis complications: fractures, pancytopenia from marrow obliteration with extramedullary hematopoiesis and hepatosplenomegaly, and cranial nerve palsies (vision and hearing loss) from narrowed foramina, more severe in the infantile autosomal recessive form.

Interpret serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and PTH to distinguish osteoporosis (all normal), osteomalacia, Paget disease (isolated high alkaline phosphatase), primary hyperparathyroidism, and renal osteodystrophy.

Explain renal osteodystrophy: phosphate retention and low calcitriol in chronic kidney disease cause secondary hyperparathyroidism, with osteitis fibrosa cystica (subperiosteal resorption, brown tumors) and defective mineralization.

Explain Marfan syndrome as an autosomal dominant FBN1 (fibrillin-1) defect with excess TGF-beta signaling, and identify tall stature, arachnodactyly, arm span exceeding height, pectus deformity, joint hypermobility, and upward lens dislocation.

Predict Marfan cardiovascular complications (aortic root dilation, aortic dissection, mitral valve prolapse) and distinguish Marfan from homocystinuria (downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, thrombosis).

Describe Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked, absent dystrophin): onset before age 5, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy from fibrofatty replacement, markedly elevated CK, dilated cardiomyopathy, and respiratory failure.
Compare Becker muscular dystrophy (later onset, milder course, truncated dystrophin) with Duchenne, and use dystrophin immunostaining and genetic testing to separate them.

Explain osteogenesis imperfecta as defective type I collagen (COL1A1 or COL1A2), and identify multiple fractures with minimal trauma, blue sclerae, conductive hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and joint laxity.
Distinguish osteogenesis imperfecta from nonaccidental trauma in a child with multiple fractures using sclerae, dentition, family history, and fracture pattern.

Describe Ehlers-Danlos syndrome as a group of collagen disorders (classic type V collagen, vascular type III collagen) with skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility and dislocation, easy bruising, and arterial or bowel rupture in the vascular type.
Identify achondroplasia findings: rhizomelic limb shortening with a normal-length trunk, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and normal intelligence.

Explain osteoarthritis pathogenesis (chondrocyte injury, proteoglycan loss, cartilage fibrillation, eburnation, subchondral sclerosis and cysts, osteophytes) and risk factors (age, obesity, prior joint injury, mechanical load).

Identify osteoarthritis findings: pain worse with use, morning stiffness under 30 minutes, Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodes, asymmetric weight-bearing joint involvement, and radiographic joint space narrowing with osteophytes.

Explain osteoporosis as reduced bone mass with normal mineralization, driven by low peak bone mass, estrogen loss increasing RANKL-mediated resorption, aging, and secondary causes (glucocorticoids, hyperthyroidism, immobilization, alcohol, smoking).

Interpret osteoporosis findings: vertebral compression, hip, and distal radius fractures, height loss and kyphosis, normal serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase, and DEXA T-scores of minus 2.5 or lower (osteopenia between minus 1 and minus 2.5).

Explain Paget disease of bone as osteoclast overactivity followed by disorganized osteoblastic repair (lytic, mixed, and sclerotic phases) producing thick but weak mosaic lamellar bone, with isolated elevation of alkaline phosphatase.
Predict Paget disease complications in older adults: bone pain, enlarging skull, hearing loss, fractures, high-output heart failure from arteriovenous shunting, and osteosarcoma.

Explain avascular necrosis as bone infarction from interrupted blood supply, and identify causes (glucocorticoids, alcohol, sickle cell disease, SLE, decompression sickness, femoral neck and scaphoid fractures) and the femoral head as the most common site.

Distinguish pediatric hip disorders: developmental dysplasia of the hip (newborn, Ortolani and Barlow tests), Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (idiopathic femoral head osteonecrosis in young children), and slipped capital femoral epiphysis (obese adolescent, epiphysis slips off the femoral neck).

Relate disc degeneration to posterolateral nucleus pulposus herniation compressing the lower root (L4 to L5 herniation affects L5), and distinguish spondylosis (degenerative change) from spondylolisthesis (forward vertebral slip).

Distinguish adolescent knee disorders: Osgood-Schlatter disease (traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle), chondromalacia patellae (softened patellar cartilage with anterior knee pain), and osteochondritis dissecans (separation of a subchondral bone and cartilage fragment).
Describe Dupuytren contracture as myofibroblast proliferation in the palmar fascia causing flexion contracture of the ring and little fingers.

Describe chondrosarcoma as a malignant cartilage-forming tumor of older adults in the pelvis, proximal femur, and shoulder girdle, which can arise from enchondroma or osteochondroma and often carries IDH1 or IDH2 mutations.

Describe Ewing sarcoma in children and adolescents: diaphyseal or pelvic tumor of small round blue cells, CD99 positive, EWSR1-FLI1 from t(11;22), onion-skin periosteal reaction, and fever that can mimic osteomyelitis.

Describe osteoid osteoma (under 2 cm cortical nidus with a sclerotic rim in young males, night pain relieved by NSAIDs because the nidus produces prostaglandin E2) and distinguish osteoblastoma (larger, vertebral).

Describe osteosarcoma as the most common primary malignant bone tumor apart from myeloma: malignant osteoid, metaphysis around the knee, peaks in adolescents and in older adults with Paget disease or prior radiation.
Interpret osteosarcoma imaging (Codman triangle, sunburst pattern), relate risk to RB1 and TP53 loss, and predict hematogenous metastasis to lung.

Describe rhabdomyosarcoma as the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood, arising in the head and neck or genitourinary tract (sarcoma botryoides), with desmin and myogenin positive rhabdomyoblasts and PAX3 or PAX7 to FOXO1 fusions in the alveolar type.

Distinguish benign cartilage tumors: osteochondroma (EXT1 or EXT2, metaphyseal bony stalk with a cartilage cap) and enchondroma (intramedullary hyaline cartilage in hand bones, multiple in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome), with risk of chondrosarcoma.

Describe giant cell tumor of bone (epiphyseal soap-bubble lesion in young adults, RANKL-expressing stromal cells with osteoclast-like giant cells) and tenosynovial giant cell tumor (synovial or tendon sheath tumor overexpressing CSF1).

Explain why metastases are the most common malignant bone tumors, distinguish osteoblastic (prostate), osteolytic (kidney, thyroid, lung), and mixed (breast) lesions, and predict pathologic fracture and hypercalcemia as complications.

Compare soft tissue sarcomas by lineage marker, rhabdomyosarcoma (desmin, myogenin) and leiomyosarcoma (smooth muscle actin, desmin; uterus and retroperitoneum in adults), and explain their hematogenous spread to lung.
Describe hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (digital clubbing, periosteal new bone formation, and arthritis) as a paraneoplastic syndrome of lung cancer.

Explain septic arthritis pathogenesis (hematogenous seeding or direct inoculation, mostly Staphylococcus aureus, Neisseria gonorrhoeae in sexually active adults) and risk factors (rheumatoid arthritis, prosthetic joints, injection drug use, diabetes).

Interpret synovial fluid analysis: noninflammatory (under 2,000 WBC/mm3), inflammatory, and septic (usually over 50,000 WBC/mm3 with neutrophils, positive Gram stain or culture), plus crystal identification, to evaluate an acute hot swollen joint.

Explain necrotizing fasciitis as rapidly spreading infection along fascial planes, type I polymicrobial (diabetes, perineal Fournier gangrene) or type II Streptococcus pyogenes, with pain out of proportion to exam, crepitus, bullae, and systemic toxicity.

Explain why hematogenous osteomyelitis in children localizes to the metaphysis of long bones, and contrast contiguous spread from diabetic foot ulcers and vertebral osteomyelitis with discitis in adults.

Identify osteomyelitis findings and complications: sequestrum, involucrum, Brodie abscess, elevated ESR and CRP, MRI as the most sensitive imaging, chronic draining sinus, and squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic sinus tract.

Distinguish dry gangrene (coagulative necrosis after arterial occlusion, sharply demarcated) from wet gangrene (superimposed bacterial infection with liquefactive necrosis), and explain the higher risk in diabetes and peripheral artery disease.

Describe gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) after deep contaminated wounds: rapid spread, severe pain, crepitus from gas, bronze skin, hemolysis, and shock from Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin.

Describe infective myositis: pyomyositis (Staphylococcus aureus abscess in large muscles) and trichinellosis (Trichinella spiralis larvae encysting in skeletal muscle after undercooked pork or wild game, with myalgia, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia).

Sequence fracture healing (hematoma and inflammation, soft callus, hard callus, remodeling) and predict delayed union from poor blood supply, infection, instability, smoking, diabetes, and malnutrition.

Predict complications of specific fractures: scaphoid and femoral neck (avascular necrosis from retrograde or retinacular blood supply), supracondylar humerus (brachial artery and median nerve), and long bone fractures (fat embolism with hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae).
Distinguish sprain (ligament), strain (muscle or tendon), contusion (soft tissue hemorrhage), and dislocation (loss of joint congruity), and explain why ligaments heal slowly.

Explain compartment syndrome (rising pressure in a closed fascial compartment after fracture or crush, causing ischemia) and identify pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, preserved pulses early, and Volkmann ischemic contracture as a late result.
Explain rhabdomyolysis from crush injury, extreme exertion, or statins, and predict very high CK, myoglobinuria (dipstick positive for blood without red cells), hyperkalemia, and acute kidney injury.
Describe myositis ossificans as heterotopic bone in muscle after trauma, and distinguish its zonal pattern (mature bone at the periphery) from osteosarcoma.
Describe neurulation, including notochord induction of the neural plate, elevation and fusion of the neural folds, and closure of the anterior and posterior neuropores during the fourth week.

Relate the primary brain vesicles (prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon) and secondary vesicles (telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon) to the adult structures and ventricles each forms.

Distinguish neuroectoderm derivatives (CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma, retina) from neural crest derivatives (sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes) and mesoderm-derived microglia.

Distinguish spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, and anencephaly, and relate open neural tube defects to elevated maternal serum and amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein and to periconceptional folate deficiency.

Explain holoprosencephaly as failed separation of the prosencephalon into two hemispheres, linked to sonic hedgehog pathway defects and trisomy 13, and relate it to midline facial defects such as cyclopia and cleft lip.

Compare Chiari I malformation (cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum, associated with syringomyelia), Chiari II malformation (vermis and medulla herniation with lumbosacral myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus), and Dandy-Walker malformation (vermis agenesis with cystic fourth ventricle).

Identify the parts of a multipolar motor neuron (soma with Nissl substance, dendrites, axon hillock, axon, synaptic terminals) and compare it with pseudounipolar dorsal root ganglion neurons and bipolar retinal and olfactory neurons.

Describe the connective tissue layers of a peripheral nerve (endoneurium around each axon, perineurium around each fascicle, epineurium around the whole nerve) and explain the perineurium's role as a blood-nerve barrier.

Compare myelination by Schwann cells (one internode of one axon in the PNS) and oligodendrocytes (internodes of many axons in the CNS), and relate Schwann cell injury to Guillain-Barré syndrome and oligodendrocyte injury to multiple sclerosis and PML.

Identify the functions of astrocytes (blood-brain barrier support, potassium buffering, glial scar), microglia (resident CNS macrophages that form multinucleated giant cells in HIV infection), and ependymal cells lining the ventricles.

Describe Wallerian degeneration distal to an axon transection and central chromatolysis in the cell body, and explain why peripheral axons can regenerate along Schwann cell tubes while CNS axons generally do not.
Identify red neurons (shrunken cell body, eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus) as the histologic marker of irreversible neuronal injury, appearing about 12 to 24 hours after hypoxia or ischemia.
Locate the primary motor, primary somatosensory, primary visual, and primary auditory cortices and the Broca and Wernicke areas, and predict the deficit produced by a lesion of each.

Describe the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, including dopamine acting on D1 and D2 receptors, and predict how loss of substantia nigra pars compacta neurons (Parkinson disease) or caudate neurons (Huntington disease) changes movement.
Explain cerebellar function in coordination and distinguish a vermis lesion (truncal ataxia, wide-based gait) from a hemisphere lesion (ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia).

Identify the thalamic relay nuclei (VPL for body sensation, VPM for face sensation and taste, LGN for vision, MGN for hearing, VL for motor) and relate thalamic infarction to contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome.

Identify the brainstem level of the cranial nerve nuclei (midbrain III and IV; pons V to VIII; medulla IX, X, XII) and the spinal cord's gray horns, white columns, enlargements, and conus medullaris ending near L1 to L2.

Explain how damage to the ascending reticular activating system of the upper brainstem or to both cerebral hemispheres causes coma, and distinguish coma, delirium, and brain death (irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function).

Describe the meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia) and the epidural, subdural, and subarachnoid spaces, and identify which space an arterial epidural, venous subdural, and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage occupies.

Identify the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli and predict the structures compressed in subfalcine (anterior cerebral artery), uncal (CN III, posterior cerebral artery, cerebral peduncle), and tonsillar (medullary respiratory centers) herniation.

Describe the subarachnoid cisterns, including the lumbar cistern below the conus medullaris where lumbar puncture is done at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5, and the arachnoid granulations that return CSF to the dural venous sinuses.

Explain the blood-brain barrier (endothelial tight junctions, basement membrane, astrocyte foot processes) and the blood-CSF barrier (choroid plexus epithelium), and identify circumventricular organs that lack a barrier, such as the area postrema and posterior pituitary.

Interpret CSF opening pressure, cell count and type, protein, and glucose to distinguish bacterial, viral, fungal, and tuberculous meningitis, and recognize albuminocytologic dissociation in Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Classify Meissner corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles, Merkel discs, Ruffini endings, free nerve endings, muscle spindles, and Golgi tendon organs by stimulus, adaptation rate, and afferent fiber type.
Trace the dorsal column medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways from receptor to cortex, naming where each decussates, and predict the sensory loss from a lesion at a given level.

Predict the findings of Brown-Séquard hemisection (ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration and position sense, contralateral loss of pain and temperature) and syringomyelia (bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch).

Describe the monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle, Ia afferent, alpha motor neuron), the Golgi tendon organ Ib reflex, and the withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes, and identify the roots of the biceps (C5), triceps (C7), patellar (L4), and Achilles (S1) reflexes.

Explain referred pain as convergence of visceral and somatic afferents on the same spinal segments, using cardiac pain felt in the left arm and diaphragmatic irritation felt in the shoulder (C3 to C5) as examples.

Explain pain modulation by gate control and by descending inhibition from the periaqueductal gray using endogenous opioids, and identify postherpetic neuralgia, phantom limb pain, and thalamic pain as neuropathic pain from nervous system injury.

Distinguish migraine (unilateral pulsating headache with nausea and photophobia, often with aura, involving trigeminovascular activation and CGRP release), cluster headache (brief severe periorbital pain with ipsilateral lacrimation and rhinorrhea), and tension headache (bilateral band-like pressure).

Trace the visual pathway from retina through optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations (Meyer loop) to the calcarine cortex, and predict the visual field defect from a lesion at each site.

Describe the pupillary light reflex (CN II afferent, Edinger-Westphal nucleus and CN III efferent) and accommodation, and interpret anisocoria, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and an Argyll Robertson pupil.

Explain phototransduction in rods and cones (light isomerizing retinal in rhodopsin, transducin activation, cGMP breakdown by phosphodiesterase, closure of cGMP-gated sodium channels, hyperpolarization) and relate vitamin A deficiency to night blindness.

Describe aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium and drainage through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm, and describe tear film production by the lacrimal gland (CN VII parasympathetic fibers) and meibomian glands.

Trace sound transmission through the tympanic membrane, ossicles, oval window, and cochlea, explain hair cell transduction in potassium-rich endolymph and tonotopy (base high frequency, apex low), and distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss with Weber and Rinne tests.

Describe the semicircular canals (angular acceleration), utricle and saccule (linear acceleration and gravity), and vestibulo-ocular reflex, and relate vestibular imbalance to vertigo and nystagmus and sensory conflict to motion sickness.
