Trace taste (CN VII anterior two thirds, CN IX posterior third, to the nucleus solitarius and VPM) and smell (olfactory neurons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, no thalamic relay), and predict anosmia after cribriform fracture.

Unit name: Somatic and visceral motor and sensory components
Competency: Trace the lateral corticospinal tract from the precentral gyrus through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, and pyramidal decussation to the anterior horn alpha motor neuron.

Unit name: Somatic and visceral motor and sensory components
Competency: Distinguish upper from lower motor neuron lesions by tone, reflexes, Babinski sign, fasciculations, and atrophy, and apply this to ALS (mixed signs) and poliomyelitis and spinal muscular atrophy (lower motor neuron signs).

Unit name: Somatic and visceral motor and sensory components
Competency: Compare the one-neuron somatic motor pathway (acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle) with the two-neuron visceral motor pathway (preganglionic and postganglionic neurons) to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

Unit name: Somatic and visceral motor and sensory components
Competency: Predict the findings of subacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts), tabes dorsalis (dorsal columns and dorsal roots), anterior spinal artery infarction (dorsal columns spared), and complete cord transection.

Unit name: Somatic and visceral motor and sensory components
Competency: Describe visceral sensory pathways, including pain afferents that travel with sympathetic nerves and reflex afferents from carotid sinus baroreceptors (CN IX) and aortic arch baroreceptors (CN X) to the nucleus solitarius.

Identify each cranial nerve's skull foramen, components, and functions, and predict the deficit from injury, such as a down-and-out eye with ptosis and mydriasis (CN III), failed abduction (CN VI), or tongue deviation toward the lesion (CN XII).
Distinguish a central (upper motor neuron) facial lesion that weakens only the contralateral lower face from a CN VII lesion that weakens the entire ipsilateral face, including the forehead.

Describe the brachial plexus (roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches) and predict deficits from Erb palsy (C5 to C6), Klumpke palsy (C8 to T1), and injuries to the axillary, radial, median, ulnar, and long thoracic nerves.
Predict deficits from injuries to lower limb nerves: common fibular at the fibular neck (foot drop), tibial, femoral, obturator, and superior gluteal (Trendelenburg sign).
Use dermatome landmarks (C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 knee and medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot) to localize a spinal nerve root lesion.

Explain internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion (impaired adduction on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye, convergence preserved) and its association with multiple sclerosis.

Compare sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1 to L2) and parasympathetic (craniosacral, CN III, VII, IX, X and S2 to S4) outflow, including where preganglionic and postganglionic cell bodies and ganglia lie.

Identify the transmitter and receptor at each autonomic synapse (acetylcholine at nicotinic ganglia, norepinephrine at adrenergic targets, acetylcholine at muscarinic targets and sweat glands) and the G protein linked to alpha1, alpha2, beta, M1, M2, and M3 receptors.

Trace the oculosympathetic pathway (hypothalamus, ciliospinal center at C8 to T2, superior cervical ganglion, carotid plexus) and predict ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis in Horner syndrome from a Pancoast tumor or carotid dissection.

Identify the parasympathetic ganglia of the head and their targets: ciliary (CN III, pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle), pterygopalatine (CN VII, lacrimal gland), submandibular (CN VII, submandibular and sublingual glands), and otic (CN IX, parotid).

Explain autonomic dysreflexia after spinal cord injury at or above T6, linking a stimulus below the lesion (such as a full bladder) to unopposed sympathetic discharge with severe hypertension and reflex bradycardia.

Unit name: CNS blood supply and CSF flow
Competency: Trace the circle of Willis from the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems and identify the territories supplied by the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries and the lenticulostriate arteries.

Unit name: CNS blood supply and CSF flow
Competency: Predict the stroke syndrome from occlusion of the ACA (contralateral leg), MCA (contralateral face and arm, aphasia if dominant, neglect if nondominant), PCA (homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing), and lenticulostriate arteries (pure motor lacunar stroke).

Unit name: CNS blood supply and CSF flow
Competency: Predict brainstem syndromes from occlusion of the PICA (lateral medullary syndrome with dysphagia, hoarseness, and crossed pain loss), anterior spinal artery (medial medullary syndrome), AICA (lateral pontine syndrome), and basilar artery (locked-in syndrome).

Unit name: CNS blood supply and CSF flow
Competency: Trace CSF from the choroid plexus through the interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, and foramina of Luschka and Magendie to the subarachnoid space, and predict which ventricles dilate with obstruction at each site.

Unit name: CNS blood supply and CSF flow
Competency: Describe venous drainage through the dural venous sinuses to the internal jugular veins, and relate tearing of bridging veins to subdural hematoma and dural sinus thrombosis to raised intracranial pressure.

Unit name: CNS blood supply and CSF flow
Competency: Explain autoregulation of cerebral blood flow and its sensitivity to PaCO2 (hypercapnia dilates, hypocapnia constricts), and use cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP minus ICP) to explain the Cushing reflex of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing.

Describe prefrontal association cortex functions (executive function, planning, judgment, personality) and predict disinhibition, apathy, and poor judgment after frontal lobe damage, as in frontotemporal dementia.

Explain the role of parietal association cortex in spatial attention, and predict hemispatial neglect after a nondominant (usually right) parietal lesion and Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right confusion) after a dominant angular gyrus lesion.

Distinguish Broca aphasia (nonfluent, comprehension intact), Wernicke aphasia (fluent, comprehension impaired), conduction aphasia (repetition impaired, arcuate fasciculus), and global aphasia by lesion site.

Compare the dorsal (occipitoparietal, spatial location and motion) and ventral (occipitotemporal, object and face recognition) visual association streams, and predict prosopagnosia after fusiform gyrus damage.
Relate EEG patterns to arousal and sleep stages (beta awake, alpha relaxed with eyes closed, theta in N1, sleep spindles and K complexes in N2, delta in N3, low-voltage beta-like activity in REM).

Identify hypothalamic nuclei and functions: supraoptic and paraventricular (ADH, oxytocin), arcuate (dopamine, GHRH), lateral (hunger), ventromedial (satiety), anterior (heat loss), posterior (heat conservation), and suprachiasmatic (circadian rhythm).

Explain hypothalamic thermoregulation, including how pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) raise the set point through prostaglandin E2 in fever, and predict hyperphagia after ventromedial lesions and anorexia after lateral lesions.

Describe the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix, mammillary bodies) and relate hippocampal damage to anterograde amnesia, mammillary body damage to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, and bilateral amygdala damage to Klüver-Bucy syndrome.

Explain how the suprachiasmatic nucleus, driven by retinal light input, sets circadian rhythm through pineal melatonin, and relate loss of lateral hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons to narcolepsy with cataplexy.

Distinguish REM sleep behavior disorder (loss of REM atonia, often preceding Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia), N3 parasomnias of childhood (sleepwalking, sleep terrors), and restless legs syndrome (urge to move at rest, linked to iron deficiency).

Explain the resting membrane potential using the Na+/K+ ATPase, potassium leak channels, and the Nernst equation, and predict how changes in extracellular potassium alter neuronal and muscle excitability.

Describe the phases of the action potential (voltage-gated sodium channel activation and inactivation, delayed potassium efflux, afterhyperpolarization), threshold, and the absolute and relative refractory periods.
Compare graded potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs) with action potentials and explain temporal and spatial summation at the axon hillock.

Explain how myelin speeds conduction by saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier, how axon diameter affects velocity, and why demyelination in multiple sclerosis and Guillain-Barré syndrome slows or blocks conduction.

Describe neuromuscular transmission (calcium entry, SNARE-mediated vesicle release, acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors, acetylcholinesterase) and predict how botulinum toxin, myasthenia gravis, and Lambert-Eaton syndrome each disrupt it.

Classify seizures as focal (with or without impaired awareness) or generalized (tonic-clonic, absence with 3 Hz spike-and-wave), explain them as excess synchronous neuronal firing from an excitation and inhibition imbalance, and describe febrile seizures in young children.

Explain hypokalemic periodic paralysis as an inherited skeletal muscle ion channelopathy causing episodes of flaccid weakness with low serum potassium, often triggered by carbohydrate-rich meals or rest after exercise.

Explain why the brain depends on glucose (entering through GLUT1 at the blood-brain barrier and GLUT3 on neurons) and shifts to ketone bodies in prolonged fasting, and predict neuroglycopenic symptoms of hypoglycemia.

Explain thiamine pyrophosphate as a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, and relate deficiency to Wernicke encephalopathy, dry beriberi, and worsening when glucose is given before thiamine.

Explain vitamin B12 as a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and use elevated methylmalonic acid to distinguish B12 deficiency, which damages myelin, from folate deficiency, which spares the nervous system.

Relate neurologic findings to deficiencies of vitamin B6 (seizures and neuropathy from impaired GABA and transmitter synthesis), niacin (pellagra with dementia), and vitamin E (spinocerebellar ataxia and dorsal column degeneration).
Explain how hyperammonemia from liver failure or urea cycle defects injures the brain, linking astrocyte glutamine synthetase activity to astrocyte swelling and Alzheimer type II astrocytes.

Describe the lipid composition of myelin (cholesterol, galactocerebroside, sulfatide, sphingomyelin) and relate defects in lysosomal sphingolipid breakdown to neurodegeneration in the sphingolipidoses and leukodystrophies.
Explain how lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, and relate lead poisoning to encephalopathy in children and to wrist and foot drop from peripheral motor neuropathy in adults.

Trace catecholamine synthesis from tyrosine through L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate limiting), dopamine, norepinephrine (dopamine beta-hydroxylase, vitamin C dependent), and epinephrine (PNMT, induced by cortisol).

Describe catecholamine breakdown by MAO and COMT to homovanillic acid (from dopamine) and vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrines (from norepinephrine and epinephrine), and relate elevated urinary HVA and VMA to neuroblastoma.
Trace serotonin synthesis from tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase in the raphe nuclei, its conversion to melatonin in the pineal gland, and its breakdown by MAO to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

Explain GABA synthesis from glutamate by pyridoxal phosphate-dependent glutamate decarboxylase, contrast glutamate (excitatory, NMDA and AMPA receptors) with GABA and glycine (inhibitory), and relate glutamate excitotoxicity to ischemic neuronal death.

Describe acetylcholine synthesis by choline acetyltransferase from acetyl-CoA and choline and its breakdown by acetylcholinesterase, and relate loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert to Alzheimer disease.

Identify the main source nuclei of dopamine (substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area), norepinephrine (locus coeruleus), and serotonin (raphe), and relate decreased dopamine to Parkinson disease and decreased GABA and acetylcholine to Huntington disease.

Explain trinucleotide repeat expansion in Huntington disease (CAG, HTT), fragile X syndrome (CGG, FMR1 hypermethylation), myotonic dystrophy (CTG, DMPK), and Friedreich ataxia (GAA, frataxin), including each inheritance pattern and anticipation in the first three.

Explain the chromosomal mechanisms of Down syndrome (maternal meiotic nondisjunction, Robertsonian translocation, mosaicism) and relate an extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21 to early-onset Alzheimer disease.

Explain how loss of tumor suppressor genes causes autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndromes: NF1 (neurofibromin, chromosome 17), NF2 (merlin, chromosome 22), tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin, mTOR activation), and von Hippel-Lindau (VHL, chromosome 3).
Describe Sturge-Weber syndrome as a sporadic somatic GNAQ mutation causing a facial port-wine stain in the CN V1 distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and glaucoma.

Explain spinal muscular atrophy as autosomal recessive loss of SMN1 causing degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons, with a floppy infant, tongue fasciculations, and areflexia in the severe infantile form.

Relate driver gene defects to nervous system tumors: two-hit RB1 tumor suppressor loss in retinoblastoma, IDH mutation with 1p/19q codeletion in oligodendroglioma, and MYCN oncogene amplification predicting aggressive neuroblastoma.

Describe the hypophyseal portal system and the hypothalamic hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) that control the anterior pituitary, and explain why dopamine is the main inhibitor of prolactin.

Explain ADH and oxytocin synthesis in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei with axonal transport to the posterior pituitary, and predict central diabetes insipidus or SIADH after head trauma, neurosurgery, or a CNS tumor.
Predict the effects of a pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma compressing the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia) and pituitary stalk (hyperprolactinemia from loss of dopamine inhibition).
Explain the neuroendocrine stress response linking the hypothalamus to the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla (catecholamines) and to the HPA axis (CRH, ACTH, cortisol).

Relate thyroid hormone to nervous system function, including impaired brain development in congenital hypothyroidism, delayed reflex relaxation in hypothyroidism, and tremor and hyperreflexia in hyperthyroidism.

Describe how the blood-brain barrier and resident microglia shape CNS innate immunity, and explain how cytokine release (IL-1, TNF) in bacterial meningitis increases barrier permeability and causes cerebral edema.
Explain multiple sclerosis as T cell-mediated (Th1 and Th17) autoimmune injury to CNS myelin, with HLA-DR2 association, CSF oligoclonal IgG bands, and periventricular white matter plaques.

Explain molecular mimicry in Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter jejuni infection, with antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides, and relate anti-GQ1b antibodies to the Miller Fisher variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia).

Classify myasthenia gravis (antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, associated with thymoma and thymic hyperplasia) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels) as type II hypersensitivity, and MS and ADEM as T cell-mediated.

Explain neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes as immune responses to tumor antigens shared with neurons: anti-Hu (small cell lung cancer, sensory neuronopathy, limbic encephalitis), anti-Yo (cerebellar degeneration), and anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (ovarian teratoma).

Explain how conjugate polysaccharide vaccines against H. influenzae type b, S. pneumoniae, and N. meningitidis produce T cell-dependent responses, and compare inactivated (Salk) with live oral (Sabin) polio vaccines for mucosal IgA immunity.

Compare the morphology and capsule-based virulence of Streptococcus pneumoniae (gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci), Neisseria meningitidis (gram-negative diplococci with lipooligosaccharide endotoxin), and Haemophilus influenzae type b (gram-negative coccobacillus with polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule).

Describe the neonatal meningitis pathogens Streptococcus agalactiae (group B, maternal vaginal colonization), Escherichia coli with the K1 capsule, and Listeria monocytogenes (gram-positive rod, tumbling motility, actin-based cell spread, unpasteurized dairy and deli meats).

Contrast botulinum toxin (cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking acetylcholine release and causing flaccid paralysis) with tetanospasmin (retrograde transport to spinal inhibitory interneurons, blocking GABA and glycine release and causing spastic paralysis).

Describe DNA viruses of the nervous system: herpesviruses (enveloped dsDNA, latency in sensory ganglia, spread along axons) and JC polyomavirus (nonenveloped dsDNA, latent in the kidney, reactivated in immunosuppression).

Describe RNA viruses of the nervous system: enteroviruses (nonenveloped positive-sense picornaviruses, fecal-oral), West Nile virus (flavivirus spread by Culex mosquitoes from bird reservoirs), and rabies virus (bullet-shaped negative-sense rhabdovirus, retrograde axonal transport).

Identify Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated yeast in pigeon droppings, seen with India ink, detected by capsular antigen), Mucor and Rhizopus (broad nonseptate hyphae favored by ketoacidosis), and Coccidioides (spherules, southwestern US soil).

Compare Treponema pallidum (spirochete detected with darkfield, VDRL, and FTA-ABS), Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete spread by Ixodes ticks), and Mycobacterium leprae (acid-fast, prefers cooler body sites, infects Schwann cells, armadillo reservoir in the US).

Distinguish thrombotic cerebral infarction (atherosclerosis at the carotid bifurcation, MCA, or basilar artery) from embolic infarction (cardiac sources such as atrial fibrillation, often with hemorrhagic conversion) and lacunar infarcts from hypertensive arteriolosclerosis.

Describe the time course of cerebral infarction: red neurons by 12 to 24 hours, neutrophils in the first days, macrophages clearing debris over weeks, and reactive gliosis around a fluid-filled cyst from liquefactive necrosis.

Distinguish ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and transient ischemic attack by mechanism, list shared risk factors (hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia), and explain why noncontrast CT is used first to exclude hemorrhage.

Explain global hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, identifying the most vulnerable neurons (hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, neocortical pyramidal cells with laminar necrosis) and watershed infarcts between arterial territories after severe hypotension.

Compare epidural hematoma (middle meningeal artery tear with temporal bone fracture, lucid interval, biconvex and limited by sutures) with subdural hematoma (bridging vein tear in elderly, alcohol use, or shaken infants, crescent-shaped and crossing sutures).

Explain subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured saccular aneurysm, most often near the anterior communicating artery, with sudden worst headache and xanthochromic CSF, risk factors ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and complications vasospasm and hydrocephalus.

Explain hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum, and contrast it with lobar hemorrhage from cerebral amyloid angiopathy in older adults.

Describe the spinal cord blood supply (one anterior and two posterior spinal arteries, artery of Adamkiewicz) and predict anterior spinal artery syndrome after aortic surgery or dissection: paralysis and loss of pain and temperature with vibration and position sense spared.

Describe arteriovenous malformations (tangles of arteries draining directly into veins without a capillary bed) and other vascular malformations as causes of intracerebral hemorrhage and seizures in young adults.

Explain carotid and vertebral artery dissection as a cause of stroke in young adults after neck trauma, and subclavian steal syndrome (proximal subclavian stenosis reversing vertebral flow, with arm claudication and unequal arm blood pressures).

Explain cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in hypercoagulable states such as pregnancy and estrogen use, and hypertensive encephalopathy and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome as vasogenic edema, mainly of posterior white matter, during severe hypertension.

Explain Alzheimer disease pathogenesis: amyloid precursor protein cleavage by beta and gamma secretase into amyloid beta plaques, hyperphosphorylated tau tangles, and risk from age, APOE e4, Down syndrome, and APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutations.

Identify Alzheimer disease findings: cortical atrophy with hydrocephalus ex vacuo, hippocampal involvement, neuritic plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid angiopathy, and a course beginning with short-term memory loss.

Explain ALS as degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons (some familial cases with SOD1 or C9orf72 mutations) causing mixed UMN and LMN signs with sensation, bladder control, and eye movements spared, and death from respiratory failure.

Explain Parkinson disease as loss of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies, causing resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability, and identify secondary parkinsonism from MPTP and dopamine-blocking drugs.

Explain Huntington disease as an autosomal dominant CAG expansion in HTT on chromosome 4 with caudate atrophy and GABAergic neuron loss, causing chorea, dementia, and depression in midlife, with anticipation through paternal transmission.

Explain Friedreich ataxia (autosomal recessive GAA expansion in frataxin, mitochondrial iron accumulation) as spinocerebellar degeneration of dorsal columns, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes, kyphoscoliosis, and pes cavus.

Explain Guillain-Barré syndrome as acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy after infection, causing ascending symmetric flaccid weakness with areflexia, and complications of respiratory failure and autonomic instability.

Describe multiple sclerosis risk factors (women aged 20 to 40, higher latitude), relapsing-remitting course, and findings including optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss, heat-worsened symptoms, and periventricular MRI plaques.
Distinguish acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (monophasic, mostly in children, after viral infection or rarely vaccination, perivenular demyelination) from relapsing multiple sclerosis.

Distinguish dementia with Lewy bodies (cortical Lewy bodies, visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism), frontotemporal dementia (early personality change, tau Pick bodies or TDP-43 inclusions), and progressive supranuclear palsy (tau, vertical gaze palsy, early falls).

Distinguish vascular dementia (stepwise decline after multiple infarcts or diffuse small vessel disease) and mild cognitive impairment (measurable decline with daily function preserved) from Alzheimer disease.
Describe transverse myelitis as acute inflammation across a spinal cord segment, often after infection or with MS, causing bilateral weakness, a sensory level, and bladder dysfunction.

Distinguish essential tremor (often familial, postural and action tremor that may improve with alcohol) from parkinsonian resting tremor and cerebellar intention tremor, and describe cervical dystonia (torticollis) as sustained involuntary neck muscle contraction.

Compare vasogenic edema (blood-brain barrier disruption from tumor, abscess, or trauma), cytotoxic edema (cell swelling from ischemia or hypoxia), and interstitial edema (hydrocephalus), and predict papilledema, Cushing triad, and herniation as complications.

Distinguish noncommunicating hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker, tumor) from communicating hydrocephalus (arachnoid granulation scarring after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage) and from hydrocephalus ex vacuo, and explain head enlargement in infants.

Describe normal pressure hydrocephalus in older adults as enlarged ventricles without consistently raised opening pressure, causing urinary incontinence, magnetic gait, and dementia that may improve after CSF drainage.

Describe idiopathic intracranial hypertension in obese women of childbearing age (headache, papilledema, vision loss, CN VI palsy, normal imaging, raised opening pressure) and its associations with vitamin A excess and tetracyclines.

Explain hepatic encephalopathy from ammonia and other gut-derived toxins bypassing the liver in cirrhosis or portosystemic shunts, its precipitants (GI bleeding, infection, high protein intake, constipation, hypokalemia), and findings of confusion and asterixis.

Classify peripheral neuropathy by pattern (distal symmetric, mononeuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex) and by axonal or demyelinating injury, and list major causes: diabetes, alcohol, B12 and thiamine deficiency, vasculitis, leprosy, HIV, and neurotoxic chemotherapy.

Explain diabetic neuropathy (sorbitol accumulation, advanced glycation end products, microvascular injury) and its findings: stocking-glove sensory loss, autonomic dysfunction (gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension), neuropathic foot ulcers, and pupil-sparing CN III palsy.

Identify causes of B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia, strict vegan diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease, Diphyllobothrium latum) and its neurologic findings: subacute combined degeneration with lost vibration and position sense, positive Romberg sign, spasticity, neuropathy, and dementia.

Explain Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and its progression to Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia with confabulation), with mammillary body and medial thalamic damage, in alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, or hyperemesis.

Describe Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease as a group of inherited motor and sensory neuropathies (most often autosomal dominant PMP22 duplication) causing distal weakness, foot drop, pes cavus, and hammer toes.

Explain osmotic demyelination syndrome after overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, with demyelination of the central pons causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and possible locked-in syndrome.

Describe the neurologic and associated features of Down syndrome: intellectual disability, hypotonia, early-onset Alzheimer disease, atlantoaxial instability, and associated duodenal atresia, atrioventricular septal defects, and increased leukemia risk.

Compare the leukodystrophies: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1, very long chain fatty acid buildup from impaired peroxisomal oxidation, adrenal insufficiency), metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A, sulfatides), and Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase, globoid cells).

Explain phenylketonuria as autosomal recessive phenylalanine hydroxylase or BH4 deficiency, making tyrosine essential, and relate phenylalanine buildup to intellectual disability, seizures, musty odor, fair skin, and microcephaly in infants of untreated mothers.

Distinguish Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A, GM2 ganglioside, cherry-red macula, no hepatosplenomegaly) from Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase, cherry-red macula with hepatosplenomegaly and foam cells).

Describe the neurologic features of Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, painful neuropathy, angiokeratomas, early stroke), Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase, neuronopathic types 2 and 3), and Hurler (alpha-L-iduronidase, corneal clouding) versus Hunter syndrome (X-linked, no corneal clouding).

Explain Wilson disease as autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation impairing biliary copper excretion, with low ceruloplasmin, copper deposits in the basal ganglia causing tremor, dystonia, and psychiatric change, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and liver disease.

Describe fragile X syndrome (FMR1 CGG expansion with hypermethylation and silencing) as the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, with autism features, long face, large ears, and macroorchidism.

Explain maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, sweet urine odor, neonatal encephalopathy) and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (X-linked hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria) as inborn errors that injure the brain.

Explain acute intermittent porphyria (autosomal dominant porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency) with attacks of abdominal pain, neuropathy, and psychiatric symptoms, elevated urine porphobilinogen, and triggers such as alcohol, fasting, and cytochrome P450 inducers.
Identify causes of congenital microcephaly, including congenital Zika, cytomegalovirus, rubella, and toxoplasma infection, fetal alcohol syndrome, and maternal phenylketonuria.

Describe medulloblastoma as the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood: a small round blue cell tumor of the cerebellum with Homer Wright rosettes that can block the fourth ventricle and seed the CSF as drop metastases.

Describe meningioma as a dural-based extra-axial tumor of arachnoid cap cells, common in adult women, with whorls and psammoma bodies, associations with NF2 and prior radiation, and seizures or focal deficits from compression.

Describe neuroblastoma as a neural crest tumor of young children, usually in the adrenal medulla, presenting as an abdominal mass with elevated urinary HVA and VMA, Homer Wright rosettes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, and worse prognosis with MYCN amplification.

Describe glioblastoma as the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults: an IDH-wildtype astrocytic tumor that can cross the corpus callosum, with pseudopalisading necrosis, microvascular proliferation, GFAP staining, and poor survival.

Distinguish pilocytic astrocytoma (children, cerebellum, cystic with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers, BRAF alteration, good prognosis) from IDH-mutant diffuse astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma (frontal lobe, fried-egg cells, chicken-wire capillaries, calcification, seizures).

Describe neuronal and mixed neuronal-glial tumors such as ganglioglioma, a slow-growing temporal lobe tumor of children and young adults that presents with seizures, and central neurocytoma within the lateral ventricles.

Describe schwannoma (S-100 positive Schwann cells, Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies and Antoni B areas) and predict hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance from a vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle, bilateral in NF2.

Describe neurofibromatosis type 1: café-au-lait macules, cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas with risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, and pheochromocytoma.

Describe brain metastases as the most common intracranial tumors in adults (from lung, breast, melanoma, and other primaries, often at the gray-white junction) and primary CNS lymphoma (diffuse large B cell, EBV-related in AIDS).
Describe retinoblastoma (leukocoria in young children, bilateral in hereditary RB1 cases, later osteosarcoma risk) and uveal melanoma as the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults.

Describe the CNS lesions of tuberous sclerosis (cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma, seizures, with ash-leaf spots and cardiac rhabdomyoma) and von Hippel-Lindau disease (cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma).

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe arboviral encephalitis (West Nile, St. Louis, and eastern and western equine encephalitis viruses) transmitted by mosquitoes from bird reservoirs, with humans as dead-end hosts, and West Nile acute flaccid paralysis in older adults.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Distinguish foodborne botulism (preformed toxin), infant botulism (ingested spores, honey, floppy baby with constipation), and wound botulism, all causing descending symmetric flaccid paralysis starting with cranial nerves, without fever or sensory loss.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Explain brain abscess spread from contiguous infection (sinusitis, otitis, mastoiditis, dental) or hematogenous seeding (endocarditis, lung infection, right-to-left cardiac shunts), common organisms (streptococci, staphylococci, anaerobes), and a ring-enhancing lesion with fever and focal deficits.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe the histology of viral encephalitis (perivascular lymphocytic cuffs, microglial nodules, neuronophagia), and rabies acquired from bat, raccoon, or dog bites, with Negri bodies, agitation, and hydrophobia.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe parasitic CNS infection: Toxoplasma gondii (ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS), Taenia solium neurocysticercosis (ingested eggs, brain cysts, seizures), and Naegleria fowleri (freshwater exposure, cribriform plate entry, rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis).

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS (raised opening pressure, positive capsular antigen) and rhinocerebral mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis (necrotic nasal or palatal eschar spreading to the orbit and brain).

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Distinguish CNS herpesvirus diseases: HSV-1 hemorrhagic temporal lobe encephalitis, HSV-2 meningitis and neonatal encephalitis, CMV encephalitis in advanced AIDS and congenital periventricular calcifications, and EBV-associated primary CNS lymphoma.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Compare tuberculoid leprosy (strong Th1 response, few bacilli, few anesthetic hypopigmented plaques, thickened nerves) with lepromatous leprosy (Th2 response, many bacilli, leonine facies, symmetric glove-and-stocking neuropathy).

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Identify the common causes of bacterial meningitis by age: group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria in neonates; S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis in children and adults; and S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and Listeria in older adults.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe the findings and complications of meningitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, petechial rash in meningococcemia, sensorineural hearing loss, hydrocephalus, seizures), including tuberculous basilar meningitis with cranial nerve palsies.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe neurosyphilis forms in tertiary syphilis: meningovascular disease, general paresis, and tabes dorsalis (dorsal column and root degeneration with sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, Argyll Robertson pupils, and Charcot joints), with CSF VDRL testing.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Explain poliomyelitis as fecal-oral enterovirus infection that spreads to and destroys anterior horn motor neurons, causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis, fasciculations, and areflexia without sensory loss, and later post-polio syndrome.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Explain prion disease as conversion of normal alpha-helical PrP into protease-resistant beta-pleated PrP (sporadic, inherited, or acquired, including variant CJD from bovine prions), causing rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and spongiform change without inflammation.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Explain PML as JC virus reactivation in severe immunosuppression (AIDS, natalizumab, rituximab), causing lytic oligodendrocyte infection with multifocal white matter demyelination and rapidly progressive deficits.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe subacute sclerosing panencephalitis as a persistent defective measles virus infection appearing years after early childhood measles, causing progressive cognitive decline and myoclonus with high CSF anti-measles antibody levels.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe tetanus after spores enter a contaminated wound or the umbilical stump in neonates, causing trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, and spastic paralysis, and explain prevention by toxoid immunization.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Explain VZV latency in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and reactivation as dermatomal herpes zoster, including herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear vesicles), and postherpetic neuralgia.

Unit name: Infections of the CNS and PNS
Competency: Describe Lyme neuroborreliosis (facial nerve palsy, often bilateral, lymphocytic meningitis, radiculopathy) and leptospirosis acquired from water contaminated by animal urine as spirochetal causes of meningitis.

Describe concussion as trauma-induced transient neurologic dysfunction without structural imaging changes, postconcussion syndrome, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (dementia pugilistica) with tau deposits after repeated head injury.

Explain coup and contrecoup contusions at the frontal and temporal poles and diffuse axonal injury from acceleration-deceleration shearing, which causes axonal swellings and coma without a mass lesion.

Predict the progression of an expanding traumatic hematoma: rising intracranial pressure, uncal herniation with an ipsilateral dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis, secondary Duret hemorrhages in the brainstem, and death without decompression.

Explain the phases of spinal cord transection, from spinal shock (flaccid paralysis, areflexia, neurogenic hypotension) to spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia, and predict ventilator-dependent quadriplegia at or above C3 (phrenic roots C3 to C5) versus paraplegia from thoracic injury.

Distinguish spinal cord compression (back pain, sensory level, upper motor neuron signs) from cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, lost anal reflex, lower motor neuron signs), caused by metastasis, epidural abscess, or central disc herniation.

Explain Bell palsy as idiopathic lower motor neuron CN VII palsy linked to HSV reactivation, diabetes, pregnancy, and Lyme disease, with whole-face ipsilateral weakness, hyperacusis, loss of anterior tongue taste, and reduced tearing.

Explain carpal tunnel syndrome as median nerve compression under the flexor retinaculum (risks: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, dialysis amyloid), with nocturnal thumb-to-ring finger paresthesia, thenar atrophy, Tinel and Phalen signs, and spared palm sensation.

Explain disc herniation as nucleus pulposus protruding through a torn annulus fibrosus, usually posterolaterally at L4 to L5 or L5 to S1, and predict that it compresses the lower root (for example, an L4 to L5 disc affects L5).
Explain radiculopathy from nerve root entrapment by disc, osteophytes, or foraminal narrowing, and predict the dermatomal pain, weakness, and reflex loss of C6, C7, L4, L5, and S1 root lesions.
Describe sciatica as radiating pain from the buttock down the posterior thigh below the knee, usually from L5 or S1 root compression by disc herniation, reproduced by a straight leg raise test.

Explain thoracic outlet syndrome as compression of the lower brachial plexus trunk (C8 to T1), subclavian artery, or vein by a cervical rib or scalene muscles, with ulnar-side hand paresthesia, intrinsic hand weakness, and vascular symptoms.

Explain trigeminal neuralgia as paroxysmal unilateral lancinating facial pain in the V2 or V3 distribution triggered by touch or chewing, usually from vascular compression of the nerve root, and as a sign of MS in younger patients.

Predict the findings of cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve at the elbow, fourth and fifth finger paresthesia, intrinsic weakness), tarsal tunnel syndrome (tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus, sole paresthesia), and common fibular compression at the fibular neck (foot drop).

Describe lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication (leg pain worse with standing and extension, relieved by sitting or flexion) and cervical stenosis causing myelopathy with upper motor neuron signs.

Describe complex regional pain syndrome (burning pain, allodynia, swelling, and skin and temperature changes after limb injury, with type II following a nerve injury) and phantom limb pain after amputation.

Describe blepharitis (anterior from staphylococcal or seborrheic disease, posterior from meibomian gland dysfunction), and distinguish a painful hordeolum (acute gland infection, usually S. aureus) from a painless chalazion (meibomian lipogranuloma).

Explain cataract as lens protein opacification, with risks of age, diabetes (sorbitol), galactosemia (galactitol), corticosteroids, UV light, smoking, and congenital rubella, causing painless progressive blurred vision, glare, and loss of the red reflex.

Distinguish viral conjunctivitis (adenovirus, watery discharge, preauricular node), bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent; hyperacute with N. gonorrhoeae), chlamydial conjunctivitis and trachoma, and allergic conjunctivitis (type I hypersensitivity, itching).

Explain glaucoma as optic neuropathy with disc cupping, and contrast open-angle glaucoma (impaired trabecular outflow, painless peripheral vision loss) with acute angle-closure glaucoma (painful red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, halos, nausea).
Describe keratitis (HSV dendritic ulcer; Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba in contact lens wearers; corneal ulcer risk) and iritis or anterior uveitis (ciliary flush, photophobia, small irregular pupil).

Distinguish dry macular degeneration (drusen, gradual central vision loss) from wet macular degeneration (VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization, rapid central loss, distortion), with age and smoking as risk factors.
Relate anterior uveitis to HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, sarcoidosis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and posterior uveitis and chorioretinitis to toxoplasmosis and CMV retinitis in AIDS.
Explain Ménière disease as endolymphatic hydrops causing episodic vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.

Explain acute otitis media (S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis) from eustachian tube dysfunction in children, otitis media with effusion, and complications including perforation, mastoiditis, cholesteatoma, and conductive hearing loss.

Distinguish otitis externa (Pseudomonas or S. aureus, pain with tragal pressure) from malignant otitis externa (Pseudomonas skull base osteomyelitis in older diabetics, cranial nerve palsies) and auricular perichondritis after cartilage piercing.

Distinguish vestibular neuritis (acute continuous vertigo for days with normal hearing), labyrinthitis (vertigo with hearing loss), and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (otoconia in the posterior canal, brief positional vertigo, positive Dix-Hallpike test).

Distinguish central retinal artery occlusion (sudden painless monocular loss, pale retina, cherry-red spot), amaurosis fugax from carotid emboli, and central retinal vein occlusion (retinal hemorrhages and venous engorgement).

Identify findings of hypertensive retinopathy (arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots), diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms, hard exudates, neovascularization), and papilledema from raised intracranial pressure.

Describe retinal detachment (flashes, floaters, curtain-like vision loss, myopia as a risk) and retinitis pigmentosa (inherited photoreceptor degeneration with night blindness, peripheral vision loss, and bone spicule pigment).
Explain myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, and presbyopia (age-related loss of lens elasticity), and relate childhood strabismus to amblyopia from cortical suppression of the deviating eye.

Distinguish conductive hearing loss (cerumen impaction, tympanic membrane perforation, barotrauma, eustachian tube dysfunction, otosclerosis with stapes fixation, cholesteatoma) from sensorineural loss (presbycusis, noise-induced hair cell damage), and relate both to tinnitus.

Distinguish preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis from orbital cellulitis (pain with eye movement, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, usually from ethmoid sinusitis), and describe dacryocystitis and endophthalmitis.
Describe pterygium as UV-related fibrovascular conjunctival growth onto the cornea, and lens dislocation in Marfan syndrome (usually upward) and homocystinuria (usually downward).

Describe eye injuries: corneal abrasion and foreign body (fluorescein uptake), hyphema, subconjunctival hemorrhage, orbital floor fracture with inferior rectus entrapment limiting upward gaze, and alkali burns causing liquefactive necrosis.
Describe the sequence of pronephros, mesonephros, and metanephros, and identify the metanephros, appearing in the fifth week, as the source of the permanent kidney.

Explain how reciprocal induction between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme forms the collecting system (collecting ducts, calyces, pelvis, ureter) and the nephron (Bowman capsule to distal convoluted tubule), and predict renal agenesis when induction fails.
Describe the ascent of the kidneys from the pelvis to the lumbar region, and explain how fusion of the lower poles produces a horseshoe kidney trapped beneath the inferior mesenteric artery.
Explain how early splitting of the ureteric bud or formation of two buds produces a bifid or duplex ureter, and relate an ectopic ureteral orifice to obstruction or reflux.

Trace partition of the cloaca by the urorectal septum into the urogenital sinus and anorectal canal, and predict a patent urachus (urine draining from the umbilicus) or urachal cyst from failed allantois obliteration.
Explain how posterior urethral valves in male infants obstruct urine outflow, and predict bilateral hydronephrosis, a distended bladder, and oligohydramnios.

Describe the three layers of the glomerular filtration barrier (fenestrated endothelium, basement membrane with type IV collagen and negatively charged heparan sulfate, podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms) and predict albuminuria when charge or foot processes are lost.

Identify the components of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole, macula densa of the distal thick ascending limb, extraglomerular mesangial cells) and the supporting and phagocytic roles of intraglomerular mesangial cells.

Distinguish proximal tubule (cuboidal cells with brush border and abundant mitochondria), thin limb (simple squamous), distal tubule (cuboidal without brush border), and collecting duct (principal and intercalated cells) epithelium, and relate high proximal tubule energy demand to ischemic injury.
Distinguish cortical from juxtamedullary nephrons by glomerulus position, loop of Henle length, and vasa recta supply, and relate long loops to urine concentrating ability.

Describe urothelium (transitional epithelium with umbrella cells), the lamina propria, and the detrusor muscle, and explain how the urothelium stretches during bladder filling while remaining impermeable to urine.

Locate the kidneys in the retroperitoneum from about T12 to L3, explain why the right kidney lies lower than the left, and identify posterior relations (diaphragm, 12th rib, psoas major, quadratus lumborum).
Identify the anterior relations of the right kidney (liver, descending duodenum, right colic flexure) and left kidney (stomach, spleen, pancreatic tail, jejunum, left colic flexure).
Describe the renal coverings (fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat) and the anterior to posterior order of hilar structures (renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis).

Trace the ureter along the psoas, across the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, into the bladder wall, and predict that stones lodge at the ureteropelvic junction, pelvic brim, and ureterovesical junction.

Describe the bladder trigone, the ureteric and internal urethral orifices, and the male urethral segments (prostatic, membranous, spongy), and contrast them with the short female urethra and its higher risk of ascending infection.
Predict the site of male urethral injury from a pelvic fracture (posterior urethra at the membranous segment) versus a straddle injury (bulbous part of the spongy urethra).

Unit name: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity
Competency: Distinguish the retroperitoneal kidneys and ureters from the extraperitoneal bladder, and explain why dome rupture of a full bladder leaks urine into the peritoneal cavity while pelvic fracture causes extraperitoneal extravasation.

Unit name: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity
Competency: Describe the peritoneal reflections over the bladder, including the rectovesical pouch in males and the vesicouterine and rectouterine pouches in females.

Unit name: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity
Competency: Explain why ureteral colic radiates from the flank to the groin, relating the pain to visceral afferents that enter the lower thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord.

Unit name: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity
Competency: Relate the posterior position of the kidney against the 12th rib and posterior abdominal wall to costovertebral angle tenderness in pyelonephritis and to the spread of a perinephric abscess within the renal fascia.

Unit name: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity
Competency: Explain why the ureter is at risk during hysterectomy, where it passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix, and predict hydronephrosis or urine leak after ligation or transection.

Unit name: Urinary system in the abdominopelvic cavity
Competency: Relate pelvic floor and urethral support to stress incontinence and cystocele, and distinguish stress, urge (detrusor overactivity), and overflow incontinence by mechanism.

Trace renal blood flow from the renal artery through segmental, interlobar, arcuate, and cortical radiate arteries, afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, and peritubular capillaries or vasa recta to the renal vein.
Explain why segmental and interlobar arteries behave as end arteries, and predict a wedge-shaped cortical infarct after embolic occlusion.
Predict how afferent versus efferent arteriolar constriction or dilation changes renal plasma flow, GFR, and filtration fraction.
Explain renal autoregulation of blood flow and GFR by the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback through the macula densa.
Explain how slow vasa recta flow and its countercurrent arrangement preserve medullary hypertonicity, and relate the low medullary oxygen tension to papillary necrosis and sickling in the vasa recta.

Describe the course of the left renal vein between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery and its gonadal tributary, and predict a left varicocele when renal cell carcinoma invades the left renal vein.
Explain how glomerular capillary hydrostatic and oncotic pressures and Bowman space pressure set GFR, and predict the GFR change with ureteral obstruction, hypoalbuminemia, and dehydration.

Calculate clearance (urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration), GFR from inulin or creatinine, effective renal plasma flow from PAH, and filtration fraction, and interpret clearance above or below GFR as net secretion or reabsorption.

Describe proximal tubule reabsorption (about two thirds of filtered sodium and water, nearly all glucose and amino acids, Na+/H+ exchange) and thick ascending limb transport (Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransport, water impermeability, paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption).
Explain how aldosterone acts on principal cells (ENaC, Na+/K+-ATPase, K+ secretion), ADH inserts aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct, and PTH increases distal tubule calcium reabsorption.

Explain countercurrent multiplication and ADH-dependent urine concentration, and distinguish central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, SIADH, and primary polydipsia by serum sodium, urine osmolality, and response to water deprivation and desmopressin.

Predict changes in extracellular and intracellular fluid volume and osmolality after isotonic, hypotonic, and hypertonic fluid gain or loss, and apply them to dehydration, hypovolemia, and volume overload.

Describe the micturition reflex (pelvic parasympathetic detrusor contraction, sympathetic and pudendal sphincter control, pontine micturition center), and predict a reflex spastic bladder above the sacral cord versus a flaccid overflow bladder at the sacral cord.

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Explain how the proximal tubule reclaims filtered bicarbonate using carbonic anhydrase and Na+/H+ exchange, and how the kidney generates new bicarbonate by excreting H+ as titratable acid (mainly phosphate) and as ammonium made from glutamine in the proximal tubule.

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Interpret arterial blood gases to classify metabolic and respiratory acidosis and alkalosis, judge compensation (Winters formula, acute versus chronic renal compensation), and identify mixed disturbances.

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Calculate the anion gap and distinguish high anion gap metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, uremia, methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates) from normal anion gap acidosis (diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis).

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Distinguish renal tubular acidosis type 1 (distal, urine pH above 5.5, hypokalemia, calcium phosphate stones), type 2 (proximal bicarbonate wasting, hypokalemia, Fanconi syndrome), and type 4 (hypoaldosteronism, hyperkalemia).

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Explain how vomiting causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, and why volume depletion and aldosterone maintain it and produce paradoxical aciduria.

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Trace renin release (low perfusion pressure at juxtaglomerular cells, low NaCl at the macula densa, beta-1 sympathetic input) through angiotensin II and aldosterone actions, and contrast the opposing effects of atrial natriuretic peptide.

Unit name: Kidney in acid-base and blood pressure control
Competency: Explain pressure natriuresis as the kidney's long-term control of arterial pressure, and predict hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin in primary hyperaldosteronism.

Explain sodium-coupled (SGLT2) glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule with a transport maximum, and predict glucosuria and osmotic diuresis when plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold (about 200 mg/dL) in diabetes mellitus.
Distinguish glomerular proteinuria (albumin), overflow proteinuria (Bence Jones light chains), and tubular proteinuria (failed proximal reabsorption of small filtered proteins).

Describe PTH and low phosphate stimulation of vitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylation in the proximal tubule, predict serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH in chronic kidney disease, primary hyperparathyroidism, and vitamin D deficiency, and explain refractory hypocalcemia in hypomagnesemia.

Explain potassium shifts into cells (insulin, beta-adrenergic stimulation, alkalosis) and out of cells (acidosis, cell lysis, insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality), and predict ECG findings of hyperkalemia (peaked T waves, wide QRS) and hypokalemia (U waves).

Describe erythropoietin release by renal peritubular interstitial cells in response to hypoxia, and relate it to normocytic anemia in chronic kidney disease and secondary polycythemia in renal cell carcinoma.

Explain how NAD+-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase starts the conversion of ethylene glycol to glycolic and oxalic acids, producing high anion gap metabolic acidosis, an osmolal gap, calcium oxalate crystals in urine, and acute tubular injury.

Explain the hyperlipidemia of nephrotic syndrome (increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis and reduced lipoprotein catabolism) and identify lipiduria as oval fat bodies and fatty casts showing Maltese cross birefringence under polarized light.

Explain how autosomal dominant PKD1 (polycystin-1, chromosome 16) and PKD2 (polycystin-2, chromosome 4) mutations and autosomal recessive PKHD1 (fibrocystin) mutations cause polycystic kidney disease, and predict inheritance in a pedigree.

Explain how mutations in the alpha-3, alpha-4, or alpha-5 chains of type IV collagen (most often X-linked COL4A5) cause Alport syndrome, and how heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 mutations cause thin basement membrane disease.

Explain two-hit loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3p, with HIF stabilization driving VEGF expression, in sporadic clear cell renal carcinoma and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (bilateral renal carcinoma, hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma).
Relate WT1 loss on chromosome 11p13 to Wilms tumor in WAGR and Denys-Drash syndromes, and 11p15 imprinting defects to Wilms tumor in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome.

Explain how TSC1 or TSC2 mutations in tuberous sclerosis remove hamartin and tuberin inhibition of mTOR growth signaling, and relate this to renal angiomyolipomas (blood vessels, smooth muscle, fat) and renal cysts.

Explain how an autosomal recessive defect in the proximal tubule transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine causes cystinuria with hexagonal cystine stones and a positive cyanide-nitroprusside test.
Explain how X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency in Fabry disease causes globotriaosylceramide accumulation, with angiokeratomas, painful neuropathy, hypohidrosis, and progressive renal failure.

Classify glomerular injury as type II hypersensitivity (anti-GBM antibodies to the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, linear IgG, with lung hemorrhage in Goodpasture syndrome), type III immune complex disease (granular deposits), or pauci-immune ANCA disease, and name an example of each.

Interpret serum complement in glomerular disease: low C3 in poststreptococcal and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis, low C3 and C4 in lupus nephritis, and normal levels in IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, and ANCA vasculitis.

Distinguish granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA, necrotizing granulomas of the upper and lower airways, glomerulonephritis) from microscopic polyangiitis (MPO-ANCA, no granulomas), and contrast polyarteritis nodosa, which spares glomeruli and causes renal artery microaneurysms.

Describe IgA vasculitis in children (IgA immune complex deposition after an upper respiratory infection, palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs, arthralgia, abdominal pain, intussusception) and its mesangial IgA glomerulonephritis.

Describe urinary tract defenses (one-way urine flow, complete bladder emptying, the flap-valve ureterovesical junction, urothelial shedding) and predict how obstruction, reflux, catheters, and pregnancy increase infection risk.

Explain how CD8+ T cells recognize renal cell carcinoma antigens on MHC class I and NK cells kill tumor cells that lose MHC class I, and how tumors evade immunity through PD-L1 expression and MHC class I downregulation.

Explain how the recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine induces protective anti-HBs antibodies, interpret anti-HBs alone as vaccine immunity, and relate vaccination to prevention of hepatitis B associated membranous nephropathy.

Describe uropathogenic Escherichia coli (gram-negative lactose-fermenting rod from fecal flora) as the most common urinary pathogen, and relate type 1 fimbriae to cystitis and P fimbriae to pyelonephritis.

Identify Staphylococcus saprophyticus (coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant, young sexually active women), Klebsiella (mucoid capsule), Enterococcus, and Pseudomonas (catheter-associated) as other urinary pathogens.

Explain how Proteus mirabilis urease splits urea to ammonia, raising urine pH and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) staghorn calculi, and relate swarming motility to its identification.

Interpret urine dipstick and microscopy in infection: leukocyte esterase for pyuria, nitrite from Enterobacterales nitrate reductase, WBC casts for kidney involvement, and sterile pyuria suggesting urethritis or renal tuberculosis.

Compare Neisseria gonorrhoeae (gram-negative diplococcus, pili with antigenic variation, IgA protease) and Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K (obligate intracellular, elementary and reticulate bodies) as causes of urethritis, and identify nucleic acid amplification as the diagnostic test.

Relate infections to glomerular disease: nephritogenic group A streptococci to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, hepatitis B to membranous nephropathy, hepatitis C to membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with cryoglobulinemia, and HIV to collapsing FSGS.

Describe hematogenous renal tuberculosis with caseating granulomas and sterile pyuria, and the Schistosoma haematobium life cycle (snail host, skin-penetrating cercariae, adults in vesical venules, terminal-spined eggs) leading to hematuria and bladder squamous cell carcinoma.

Distinguish nephritic syndrome (hematuria with RBC casts, hypertension, oliguria, azotemia, proteinuria under 3.5 g/day) from nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, hyperlipidemia, fatty casts).

Interpret urinary findings to localize disease: RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs (glomerulonephritis), WBC casts (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis), muddy brown granular casts (acute tubular necrosis), fatty casts (nephrotic syndrome), and waxy casts (chronic kidney disease).

Describe poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis: onset weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis or impetigo, cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, low C3, granular IgG and C3 deposits, and subepithelial humps on electron microscopy.

Distinguish IgA nephropathy (episodic gross hematuria within days of a mucosal infection, mesangial IgA deposits) from poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis by timing of hematuria after infection and complement level.

Classify rapidly progressive (crescentic) glomerulonephritis by immunofluorescence into anti-GBM (linear), immune complex (granular), and pauci-immune (ANCA) types, and identify crescents of fibrin, parietal epithelial cells, and macrophages.

Describe lupus nephritis, with diffuse proliferative disease (subendothelial wire-loop deposits, nephritic picture) as the most common and most severe class and membranous disease causing nephrotic syndrome, and interpret low complement and anti-dsDNA antibodies.

Describe membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (mesangial proliferation, tram-track basement membrane duplication), with immune complex disease linked to hepatitis B and C and dense deposit disease (a C3 glomerulopathy) linked to C3 nephritic factor.

Explain diabetic nephropathy: hyperfiltration, nonenzymatic glycation, and hyaline arteriolosclerosis of afferent and efferent arterioles lead to basement membrane thickening and mesangial expansion with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, progressing from microalbuminuria to nephrotic proteinuria and renal failure.

Describe focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (segmental sclerosis with podocyte injury and poor steroid response) and its secondary causes (HIV, heroin use, sickle cell disease, obesity), including the collapsing variant of HIV-associated nephropathy.

Explain the consequences of nephrotic syndrome: edema from hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia from increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis, hypercoagulability from urinary antithrombin III loss (renal vein thrombosis), and infection from immunoglobulin loss.

Describe minimal change disease in children: selective albuminuria, normal light microscopy and immunofluorescence, podocyte foot process effacement on electron microscopy, excellent corticosteroid response, and association with Hodgkin lymphoma.

Describe membranous nephropathy in adults: subepithelial immune deposits with spike and dome basement membrane, anti-PLA2R antibodies in primary disease, and secondary causes (lupus, hepatitis B, solid tumors, drugs such as NSAIDs).

Explain how amyloid deposition in glomeruli causes nephrotic syndrome, and identify AL (light chain) and AA (chronic inflammation) amyloid by apple-green birefringence with Congo red stain under polarized light.

Classify acute kidney injury as prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal, and interpret BUN to creatinine ratio (over 20 prerenal), fractional excretion of sodium (under 1 percent prerenal, over 2 percent tubular necrosis), and urine osmolality.

Identify diabetes and hypertension as the leading causes of chronic kidney disease, and predict its consequences: uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, platelet dysfunction), hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload, hypertension, anemia, and renal osteodystrophy.

Explain ischemic and nephrotoxic acute tubular necrosis, with injury concentrated in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb, tubular cell sloughing that obstructs flow, and muddy brown granular casts.
Describe the initiation, maintenance (oliguria, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, volume overload), and recovery (polyuria with potassium and sodium loss) phases of acute tubular necrosis.

Identify nephrotoxic causes of tubular necrosis (myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis, hemoglobin, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast, cisplatin, ethylene glycol) and predict a dipstick positive for blood without RBCs on microscopy in rhabdomyolysis.

Describe Fanconi syndrome as generalized proximal tubule dysfunction with glucosuria despite normal plasma glucose, aminoaciduria, phosphaturia, and bicarbonaturia (proximal renal tubular acidosis), and identify causes such as cystinosis, Wilson disease, and multiple myeloma.

Identify causes of hydronephrosis by age and sex (posterior urethral valves, ureteropelvic junction obstruction, calculi, pregnancy, prostatic enlargement, pelvic tumors), and explain how persistent obstruction lowers GFR and causes papillary and cortical atrophy.
Predict that unilateral hydronephrosis may stay silent while bilateral obstruction causes postrenal acute kidney injury with oliguria or anuria, and explain postobstructive diuresis after relief.

Classify kidney stones by composition and urine pH: calcium oxalate (most common, hypercalciuria), calcium phosphate (alkaline urine), struvite (urease-producing bacteria, staghorn), uric acid (acidic urine, radiolucent, gout, tumor lysis), and cystine (hexagonal crystals).
Describe renal colic (colicky flank pain radiating to the groin with hematuria) and the complications of calculi, including obstruction, hydronephrosis, and infection above the stone.

Describe drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis as a hypersensitivity reaction days to weeks after drugs such as penicillins, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, and diuretics, presenting with fever, rash, eosinophilia, pyuria with WBC casts, and rising creatinine.

Explain chronic analgesic nephropathy, with long-term combination analgesic use causing chronic interstitial nephritis and papillary necrosis, and identify other causes of papillary necrosis (diabetes, sickle cell disease, severe pyelonephritis, obstruction).

Explain how vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction leads to chronic pyelonephritis, with coarse asymmetric corticomedullary scars over blunted calyces and thyroidization of tubules filled with eosinophilic casts.

Describe xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis as a chronic destructive infection, usually with obstructing stones and Proteus, filled with lipid-laden foamy macrophages that can mimic renal cell carcinoma.
Describe interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome) as chronic pelvic pain with urgency and frequency in the absence of infection, most often in women, with Hunner ulcers in some patients.

Describe Alport syndrome: hematuria progressing to renal failure, sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus, with thinning and splitting (basket-weave) of the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy, and more severe disease in males with X-linked inheritance.

Describe autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease in adults: bilaterally enlarged cystic kidneys, flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, progressive renal failure, hepatic cysts, berry aneurysms with subarachnoid hemorrhage, and mitral valve prolapse.

Distinguish autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (bilateral enlarged kidneys in infancy, Potter sequence, congenital hepatic fibrosis with portal hypertension) from multicystic dysplastic kidney (usually unilateral, noninherited) and acquired cystic disease in long-term dialysis (renal carcinoma risk).

Explain how bilateral renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, flattened facies, limb deformities), while unilateral agenesis or a single kidney leads to compensatory hypertrophy of the other kidney.

Explain how a short intravesical ureteral segment causes primary vesicoureteral reflux, predict recurrent pyelonephritis and reflux nephropathy scarring, and identify the voiding cystourethrogram as the diagnostic study.

Explain how Shiga toxin from enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 damages endothelium in hemolytic uremic syndrome, causing microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury after bloody diarrhea in children, and contrast TTP (ADAMTS13 deficiency).

Distinguish benign nephrosclerosis (hyaline arteriolosclerosis, symmetrically shrunken kidneys with finely granular surfaces) from malignant hypertension (hyperplastic onion-skin arteriolosclerosis, fibrinoid necrosis, flea-bitten kidney, acute renal failure).

Distinguish atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (older adults, ostial or proximal lesion) from fibromuscular dysplasia (young women, string of beads), and explain renin-driven hypertension, an abdominal bruit, and atrophy of the affected kidney.
Describe renal infarction from emboli (atrial fibrillation, mural thrombus, endocarditis) or arterial thrombosis, producing a pale wedge-shaped coagulative infarct with flank pain and hematuria.

Explain how the hypoxic, hypertonic, acidic renal medulla promotes sickling in the vasa recta, and predict isosthenuria, hematuria, and papillary necrosis in sickle cell disease and sickle cell trait.

Identify causes of renal vein thrombosis (nephrotic syndrome, especially membranous nephropathy; renal cell carcinoma invading the vein; dehydration in infants) and predict flank pain, hematuria, and an enlarged kidney.

Describe clear cell renal cell carcinoma: proximal tubule origin, golden-yellow cut surface, lipid- and glycogen-filled clear cells, risk factors (smoking, obesity, hypertension, acquired cystic disease), and spread into the renal vein and inferior vena cava.

Predict renal cell carcinoma presentations: hematuria, flank pain, and a flank mass, plus paraneoplastic polycythemia (erythropoietin), hypercalcemia (PTHrP), and hypertension (renin), and hematogenous spread to lung and bone.

Distinguish papillary renal cell carcinoma (trisomy 7 and 17, papillae with foamy macrophages) and chromophobe carcinoma (intercalated cell origin) from clear cell carcinoma, and identify oncocytoma as a benign mitochondria-rich tumor.

Describe Wilms tumor in children aged 2 to 5 years: a large unilateral flank mass, often with hematuria or hypertension, triphasic histology (blastema, stroma, epithelium), and associated syndromes (WAGR, Denys-Drash, Beckwith-Wiedemann).

Describe urothelial carcinoma of the bladder and collecting system: painless hematuria, multifocal recurrence, flat carcinoma in situ versus papillary tumors, and risk factors (smoking, aromatic amine dyes, cyclophosphamide, phenacetin).
Relate bladder squamous cell carcinoma to Schistosoma haematobium infection and chronic irritation, and bladder adenocarcinoma to urachal remnants and bladder exstrophy.

Describe acute pyelonephritis: mostly ascending infection, fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, WBC casts, and neutrophilic infiltration of the interstitium and tubules, with complications of papillary necrosis, perinephric abscess, pyonephrosis, and sepsis.

Identify risk factors for cystitis (female sex, sexual intercourse, pregnancy, catheters, diabetes, obstruction) and distinguish cystitis (dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, no fever) from pyelonephritis.

Distinguish gonococcal urethritis (purulent discharge, gram-negative intracellular diplococci) from nongonococcal urethritis (Chlamydia trachomatis, scant discharge), and predict complications such as epididymitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and reactive arthritis.

Explain how SRY on the Y chromosome drives the bipotential gonad to form testes with Sertoli cells, and predict the gonadal phenotype of a 46,XY embryo with an SRY deletion or a 46,XX embryo with an SRY translocation.

Relate Sertoli cell anti-Mullerian hormone, Leydig cell testosterone, and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) to Mullerian duct regression, Wolffian duct development, and masculinization of the external genitalia and prostate.

Trace the paramesonephric (Mullerian) ducts to the uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina, and explain how failed fusion or failed septum resorption produces uterus didelphys, bicornuate uterus, and septate uterus.

Match the male and female derivatives of the genital tubercle (glans penis, clitoris), urogenital folds (ventral penile shaft and penile urethra, labia minora), and labioscrotal swellings (scrotum, labia majora).
Describe testicular descent guided by the gubernaculum through the inguinal canal, and explain how a patent processus vaginalis leads to an indirect inguinal hernia or a communicating hydrocele.

Describe placental formation from the fetal chorion frondosum (cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast) and maternal decidua basalis, and identify the umbilical cord vessels (two umbilical arteries, one umbilical vein) in Wharton jelly.

Describe breast development from the ectodermal mammary ridge (milk line), and explain how incomplete regression of the ridge produces supernumerary nipples or breast tissue between the axilla and the groin.
Distinguish Sertoli cells (tight junctions forming the blood-testis barrier, androgen-binding protein, inhibin B) from interstitial Leydig cells (testosterone) on testis histology.
Trace sperm from the seminiferous tubules through the rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, and prostatic, membranous, and spongy urethra.

Identify the epithelium of each female tract segment (ciliated simple columnar uterine tube, simple columnar endometrium and endocervix, stratified squamous ectocervix and vagina) and locate the transformation zone where cervical dysplasia arises.
Distinguish primordial, primary, secondary (antral), and mature (Graafian) follicles and the corpus luteum by their oocyte, granulosa cell, and theca cell features.
Describe the breast terminal duct lobular unit, with luminal epithelial cells over a myoepithelial cell layer, and relate it to the origin of most breast carcinomas and fibroadenomas.
Describe the peripheral, transition, and central zones of the prostate, and relate benign prostatic hyperplasia to the transition zone and most prostate carcinomas to the peripheral zone.
Compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis, including oocyte arrest in prophase I until ovulation and in metaphase II until fertilization, and the number of functional gametes produced from each meiosis.

Describe spermiogenesis (acrosome from the Golgi apparatus, flagellum from a centriole, shedding of cytoplasm), and explain capacitation in the female tract and the acrosome reaction required for fertilization.
Explain fertilization in the ampulla of the uterine tube, including the cortical reaction that blocks polyspermy and completion of the second meiotic division.
Trace the conceptus from zygote to blastocyst, and explain implantation into the endometrium about day 6 with syncytiotrophoblast invasion and hCG secretion that maintains the corpus luteum.
Predict the consequences of abnormal implantation, including tubal ectopic pregnancy (most often ampullary, with prior salpingitis as a risk factor) and placenta previa over the internal cervical os.
Describe formation of the bilaminar disc in week 2 and the trilaminar disc by gastrulation in week 3, and explain why weeks 3 to 8 are the period of greatest teratogen sensitivity.
Describe the broad ligament and its parts (mesometrium, mesosalpinx, mesovarium), and identify the rectouterine pouch as the lowest peritoneal recess where blood or pus collects in a standing woman.

Identify the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament carrying the ovarian vessels, the ovarian ligament, the round ligament through the inguinal canal, the cardinal ligament carrying the uterine vessels, and the uterosacral ligaments.
Describe uterine and vaginal support by the levator ani, perineal body, and cardinal and uterosacral ligaments, and relate weakening of these supports to uterine prolapse and pelvic relaxation.

List the layers of the scrotum and spermatic cord (skin, dartos, external spermatic fascia, cremaster, internal spermatic fascia, tunica vaginalis) and the cord contents, including the ductus deferens, testicular artery, and pampiniform plexus.
Describe the breast over the pectoralis major from about rib 2 to rib 6 with an axillary tail, and explain skin dimpling when carcinoma involves the suspensory (Cooper) ligaments.
Locate the paired corpora cavernosa, the corpus spongiosum surrounding the urethra, and the tunica albuginea, and relate rupture of the tunica albuginea to penile fracture.

Describe the perineum, bounded by the pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, and coccyx and divided into urogenital and anal triangles, and locate the prostate below the bladder and in front of the rectum for digital rectal exam.
Trace the gonadal arteries from the abdominal aorta and the gonadal veins (left to the left renal vein, right to the inferior vena cava), and explain why varicocele is more common on the left.

Trace the uterine artery from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, and explain why the ureter, passing beneath the uterine artery near the cervix, is at risk during ligation of these vessels.

Compare lymph drainage of the testis and ovary (para-aortic nodes), uterus, cervix, and proximal vagina (internal and external iliac nodes), and scrotum, vulva, and distal vagina (superficial inguinal nodes), and predict nodal spread of tumors.

Describe the nerves of the male sexual response: erection by parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4), emission by sympathetic hypogastric nerves, and ejaculation by the somatic pudendal nerve.
Trace the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) out the greater sciatic foramen, around the ischial spine, and through the lesser sciatic foramen to the perineum, and identify the ischial spine as its landmark.
