Describe breast blood supply from the internal thoracic, lateral thoracic, and thoracoacromial arteries, and lymph drainage mostly to axillary nodes with medial quadrants also draining to parasternal nodes.

Relate the follicular and luteal phases of the ovarian cycle to the proliferative, secretory, and menstrual phases of the endometrium, and explain why the luteal phase stays near 14 days while cycle length varies.
Explain erection as nitric oxide release raising cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle, causing relaxation, arterial inflow, and compression of venous outflow against the tunica albuginea.

Explain how hCG maintains the corpus luteum until the placenta takes over progesterone production near the end of the first trimester, and why placental estriol synthesis depends on fetal adrenal DHEA-S.

Predict the maternal adaptations of pregnancy: plasma volume rising more than red cell mass (dilutional anemia), higher cardiac output, lower systemic vascular resistance, higher GFR, respiratory alkalosis, and hypercoagulability.
Explain how human placental lactogen and other placental hormones increase maternal insulin resistance, and relate this to the development of gestational diabetes.

Explain lactation: alveolar development under estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin, milk secretion after placental progesterone withdrawal, suckling-driven prolactin (synthesis) and oxytocin (myoepithelial ejection), and suckling suppression of GnRH.
Explain the positive feedback of parturition, in which cervical stretch increases oxytocin release (Ferguson reflex) and oxytocin and prostaglandins increase myometrial contraction.
Explain how pulsatile GnRH stimulates LH and FSH release, and predict why continuous GnRH exposure suppresses gonadotropin secretion.

Explain the male axis: LH stimulates Leydig cell testosterone, FSH stimulates Sertoli cell androgen-binding protein and inhibin B, with negative feedback by testosterone on LH and by inhibin B on FSH.

Explain the two-cell model of ovarian steroidogenesis (LH drives theca cell androgen, FSH drives granulosa cell aromatase), and how sustained high estradiol switches to positive feedback to trigger the LH surge.
Describe sex steroid transport bound to SHBG and albumin, and predict how SHBG changes (raised by estrogen, lowered by androgens, insulin resistance, and obesity) alter free testosterone.

Distinguish DHT actions (external genitalia, prostate, male-pattern hair loss) from testosterone actions (Wolffian ducts, spermatogenesis, muscle mass, libido), and describe estrogen and progesterone effects on target tissues.
Describe puberty as reactivation of pulsatile GnRH secretion, beginning with sleep-associated LH pulses, and list the usual female sequence of thelarche, pubarche, growth spurt, and menarche.
Explain prolactin regulation by tonic hypothalamic dopamine inhibition, and predict how hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH to cause amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and hypogonadism.

Trace sex steroid synthesis from cholesterol to pregnenolone (cholesterol side-chain cleavage), then to progesterone, androstenedione, testosterone, and estradiol, naming 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, 17-alpha-hydroxylase, 17,20-lyase, 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, and aromatase.
Explain the conversion of testosterone to DHT by 5-alpha-reductase in genital skin and prostate, and predict ambiguous genitalia at birth with virilization at puberty in 5-alpha-reductase deficiency.
Explain peripheral aromatization of androstenedione to estrone in adipose tissue, and relate obesity to unopposed estrogen, endometrial hyperplasia, and gynecomastia.
Describe hCG, LH, FSH, and TSH as glycoproteins sharing a common alpha subunit with hormone-specific beta subunits, and explain why very high hCG in molar pregnancy can cause hyperthyroidism.

Describe hepatic inactivation of sex steroids by conjugation to glucuronides and sulfates for excretion, and explain why cirrhosis causes gynecomastia, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, and testicular atrophy.

Identify the seminal vesicle (fructose) and prostatic (PSA, a serine protease that liquefies the semen coagulum; citrate; zinc) contributions to semen, and explain why PSA rises in prostatitis and BPH as well as carcinoma.
Explain the role of folate in thymidylate and purine synthesis, and relate maternal folate deficiency to neural tube defects, which arise when the neural tube fails to close by about day 28.
Explain the higher iron requirement of pregnancy (expanded red cell mass, fetal and placental needs), and distinguish iron deficiency from physiologic dilutional anemia using ferritin and MCV.

Describe lactose synthesis by lactose synthase (galactosyltransferase with alpha-lactalbumin), and compare human milk content of lactose, whey proteins, and secretory IgA with its low vitamin D and vitamin K.

Explain placental glucose transfer by facilitated diffusion while maternal insulin does not cross, and predict fetal hyperinsulinemia, macrosomia, and neonatal hypoglycemia from maternal hyperglycemia.
Relate zinc deficiency to hypogonadism and delayed sexual maturation, and excess vitamin A (including retinoids) to teratogenic craniofacial, cardiac, and central nervous system defects.
Explain how low energy availability and low leptin in athletes or people with very low body fat suppress GnRH pulsatility, causing hypothalamic amenorrhea and loss of bone density.

Explain how the gonads and placenta obtain cholesterol for steroid synthesis mainly by LDL receptor-mediated uptake, and identify StAR-mediated transfer of cholesterol into mitochondria as the rate-limiting step in gonadal steroidogenesis.
Explain how meiotic nondisjunction produces 47,XXY and 45,X karyotypes, and how nondisjunction after fertilization produces mosaicism with milder phenotypes.
Explain X inactivation by XIST with Barr body formation, and predict the number of Barr bodies in 46,XX, 47,XXY, and 45,X cells.
Explain how high-risk HPV E6 promotes p53 degradation and E7 binds and inactivates Rb to release E2F, removing cell cycle checkpoints in cervical epithelium.
Relate autosomal dominant BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations (homologous recombination DNA repair genes) to hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, and BRCA2 to male breast and prostate cancer.
Relate Lynch syndrome (germline mismatch repair gene mutations, microsatellite instability) to endometrial and ovarian carcinoma as well as colorectal carcinoma.
Classify breast carcinomas by estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 (ERBB2 amplification) status, and relate triple-negative basal-like tumors to BRCA1 mutation.

Explain testicular immune privilege (Sertoli cell blood-testis barrier, local immunosuppression), predict antisperm antibodies after trauma, vasectomy, or mumps orchitis, and describe autoimmune orchitis as a cause of hypogonadism.
Explain maternal tolerance of the semiallogeneic fetus, including trophoblast expression of nonclassical HLA-G in place of HLA-A and HLA-B, which limits maternal T cell and NK cell attack.
Explain passive immunity of the newborn through FcRn-mediated placental transfer of maternal IgG (not IgM) and secretory IgA in breast milk.

Explain Rh alloimmunization, in which an Rh-negative mother forms anti-D IgG after fetomaternal hemorrhage, causing type II hypersensitivity hemolysis and possible hydrops fetalis in a later Rh-positive fetus.
Describe vaginal defenses (lactobacilli producing lactic acid to keep pH at or below 4.5, secretory IgA), and predict overgrowth of Gardnerella and anaerobes when lactobacilli are lost.

Explain how HPV vaccines made of L1 capsid virus-like particles induce neutralizing antibodies, and how cell-mediated immunity clears most HPV infections and low-grade lesions, so that immunosuppression such as HIV raises cervical cancer risk.
Explain how the inflammatory response to repeated or untreated chlamydial and gonococcal salpingitis causes tubal scarring, increasing the risk of infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

Describe Neisseria gonorrhoeae as an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose but not maltose, with pili showing antigenic variation, IgA protease, and lipooligosaccharide, cultured on Thayer-Martin agar.

Describe Chlamydia trachomatis as an obligate intracellular bacterium with an infectious elementary body and replicating reticulate body, and match serovars A to C (trachoma), D to K (genital and neonatal), and L1 to L3 (LGV).
Describe Treponema pallidum as a thin spirochete that cannot be cultured on standard media, seen by dark-field microscopy, and transmitted sexually and transplacentally.
Compare HSV-2 (enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus with latency in sacral sensory ganglia) with HPV (nonenveloped dsDNA papillomavirus), distinguishing low-risk types 6 and 11 from high-risk types 16 and 18.

Identify Trichomonas vaginalis (motile flagellated protozoan on wet mount), Candida albicans (yeast with pseudohyphae on KOH preparation), and Gardnerella vaginalis (clue cells) by their microscopic features.

Describe Haemophilus ducreyi as a gram-negative coccobacillus, and explain how Staphylococcus aureus TSST-1 acts as a superantigen by binding MHC class II and the T cell receptor outside the antigen groove.

Describe Streptococcus agalactiae (group B, beta-hemolytic, CAMP positive, bacitracin resistant) colonizing the vagina, and identify the TORCH organisms transmitted across the placenta or during delivery.

Distinguish primary amenorrhea (no menarche by age 15, or by 13 without breast development) from secondary amenorrhea (no menses for 3 months after regular cycles), naming pregnancy as the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea.
Interpret FSH, LH, prolactin, TSH, and estradiol levels to localize amenorrhea to the hypothalamus (low FSH and LH), pituitary, ovary (high FSH), or outflow tract, such as Asherman syndrome.

Explain anovulation from absent LH surge or disordered follicle development (PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease, low energy availability), and predict unopposed estrogen effects of irregular heavy bleeding and endometrial hyperplasia.

Explain anovulatory bleeding (formerly dysfunctional uterine bleeding, now abnormal uterine bleeding from ovulatory dysfunction in the PALM-COEIN system) as estrogen-driven proliferation without progesterone-induced secretory change, and distinguish it from structural causes such as polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, and malignancy.

Explain menopause as follicle depletion with loss of estradiol and inhibin feedback, raising FSH and LH, and relate estrogen loss to vasomotor symptoms, atrophic vaginitis, osteoporosis, and higher cardiovascular risk.

Describe primary ovarian insufficiency (ovarian failure before age 40) with causes including Turner syndrome, FMR1 premutation, autoimmune oophoritis, and chemotherapy or radiation, and its high FSH and low estradiol profile.

Distinguish hirsutism from virilization, and localize androgen excess to the ovary (PCOS, Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor) or adrenal (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenal tumor) using testosterone and DHEA-S levels.
Explain primary dysmenorrhea as prostaglandin-driven myometrial contraction and ischemia, and mittelschmerz as midcycle pain at ovulation from follicle rupture.
Classify female infertility as ovulatory (PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, ovarian insufficiency), tubal (prior PID), or uterine (Asherman syndrome, submucosal leiomyoma), and explain the mechanism of each.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Describe balanitis as inflammation of the glans penis, most often from Candida or bacteria, with risk factors of an uncircumcised foreskin, poor hygiene, and diabetes mellitus, and relate recurrent balanitis to phimosis.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Identify Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae as the main causes of mucopurulent cervicitis, and distinguish it from the punctate hemorrhagic strawberry cervix of trichomoniasis and the ulcerative cervicitis of HSV.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Explain endometriosis as endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus (theories of retrograde menstruation, coelomic metaplasia, vascular or lymphatic spread), and relate ovarian chocolate cysts and adhesions to dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Distinguish adenomyosis (endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, causing a uniformly enlarged, tender uterus with dysmenorrhea and heavy bleeding) from endometriosis and leiomyoma.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Distinguish acute endometritis (polymicrobial infection after delivery, miscarriage, or retained products, with fever and uterine tenderness) from chronic endometritis, identified by plasma cells in the endometrial stroma.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Distinguish mumps orchitis (postpubertal, risk of testicular atrophy and infertility) from epididymo-orchitis caused by C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae in sexually active young men and by E. coli in older men.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Explain pelvic inflammatory disease as ascending infection by C. trachomatis, N. gonorrhoeae, and vaginal flora, and identify cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, fever, and purulent cervical discharge.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Predict the complications of salpingitis, including hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, and Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis with right upper quadrant pain and violin-string adhesions.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Relate candidal vaginitis to risk factors (diabetes, antibiotic use, pregnancy, immunosuppression), and identify thick white curd-like discharge, vulvar itching, normal vaginal pH, and pseudohyphae on KOH preparation.

Unit name: Inflammatory diseases of the reproductive tract
Competency: Describe lichen sclerosus as thinned epidermis with dermal fibrosis forming white parchment-like vulvar plaques, mostly in postmenopausal women, and relate it to a small increase in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma risk.

Describe cryptorchidism (most often inguinal, more common in preterm infants), and relate it to impaired spermatogenesis from higher temperature, reduced inhibin B with raised FSH, and increased germ cell tumor risk.

Compare hypospadias (ventral urethral opening from failed fusion of the urethral folds, associated with cryptorchidism and inguinal hernia) with epispadias (dorsal opening from abnormal genital tubercle position, associated with bladder exstrophy).

Explain fragile X syndrome as an FMR1 CGG repeat expansion with hypermethylation and silencing, showing anticipation through maternal transmission, and identify intellectual disability, postpubertal macroorchidism, long face, large jaw, and large ears.
Explain imperforate hymen as failure of the hymen to perforate during development, and predict primary amenorrhea with cyclic pelvic pain, a bulging bluish membrane, and hematocolpos at menarche.

Explain Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) as seminiferous tubule dysgenesis (low inhibin B, high FSH) with Leydig cell dysfunction (low testosterone, high LH), and identify small firm testes, tall stature, gynecomastia, and infertility.

Distinguish phimosis (foreskin that cannot be retracted over the glans, physiologic in infancy or acquired from scarring) from paraphimosis (retracted foreskin trapped behind the glans, causing edema and ischemia).

Distinguish 46,XX disorders of sex development (DSD), formerly female pseudohermaphroditism (ovaries with virilized genitalia from 21-hydroxylase deficiency or excess maternal androgen), from 46,XY DSD, formerly male pseudohermaphroditism (testes with undervirilized genitalia from androgen insensitivity or 5-alpha-reductase deficiency).

Explain complete androgen insensitivity (X-linked androgen receptor defect) with female external genitalia, blind vaginal pouch, absent uterus and tubes, undescended testes, sparse pubic hair, and raised testosterone, estrogen, and LH.
Distinguish Mullerian agenesis (46,XX, normal ovaries and pubic hair, absent uterus and upper vagina) from complete androgen insensitivity as causes of primary amenorrhea with a blind vaginal pouch.

Explain septate uterus as failed resorption of the midline septum after Mullerian duct fusion and a cause of recurrent pregnancy loss, and describe longitudinal and transverse vaginal septa from abnormal fusion or canalization.
Explain Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaic) as ovarian dysgenesis with streak ovaries, and predict primary amenorrhea, absent breast development, low estradiol, and high FSH and LH.

Identify the associated findings of Turner syndrome: short stature (SHOX loss), webbed neck from fetal cystic hygroma, lymphedema of hands and feet, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, and horseshoe kidney.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Classify erectile dysfunction as vascular (atherosclerosis), neurogenic (diabetes, spinal cord injury, pelvic surgery), endocrine (hypogonadism, hyperprolactinemia), drug-induced, or psychogenic, and use preserved nocturnal erections to identify a psychogenic cause.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Describe hematocele as blood within the tunica vaginalis after trauma, torsion, or tumor, and distinguish it from hydrocele by its failure to transilluminate.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Distinguish a communicating congenital hydrocele (patent processus vaginalis) from a noncommunicating hydrocele (infection, trauma, tumor), and identify a smooth scrotal fluid collection around the testis that transilluminates.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Describe spermatocele as a cystic dilation of the epididymis containing sperm, felt as a transilluminating mass separate from the testis, and compare it with a simple epididymal cyst.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Explain varicocele as dilation of the pampiniform plexus, felt as a bag of worms that enlarges on standing and does not transilluminate, and relate it to infertility and, when new on the left, renal cell carcinoma.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Explain testicular torsion as twisting of the spermatic cord (bell-clapper deformity) causing venous then arterial occlusion, and identify sudden severe pain, a high-riding testis, and an absent cremasteric reflex.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Describe priapism as a painful erection lasting over 4 hours, with sickle cell disease and drugs as causes of the ischemic type, and predict cavernosal fibrosis and erectile dysfunction if it persists.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Describe Peyronie disease as a fibrous plaque of the tunica albuginea causing penile curvature and painful erection.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the penis and scrotum
Competency: Classify male infertility as pretesticular (hypogonadotropic hypogonadism), testicular (Klinefelter syndrome, cryptorchidism, varicocele, mumps orchitis), or post-testicular (obstruction, congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens in cystic fibrosis).

Distinguish nonproliferative fibrocystic change (cysts, apocrine metaplasia, fibrosis; no added cancer risk) from proliferative change without atypia (slightly raised risk) and atypical hyperplasia (moderately raised risk).
Describe galactocele as a milk-filled cystic dilation of a duct during lactation or weaning, and predict that it may rupture and cause local inflammation.

Describe mammary duct ectasia as dilated subareolar ducts with thick secretions and periductal chronic inflammation rich in plasma cells, in older multiparous women, and explain why nipple retraction can mimic carcinoma.
Explain acute mastitis as Staphylococcus aureus infection entering through nipple fissures during breastfeeding, with a red, painful, warm breast, fever, and possible abscess.
Describe periductal mastitis in smokers as squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts with keratin plugging, producing a painful subareolar mass or abscess.

Describe traumatic fat necrosis as nonenzymatic necrosis of breast fat after trauma or surgery, with foamy macrophages, giant cells, and calcification, forming a firm mass that can mimic carcinoma on exam and mammography.
Describe fibroadenoma as the most common benign breast tumor in young women, a small, firm, mobile mass of proliferating stroma and ducts that enlarges with estrogen in pregnancy.
Distinguish phyllodes tumor (leaf-like projections of overgrown, hypercellular stroma, usually in older women, with potential to recur or metastasize) from fibroadenoma.
Describe intraductal papilloma as a benign subareolar papillary growth in a large duct and identify it as a common cause of bloody nipple discharge.

Relate breast carcinoma risk to age, prolonged estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, late first pregnancy, postmenopausal obesity), atypical hyperplasia, and family history, and identify the upper outer quadrant as the most common site.

Distinguish ductal carcinoma in situ (confined by basement membrane, mammographic microcalcifications, comedo necrosis) from invasive ductal carcinoma (most common type, firm stellate mass with desmoplastic stroma).
Explain lobular carcinoma as loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) causing discohesive cells that invade in single-file lines, and relate it to frequent bilateral and multifocal disease.
Describe Paget disease of the breast as eczematous nipple and areolar change from large Paget cells with clear cytoplasm in the epidermis, nearly always with underlying ductal carcinoma.
Distinguish inflammatory breast carcinoma (tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics causing erythema, edema, and peau d'orange) from acute mastitis.

Distinguish gynecomastia (benign ductal and stromal proliferation from a raised estrogen to androgen ratio) from male breast carcinoma, and relate male breast carcinoma to BRCA2 mutation and Klinefelter syndrome.

Unit name: Infectious diseases and hyperplasia of the prostate
Competency: Explain benign prostatic hyperplasia as DHT-dependent nodular hyperplasia of glands and stroma in the transition (periurethral) zone of older men, and state that it is not a precursor of carcinoma.

Unit name: Infectious diseases and hyperplasia of the prostate
Competency: Predict the urinary findings and complications of benign prostatic hyperplasia: hesitancy, weak stream, frequency, nocturia, urinary retention, bladder wall hypertrophy, infection, and hydronephrosis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases and hyperplasia of the prostate
Competency: Identify E. coli and other gram-negative rods as the usual cause of acute bacterial prostatitis in older men (C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae in younger men), with fever, chills, dysuria, and a tender, boggy prostate.

Unit name: Infectious diseases and hyperplasia of the prostate
Competency: Distinguish acute bacterial prostatitis from chronic bacterial prostatitis (recurrent urinary tract infection with the same organism) and chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain without bacteria).

Distinguish follicular cysts (unruptured follicle, may secrete estrogen), corpus luteum cysts (may hemorrhage into the peritoneum), and bilateral theca lutein cysts from high hCG in molar or multiple pregnancy.

Explain ovarian torsion as twisting of the ovary on its ligaments, usually when enlarged by a cyst or tumor, with venous then arterial occlusion causing sudden severe pelvic pain and possible infarction.
Describe paraovarian cysts as thin-walled cysts in the broad ligament arising from Mullerian or Wolffian remnants, separate from the ovary, and predict torsion or rupture as complications.

Explain PCOS pathogenesis: raised LH to FSH ratio driving theca androgen, insulin resistance raising ovarian androgen and lowering SHBG, and arrested follicles forming multiple small peripheral ovarian cysts.

Identify the findings and complications of PCOS: oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricans, infertility, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma from unopposed estrogen.
Describe tubo-ovarian cysts and abscesses as sequelae of PID in which an inflamed or fluid-filled tube adheres to the ovary, and predict rupture with peritonitis and later infertility.
Compare complete mole (usually 46,XX, all paternal from an empty ovum, no fetal parts, diffuse villous swelling, p57 negative) with partial mole (triploid, fetal parts, focal swelling, p57 positive).

Predict the findings of complete hydatidiform mole: vaginal bleeding, uterus large for dates, very high hCG, hyperemesis, theca lutein cysts, hyperthyroidism, preeclampsia before 20 weeks, and higher choriocarcinoma risk.
Describe invasive mole as hydropic villi penetrating the myometrium, which can cause uterine perforation and hemorrhage and persistent hCG elevation after evacuation.

Describe gestational choriocarcinoma as malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without villi, arising after a mole, abortion, or normal pregnancy, with very high hCG and early hematogenous spread to lung, vagina, and brain.

Explain preeclampsia as abnormal placentation with failed spiral artery remodeling, placental ischemia, and release of antiangiogenic factors (sFlt-1, soluble endoglin) that cause maternal endothelial dysfunction.

Identify preeclampsia as new hypertension (140/90 mm Hg or higher) after 20 weeks with proteinuria or end-organ damage, its risk factors (nulliparity, chronic hypertension, diabetes, multiple gestation), and its complications of eclampsia, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, and fetal growth restriction.
Distinguish placental abruption (premature separation with painful bleeding, linked to hypertension, cocaine, and trauma, risking DIC) from placenta previa (painless third-trimester bleeding).
Explain placenta accreta as villi attaching to or invading the myometrium through a deficient decidua basalis, with prior cesarean delivery and placenta previa as major risk factors.

Relate oligohydramnios to reduced fetal urine output (bilateral renal agenesis, urinary obstruction) with Potter sequence, and polyhydramnios to impaired fetal swallowing (esophageal atresia, anencephaly) or maternal diabetes.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the vagina and vulva
Competency: Describe a Bartholin cyst as obstruction of the Bartholin gland duct, forming a mass in the posterolateral vulvar vestibule that may become an abscess, and identify its occurrence in reproductive-age women.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the vagina and vulva
Competency: Explain cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele as herniation through weakened pelvic floor and endopelvic fascia, with risk factors of vaginal childbirth, aging, estrogen loss, obesity, and chronic straining or cough.

Unit name: Benign conditions of the vagina and vulva
Competency: Distinguish cystocele (bladder bulging into the anterior vaginal wall, incomplete emptying), urethrocele (urethra into the distal anterior wall, stress incontinence), and rectocele (rectum into the posterior wall, difficult defecation).

Explain cervical intraepithelial neoplasia as high-risk HPV infection of the transformation zone with koilocytes, graded CIN 1 to 3 by the thickness of epithelium replaced by atypical immature cells (CIN 1 as LSIL, CIN 2 and 3 as HSIL).
Relate cervical dysplasia risk to persistent HPV 16 or 18 infection, many sexual partners, early sexual activity, smoking, and immunodeficiency such as HIV, and predict that most CIN 1 regresses.

Describe invasive cervical carcinoma (mostly squamous cell, some adenocarcinoma) with postcoital bleeding, and explain how lateral spread can obstruct the ureters, causing hydronephrosis and renal failure.

Relate endometrial hyperplasia to unopposed estrogen (obesity, anovulation, PCOS, estrogen-only therapy, granulosa cell tumor) and PTEN loss, and identify atypical hyperplasia as the precursor of endometrioid carcinoma.

Compare endometrioid endometrial carcinoma (estrogen-related, arising from hyperplasia, PTEN and Lynch syndrome mutations) with serous carcinoma (older women, atrophic endometrium, TP53 mutation, aggressive), both presenting with postmenopausal bleeding.
Describe endometrial and endocervical polyps as benign localized overgrowths of glands and stroma that cause abnormal or intermenstrual bleeding.

Describe leiomyoma as a benign, estrogen-sensitive, well-circumscribed smooth muscle tumor with a whorled pattern, more common in Black women, causing heavy bleeding, pelvic pressure, anemia, and infertility.
Distinguish leiomyosarcoma (arising de novo in older women, a single large soft mass with necrosis, nuclear atypia, and high mitotic rate) from leiomyoma, which does not transform into it.
Relate prostate adenocarcinoma to age, Black race, family history, and BRCA2, and explain its origin in the peripheral zone, Gleason grading by gland pattern, and raised PSA.
Predict osteoblastic bone metastases of prostate carcinoma to the lumbar spine and pelvis through the vertebral venous plexus, with bone pain and raised alkaline phosphatase.

Classify ovarian tumors by origin as surface epithelial (serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, Brenner), germ cell (teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma), or sex cord-stromal (granulosa cell, Sertoli-Leydig cell, fibroma, thecoma).
Relate high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma to BRCA1, BRCA2, and TP53 mutations and the fallopian tube fimbria, and identify psammoma bodies, raised CA-125, ascites, and peritoneal and omental spread.

Identify mature cystic teratoma (most common ovarian germ cell tumor), struma ovarii (a monodermal teratoma of thyroid tissue that can cause hyperthyroidism), dysgerminoma (sheets of clear cells, raised LDH), and yolk sac tumor (Schiller-Duval bodies, raised AFP).

Predict the effects of hormonally active ovarian stromal tumors: granulosa cell tumor (estrogen, Call-Exner bodies, precocious puberty or endometrial hyperplasia), Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor (virilization), and fibroma with ascites and hydrothorax (Meigs syndrome).
Identify Krukenberg tumor as bilateral ovarian metastasis of signet ring cell adenocarcinoma, most often from the stomach.
Relate squamous cell carcinoma of the penis to HPV 16, lack of circumcision, phimosis, and smoking, and identify Bowen disease, erythroplasia of Queyrat, and bowenoid papulosis as carcinoma in situ.

Classify testicular tumors as germ cell (most, with isochromosome 12p and germ cell neoplasia in situ) or sex cord-stromal, and identify a painless firm mass that does not transilluminate, with cryptorchidism and Klinefelter syndrome as risks.

Distinguish seminoma (most common, uniform clear cells with lymphocytes, placental alkaline phosphatase, radiosensitive, good prognosis) from embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor (AFP), choriocarcinoma (hCG), and teratoma.
Describe Leydig cell tumor (Reinke crystals, androgen or estrogen excess causing precocious puberty or gynecomastia) and testicular lymphoma as the most common testicular tumor in men over 60.

Distinguish vaginal squamous cell carcinoma (older women, HPV, vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia), clear cell adenocarcinoma (in utero DES exposure), and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides, grape-like mass in young girls, desmin positive).

Compare HPV-related vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (younger women, from HPV-related intraepithelial neoplasia) with HPV-independent vulvar carcinoma (older women, lichen sclerosus, differentiated VIN with TP53 mutation).

Distinguish usual (HPV-related) vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia from differentiated VIN, and distinguish extramammary Paget disease of the vulva (intraepithelial adenocarcinoma, usually without underlying carcinoma) from Paget disease of the breast.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Distinguish chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi; painful ulcer with ragged edges and gray exudate, painful suppurative inguinal nodes) from the painless indurated chancre of primary syphilis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Explain bacterial vaginosis as replacement of lactobacilli by Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes, causing thin gray discharge with fishy odor, pH above 4.5, positive amine (whiff) test, clue cells, and few neutrophils.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Use vaginal pH, the KOH whiff test, and wet mount findings to distinguish bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, and candidal vaginitis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Identify genital chlamydial infection as often asymptomatic and the cause of urethritis, cervicitis, epididymitis, PID, reactive arthritis, and neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Describe lymphogranuloma venereum (C. trachomatis L1 to L3) as a small painless genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes) and possible proctocolitis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Identify gonococcal urethritis with purulent discharge and intracellular gram-negative diplococci, cervicitis, PID, neonatal conjunctivitis, and disseminated infection (septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustules), and relate recurrent infection to C5 to C9 deficiency.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Describe genital herpes as painful grouped vesicles that ulcerate, with systemic symptoms in primary infection, recurrence from sacral ganglia, multinucleated giant cells, and neonatal infection acquired during delivery.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Distinguish condylomata acuminata (HPV 6 and 11, koilocytes) from condylomata lata of secondary syphilis, and relate high-risk HPV to cervical, vulvar, vaginal, penile, anal, and oropharyngeal carcinoma.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Identify the causes of nongonococcal urethritis (C. trachomatis most often, also Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis), and relate it to reactive arthritis with conjunctivitis in HLA-B27-positive men.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Describe the stages of syphilis: primary painless chancre, secondary rash on palms and soles with condylomata lata and lymphadenopathy, latency, and tertiary gummas, aortitis of the ascending aorta, and tabes dorsalis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Interpret nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR; anticardiolipin antibodies, false positives in pregnancy, SLE, and viral infection) and treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, which stays positive for life) in syphilis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Identify the findings of congenital syphilis: rhinitis (snuffles), rash, saddle nose, Hutchinson teeth, mulberry molars, saber shins, and sensorineural deafness.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Explain toxic shock syndrome as TSST-1 superantigen release by S. aureus (retained tampons, nasal packing, wounds) causing polyclonal T cell cytokine release, fever, hypotension, diffuse rash with later palm and sole desquamation, and multiorgan injury.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the genitourinary system (including STDs)
Competency: Describe trichomoniasis as a sexually transmitted flagellated protozoan infection causing frothy yellow-green malodorous discharge, strawberry cervix, pH above 4.5, and motile trophozoites on wet mount.

Describe how the respiratory diverticulum (lung bud) arises from ventral foregut endoderm in week 4, and distinguish endodermal airway epithelium and glands from the splanchnic mesoderm that forms cartilage, smooth muscle, and connective tissue.
Explain how the tracheoesophageal ridges fuse to form the tracheoesophageal septum, and relate faulty septation to esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

Sequence the pseudoglandular, canalicular, saccular, and alveolar stages of lung development, and explain why survival with support first becomes possible near the end of the canalicular stage, once respiratory bronchioles and capillaries appear (about weeks 24 to 26).

Explain the timing of surfactant production by type II pneumocytes (beginning in the second trimester and reaching mature levels by about week 35), and interpret an amniotic lecithin to sphingomyelin ratio above 2 as a sign of fetal lung maturity.
Explain how oligohydramnios (for example from bilateral renal agenesis) and congenital diaphragmatic hernia cause pulmonary hypoplasia, and predict respiratory failure at birth.

Trace the change in airway epithelium from pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells in the trachea and bronchi, to simple cuboidal with club cells in terminal bronchioles, to type I and type II pneumocytes in alveoli.

Distinguish bronchi from bronchioles by the presence of cartilage plates, submucosal glands, and goblet cells, and explain why bronchioles depend on smooth muscle tone and radial traction from surrounding alveoli to stay open.

Describe the functions of type I pneumocytes (thin gas exchange surface), type II pneumocytes (surfactant secretion and regeneration of type I cells), club cells (secretion, cytochrome P450 detoxification, progenitors), and alveolar macrophages.

Explain mucociliary clearance by cilia with a 9 plus 2 microtubule axoneme and dynein arms, and predict how smoking-induced squamous metaplasia or ciliary dysfunction leads to retained mucus and recurrent infection.
Describe the layers of the blood-air barrier (type I pneumocyte, fused basement membranes, capillary endothelium), and relate interstitial fibrosis or edema that thickens it to impaired diffusion.
Identify the nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium of the true vocal folds and oropharynx, and relate it to squamous cell carcinoma as the main malignant tumor of the larynx.

Describe the nasal conchae and meatuses and identify sinus drainage: frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid into the middle meatus; posterior ethmoid into the superior meatus; sphenoid into the sphenoethmoidal recess; nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus.

Explain why the maxillary sinus is the sinus most often infected (ostium high on its medial wall, poor gravity drainage), and relate the closeness of maxillary molar roots to its floor to odontogenic sinusitis.

Locate Kiesselbach area on the anterior nasal septum, name the arteries that anastomose there (sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, superior labial), and contrast it with posterior epistaxis from sphenopalatine branches.

Describe the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx, the tonsils of Waldeyer ring, and the pharyngotympanic tube opening, and relate adenoid enlargement to mouth breathing, snoring, and otitis media.

Identify the laryngeal cartilages and intrinsic muscles, state that the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal folds, and predict hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, noting that the left nerve loops under the aortic arch.

Distinguish laryngeal innervation by the internal laryngeal nerve (sensation above the vocal folds), external laryngeal nerve (cricothyroid), and recurrent laryngeal nerve (other intrinsic muscles, sensation below the folds), and relate supraglottic sensory loss to aspiration.

Describe the surface projections of the lungs (ribs 6, 8, and 10) and pleura (ribs 8, 10, and 12) at the midclavicular, midaxillary, and paravertebral lines, and explain why a thoracentesis needle passes just above a rib.

Compare the right lung (three lobes, horizontal and oblique fissures) with the left (two lobes, lingula, cardiac notch), and predict where aspirated material lodges when upright (right lower lobe) or supine (superior segment of right lower lobe).
Identify the relationships of the pulmonary artery, main bronchus, and pulmonary veins at each hilum, noting that the right pulmonary artery lies anterior and the left lies superior to its bronchus.

Describe the superior, anterior, middle, and posterior mediastinum and their contents, and predict typical masses in each, such as thymoma, teratoma, lymphoma, and retrosternal thyroid anteriorly and neurogenic tumors posteriorly.

Compare the pain-sensitive parietal pleura (intercostal and phrenic nerves) with the visceral pleura (autonomic supply), and explain why irritation of the central diaphragmatic pleura refers pain to the shoulder (C3 to C5).
Identify the diaphragmatic openings (inferior vena cava at T8, esophagus and vagal trunks at T10, aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein at T12) and the phrenic nerve supply of the diaphragm.
Trace the thoracic duct from the cisterna chyli through the aortic hiatus to the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins, and relate its injury to chylothorax.

Compare the low-pressure, low-resistance pulmonary circulation with the systemic bronchial circulation, and explain why dual blood supply makes pulmonary infarction uncommon after embolism unless bronchial flow is also compromised.

Explain hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, contrast it with hypoxic vasodilation in systemic arterioles, and relate chronic alveolar hypoxia to pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular hypertrophy (cor pulmonale).

Describe West zones 1, 2, and 3 by the relationship of alveolar, arterial, and venous pressures, and predict that ventilation-perfusion ratio is highest at the apex, explaining why reactivation tuberculosis favors the apices.

Trace airflow through the conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles, anatomic dead space about 150 mL) and the respiratory zone (respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveoli), and explain why medium-sized bronchi contribute the most airway resistance.

Apply Poiseuille law to show that airway resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of the radius, and predict how bronchoconstriction, lung volume, and gas density change resistance and airflow.

Explain why pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at functional residual capacity and rises at low lung volumes (narrowed extra-alveolar vessels) and high lung volumes (compressed alveolar vessels).

Identify tidal volume, inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes, residual volume, functional residual capacity, vital capacity, and total lung capacity, and explain why residual volume requires helium dilution or body plethysmography rather than simple spirometry.
Calculate minute and alveolar ventilation, and physiologic dead space with the Bohr equation, and predict why rapid shallow breathing lowers alveolar ventilation at the same minute ventilation.

Explain lung and chest wall compliance, elastic recoil, the negative intrapleural pressure at functional residual capacity, and how surfactant lowers surface tension to stabilize small alveoli according to the law of Laplace.

Interpret spirometry and flow-volume loops to distinguish obstructive disease (reduced FEV1/FVC, normal or increased TLC) from restrictive disease (normal or increased FEV1/FVC, reduced TLC) and fixed upper airway obstruction.

Describe medullary control of breathing (dorsal respiratory group for inspiration, ventral group for forced breathing), the pontine pneumotaxic and apneustic centers, and the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex.

Compare central chemoreceptors, which respond to CSF hydrogen ion generated from arterial CO2, with carotid and aortic body chemoreceptors, which respond mainly to PaO2 below about 60 mmHg, and predict the ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxemia.

Distinguish obstructive sleep apnea (pharyngeal collapse despite respiratory effort), central sleep apnea (absent effort), and obesity hypoventilation syndrome (daytime PaCO2 above 45 mmHg with BMI 30 or more), and predict pulmonary hypertension and secondary polycythemia.
Calculate PAO2 with the alveolar gas equation (PAO2 = FiO2 times (Patm minus 47) minus PaCO2/0.8) and the A-a gradient, and interpret a normal versus a widened gradient.

Classify causes of hypoxemia (low inspired O2, hypoventilation, diffusion limitation, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, right-to-left shunt), and predict which have a normal A-a gradient and which fail to correct with supplemental oxygen.

Contrast dead space (V/Q approaching infinity, as in pulmonary embolism) with shunt (V/Q of zero, as in airway obstruction or alveoli filled by pneumonia or edema), and predict the effect of each on PaO2 and PaCO2.

Apply Fick law of diffusion, distinguish perfusion-limited exchange (N2O, O2 at rest) from diffusion-limited exchange (CO, O2 in fibrosis or strenuous exercise at altitude), and interpret reduced DLCO in emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis.
Distinguish hypoxemia from tissue hypoxia, and classify hypoxia as hypoxemic, anemic, circulatory, or histotoxic (cyanide), predicting PaO2, SaO2, and O2 content in each.

Explain acclimatization to high altitude (hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis, renal bicarbonate excretion, increased erythropoietin and 2,3-BPG, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) and relate it to acute mountain sickness, high altitude pulmonary edema, and cerebral edema.
Calculate arterial O2 content (1.34 times Hb times SaO2, plus 0.003 times PaO2), and predict how anemia, polycythemia, and carbon monoxide poisoning change PaO2, SaO2, and O2 content.

Interpret the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, explain cooperative binding between T and R states, and name factors that shift it right (increased H+, CO2, temperature, 2,3-BPG) or left (fetal hemoglobin, CO, methemoglobin).
Describe CO2 transport as bicarbonate (about 70 percent), carbaminohemoglobin, and dissolved CO2, including red cell carbonic anhydrase and the chloride shift.
Explain the Bohr effect in tissues and the Haldane effect in the lungs, and relate them to O2 unloading and CO2 loading and unloading.

Explain how carbon monoxide (about 200 times the affinity of O2, left shift) and methemoglobin (ferric iron, chocolate-colored blood) impair O2 delivery, and predict why pulse oximetry misleads while PaO2 stays normal.

Interpret arterial blood gases in respiratory acidosis and alkalosis, applying expected renal compensation (bicarbonate rises about 1 mEq/L acutely and 3 to 4 mEq/L chronically per 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2), and identify mixed disturbances.

Describe surfactant composition (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine as the main lipid, phosphatidylglycerol, surfactant proteins), and explain why fetal cortisol and thyroid hormone promote its synthesis while fetal hyperinsulinemia in maternal diabetes delays it.

Explain the protease and antiprotease balance in the lung, in which alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase, and predict how oxidants in cigarette smoke and recruited neutrophils tip it toward alveolar wall destruction.

Relate elastin (cross-linked by copper-dependent lysyl oxidase) to lung recoil, and contrast increased compliance from elastin loss in emphysema with decreased compliance from collagen deposition in fibrosis.

Explain how vitamin A deficiency causes squamous metaplasia of respiratory epithelium and increases respiratory infections, and why pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis causes deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

Explain how high inspired oxygen concentrations and cigarette smoke generate reactive oxygen species that injure the lung, and describe protection by superoxide dismutase, catalase, and selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase.

Describe airway mucus as heavily O-glycosylated mucin glycoproteins secreted by goblet cells and submucosal glands, and relate mucous gland hyperplasia in chronic bronchitis and dehydrated mucus in cystic fibrosis to impaired clearance.

Describe cystic fibrosis as an autosomal recessive CFTR defect on chromosome 7, and explain how the common F508 deletion causes misfolding and proteasomal degradation, reducing chloride secretion and leaving dehydrated, thick airway mucus.

Explain alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (codominant SERPINA1 alleles, PiZZ most severe), and predict panacinar lower lobe emphysema plus cirrhosis with PAS-positive globules from misfolded protein retained in hepatocytes.
Relate dynein arm defects in primary ciliary dyskinesia (autosomal recessive) to bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and infertility, and explain situs inversus in Kartagener syndrome.
Describe how p53 and Rb restrain the G1 to S transition, and explain how tobacco carcinogens such as benzo[a]pyrene form DNA adducts that cause mutations, including in TP53.

Identify common driver alterations in lung cancer (EGFR mutations, ALK rearrangements, and KRAS mutations in adenocarcinoma; TP53 and RB1 loss in small cell carcinoma), and relate EGFR mutations to adenocarcinoma in nonsmokers.

Unit name: Energy production and the respiratory system
Competency: Relate O2 as the final electron acceptor at cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) to ATP production, and predict the shift to anaerobic glycolysis with lactic acidosis when tissue O2 delivery fails.

Unit name: Energy production and the respiratory system
Competency: Explain how cyanide from burning plastics and carbon monoxide in smoke inhalation inhibit complex IV, and predict lactic acidosis with a normal PaO2 and, in cyanide poisoning, a high venous O2 saturation.

Unit name: Energy production and the respiratory system
Competency: Calculate the respiratory quotient (CO2 produced divided by O2 consumed) for carbohydrate (1.0), fat (about 0.7), and protein (about 0.8), and predict how fuel mix changes CO2 production and ventilatory demand.

Unit name: Energy production and the respiratory system
Competency: Explain how 2,3-BPG made in the red cell glycolytic shunt lowers hemoglobin O2 affinity, and predict how high altitude and pyruvate kinase deficiency increase 2,3-BPG and O2 unloading.

Unit name: Energy production and the respiratory system
Competency: Relate the increased work of breathing in severe emphysema to higher resting energy expenditure and the weight loss seen in these patients.

Describe innate lung defenses (nasal filtration, mucociliary escalator, cough, secretory IgA, alveolar macrophages, surfactant proteins A and D acting as opsonins), and relate their impairment by smoking, alcohol, and ciliary defects to pneumonia risk.

Explain type I hypersensitivity in allergic asthma and rhinitis, including Th2 cytokines (IL-4 for IgE class switching, IL-5 for eosinophils, IL-13 for mucus), mast cell degranulation, and the early and late phase responses.

Explain granuloma formation in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis (Th1 cells, IFN-gamma activation of macrophages, TNF-alpha maintenance of granulomas), and predict tuberculosis reactivation when TNF-alpha is blocked.

Distinguish hypersensitivity pneumonitis (type III and IV reactions to inhaled organic antigens such as thermophilic actinomycetes in farmer lung, with poorly formed interstitial granulomas) from asthma.

Contrast Goodpasture syndrome (type II hypersensitivity against type IV collagen, pulmonary hemorrhage, glomerulonephritis) with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3-ANCA, necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis of upper and lower airways and kidney).

Explain how toxoid vaccines (diphtheria, tetanus), acellular pertussis vaccine, and polysaccharide-protein conjugate vaccines (Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcus) induce protection, contrasting T-cell independent polysaccharide responses with T-cell dependent conjugate responses.

Explain how lung cancers evade immunity by reducing MHC class I and expressing PD-L1, and relate antibodies to shared tumor and neural antigens (anti-Hu, anti-voltage-gated calcium channel) to paraneoplastic neurologic syndromes.

Describe Streptococcus pneumoniae (gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci, alpha-hemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble, polysaccharide capsule, IgA protease) as the most common cause of community-acquired and lobar pneumonia.

Compare gram-negative respiratory pathogens: Haemophilus influenzae (needs factors X and V), Klebsiella pneumoniae (mucoid capsule, alcoholics), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (oxidase positive, cystic fibrosis and ventilated patients), and Legionella (charcoal yeast extract agar, contaminated water).
Explain the toxins of Corynebacterium diphtheriae (prophage-encoded, ADP-ribosylates EF-2) and Bordetella pertussis (ADP-ribosylates Gi, raising cAMP), and link each to its clinical picture.
Describe Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast mycolic acid wall, cord factor, sulfatides), its spread by airborne droplet nuclei, and its survival in macrophages by blocking phagolysosome fusion.

Compare influenza (segmented negative-sense RNA, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, antigenic drift and shift), respiratory syncytial virus (a pneumovirus, formerly classed as a paramyxovirus, whose F protein forms syncytia), and coronaviruses (enveloped positive-sense RNA; SARS-CoV-2 spike binds ACE2).

Distinguish the dimorphic fungi by geography and tissue form: Histoplasma (Ohio and Mississippi valleys, bird and bat droppings, small yeasts in macrophages), Blastomyces (Great Lakes and Ohio and Mississippi basins, broad-based budding yeast), and Coccidioides (southwestern United States, spherules with endospores).

Identify Aspergillus (septate hyphae branching at acute angles) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (cysts on methenamine silver stain), and relate each to the host defect that allows infection (neutropenia, CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3).

Explain neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency from prematurity, maternal diabetes, or cesarean delivery) leading to atelectasis and hyaline membranes, and predict patent ductus arteriosus, plus bronchopulmonary dysplasia and retinopathy of prematurity from oxygen therapy.

Explain acute respiratory distress syndrome as diffuse alveolar damage after sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, trauma, or pancreatitis, with neutrophil-mediated capillary leak, hyaline membranes, bilateral infiltrates, and hypoxemia (PaO2/FiO2 of 300 or less) not explained by heart failure.

Describe idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (repeated alveolar epithelial injury with TGF-beta driven fibrosis), its usual interstitial pneumonia pattern (patchy subpleural and basal fibrosis, fibroblastic foci, honeycombing), clubbing, and restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO.

Compare pneumoconioses: coal workers (upper lobes, progressive massive fibrosis), silicosis (upper lobes, eggshell calcified hilar nodes, tuberculosis risk), asbestosis (lower lobes, ferruginous bodies), and berylliosis (noncaseating granulomas, aerospace work).

Describe sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, elevated ACE, hypercalcemia from macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase), its higher incidence in Black women, and Lofgren syndrome (erythema nodosum, hilar lymphadenopathy, arthritis, fever).

Distinguish intrinsic restrictive disease (reduced DLCO) from extrapulmonary restriction caused by obesity, kyphoscoliosis, or neuromuscular weakness (usually normal DLCO and a normal A-a gradient with hypoventilation).

Distinguish desquamative interstitial pneumonia (smokers, macrophages filling alveoli), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (uniform interstitial inflammation and fibrosis), and cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (polypoid fibroblast plugs, Masson bodies).

Identify occupational causes of lung disease: byssinosis (cotton dust), bagassosis (moldy sugarcane, hypersensitivity pneumonitis), and silo-filler disease (nitrogen dioxide causing bronchiolitis and pulmonary edema).
Identify bleomycin, amiodarone, busulfan, and methotrexate as causes of drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis to be distinguished from idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Explain asthma pathogenesis (atopic Th2 inflammation and nonatopic triggers such as viral infection, cold air, exercise, and aspirin), and identify Curschmann spirals, Charcot-Leyden crystals, goblet cell hyperplasia, basement membrane thickening, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.

Predict findings in acute asthma (wheezing, prolonged expiration, pulsus paradoxus, reversible obstruction on spirometry), and interpret a normal or rising PaCO2 after early respiratory alkalosis as a sign of tiring and impending respiratory failure.

Explain bronchiectasis as permanent airway dilation from obstruction plus necrotizing infection, identify causes (cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, tumor or foreign body), and predict copious purulent sputum, hemoptysis, clubbing, and amyloidosis.

Describe chronic bronchitis (productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years), mucous gland hyperplasia with a Reid index above 0.5, and the hypoxemia, hypercapnia, cyanosis, and cor pulmonale of the blue bloater.

Compare centriacinar emphysema (smoking, upper lobes), panacinar emphysema (alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, lower lobes), and paraseptal emphysema (subpleural bullae, spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults), and predict barrel chest, air trapping, and pursed-lip breathing.

Interpret COPD testing (FEV1/FVC below 0.7, increased TLC and residual volume), and contrast DLCO and blood gases in predominant emphysema (low DLCO, near normal gases until late) with predominant chronic bronchitis (normal DLCO, early hypoxemia and hypercapnia).

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Explain acute bronchitis as a mostly viral, self-limited inflammation of the large airways causing cough for up to about 3 weeks, and distinguish it from pneumonia (no consolidation) and from chronic bronchitis.

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe epiglottitis (classically Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children) with sudden fever, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod posture, and a thumb sign on lateral neck radiograph, and predict sudden airway obstruction.

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Distinguish acute laryngitis (usually viral, hoarseness) from croup (parainfluenza virus laryngotracheobronchitis, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, steeple sign) and bacterial tracheitis (toxic child, purulent tracheal secretions, often Staphylococcus aureus).

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Compare allergic rhinitis (IgE, eosinophils, pale boggy mucosa, seasonal or perennial) with infectious rhinitis (rhinovirus, an acid-labile picornavirus binding ICAM-1, as the main cause of the common cold) and nonallergic vasomotor rhinitis.

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Explain sinusitis from ostial obstruction (mostly viral; bacterial Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis), and predict complications such as orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, and mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis.

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Distinguish Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis (beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, M protein; fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough) from viral pharyngitis, and predict rheumatic fever (molecular mimicry) and poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.

Unit name: Diseases of the upper respiratory tract
Competency: Distinguish streptococcal tonsillitis from infectious mononucleosis (EBV, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical nodes, atypical lymphocytes, heterophile antibodies, splenomegaly), and predict peritonsillar abscess (uvular deviation, trismus, muffled voice).

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Explain chylothorax from thoracic duct disruption (trauma, surgery, lymphoma), and identify milky pleural fluid with triglycerides above 110 mg/dL and chylomicrons.

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Describe hemothorax from chest trauma, vascular rupture, or malignancy, define it by a pleural fluid hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit, and predict hypovolemic shock and later fibrothorax.

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Explain obstructive (resorption) atelectasis from absorption of trapped alveolar air beyond a mucus plug, tumor, or foreign body, predict mediastinal shift toward the collapse, and contrast compression atelectasis, which shifts the mediastinum away.

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Describe asbestos-related pleural disease (calcified parietal pleural plaques, effusion, diffuse pleural fibrosis), ferruginous bodies, and the increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma (synergistic with smoking) and mesothelioma.

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Compare primary spontaneous pneumothorax (tall thin young men, ruptured apical blebs), secondary pneumothorax (COPD, cystic fibrosis), and tension pneumothorax (tracheal deviation away, hypotension, distended neck veins), and predict hyperresonance with absent breath sounds.

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Classify pleural effusions with Light criteria (exudate if pleural to serum protein above 0.5, LDH ratio above 0.6, or LDH above two thirds of the serum upper limit), and identify transudative (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome) versus exudative causes.

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Identify empyema (purulent exudate after pneumonia), mediastinitis (esophageal perforation, sternotomy, inhalational anthrax), pneumomediastinum (subcutaneous crepitus, Hamman crunch), and costochondritis (reproducible chest wall tenderness).

Unit name: Disorders of the pleural cavity and lung expansion
Competency: Predict findings of chest trauma: flail chest (paradoxical segment motion), pulmonary contusion (hemorrhage with worsening hypoxemia), open pneumothorax from a penetrating wound, and diaphragmatic rupture (bowel in the left hemithorax).

Explain pulmonary edema using Starling forces, contrasting cardiogenic edema (raised capillary hydrostatic pressure, wedge pressure above 18 mmHg, hemosiderin-laden macrophages) with noncardiogenic edema from capillary injury, low oncotic pressure, or lymphatic obstruction.

Explain pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis (Virchow triad), and predict sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis, a widened A-a gradient, raised D-dimer, and acute right heart strain with saddle emboli.

Distinguish fat embolism (long bone fracture, hypoxemia, neurologic changes, petechial rash within 24 to 72 hours), air embolism (venous catheters, diving decompression), and amniotic fluid embolism (sudden collapse and DIC during delivery).

Describe pulmonary infarction as a wedge-shaped hemorrhagic infarct based on the pleura, occurring when an embolus blocks a medium or small artery and bronchial flow is reduced (as in heart failure), and predict hemoptysis and pleuritic pain.

Classify pulmonary hypertension (pulmonary arterial including BMPR2 mutation, left heart disease, lung disease or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolism), and describe medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, plexiform lesions, and progression to cor pulmonale.

Describe pulmonary arteriovenous malformations in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (autosomal dominant), and predict hypoxemia from right-to-left shunting, hemoptysis, and paradoxical embolic stroke or brain abscess.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe adenocarcinoma as the most common lung cancer overall and in nonsmokers and women, typically peripheral and mucin producing, and identify adenocarcinoma in situ by lepidic growth along alveolar walls without invasion.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe bronchial carcinoid as a low-grade neuroendocrine tumor (nests of uniform cells, chromogranin positive, often a central polypoid mass, not linked to smoking) that may obstruct a bronchus and rarely produces carcinoid syndrome.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Compare esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (upper and middle third; smoking, alcohol, very hot drinks, achalasia, nitrosamines) with adenocarcinoma (distal third; GERD, Barrett esophagus, obesity), and predict progressive dysphagia, weight loss, and tracheoesophageal fistula.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (smoking and alcohol, early hoarseness when glottic), and contrast it with benign vocal fold nodules from voice overuse and juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis from HPV types 6 and 11.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe malignant mesothelioma (asbestos exposure decades earlier, no smoking link, recurrent hemorrhagic effusion, tumor encasing the lung, calretinin and cytokeratin positive, long slender microvilli), and distinguish it from metastatic pleural adenocarcinoma.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe nasopharyngeal carcinoma (EBV association, higher incidence in southern China and parts of Africa, nonkeratinizing or undifferentiated histology), and predict cervical lymph node metastasis and unilateral serous otitis media from eustachian tube blockage.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Explain nasal polyps (chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with asthma, cystic fibrosis in a child) and vocal fold polyps (voice strain, smoking), and predict nasal obstruction, anosmia, and hoarseness.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe small cell carcinoma (central, strongly linked to smoking, small neuroendocrine cells with scant cytoplasm and nuclear molding, chromogranin and synaptophysin positive), and predict early metastasis and ACTH, ADH, and Lambert-Eaton paraneoplastic syndromes.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Compare non-small-cell carcinomas: squamous cell (central, smoking, keratin pearls, intercellular bridges, cavitation, PTHrP hypercalcemia) and large cell (peripheral, poorly differentiated, poor prognosis), alongside adenocarcinoma.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Match lung cancer paraneoplastic syndromes to type: PTHrP hypercalcemia (squamous cell), ACTH Cushing syndrome and SIADH (small cell), Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (small cell), and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy with clubbing (especially adenocarcinoma).

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Predict local effects of lung cancer spread: superior sulcus (Pancoast) tumor with Horner syndrome and brachial plexus deficits, superior vena cava syndrome, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion, and diaphragm elevation from phrenic nerve invasion.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Distinguish metastases to the lung (multiple well-circumscribed nodules, more common than primary lung cancer) from a benign hamartoma (cartilage and fat, popcorn calcification) when evaluating a solitary pulmonary nodule.

Unit name: Neoplasms of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Relate HPV type 16 to oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil and base of tongue, and contrast it with tobacco and alcohol related squamous carcinoma of the oral cavity and pharynx.

Predict the clinical picture of cystic fibrosis: meconium ileus, pancreatic insufficiency with steatorrhea, chronic Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus aureus infection, bronchiectasis, nasal polyps, male infertility from absent vas deferens, and sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher.

Explain why sweat is salty in cystic fibrosis (failed chloride reabsorption in the sweat duct) while airway surface liquid is depleted (failed chloride secretion with excess sodium absorption through ENaC).

Describe tracheoesophageal fistula, most often esophageal atresia with a distal fistula, and predict polyhydramnios, drooling, choking and cyanosis with feeds, a gastric air bubble, and failure to pass a nasogastric tube, noting the VACTERL association.

Describe congenital diaphragmatic hernia (usually left posterolateral, failed pleuroperitoneal fold closure) with abdominal contents in the chest, pulmonary hypoplasia, and a scaphoid abdomen at birth.

Distinguish pulmonary sequestration (nonfunctioning lung tissue with systemic arterial supply from the aorta and no bronchial connection) from bronchogenic cyst (abnormal foregut budding, fluid-filled, usually mediastinal), and predict recurrent infection.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Compare lobar pneumonia (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella; congestion, red hepatization, gray hepatization, resolution; dullness, egophony, increased fremitus) with bronchopneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas; patchy, often multilobar, centered on bronchioles).

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe atypical pneumonia (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which lacks a cell wall, with cold agglutinins in young adults in close quarters; Chlamydia pneumoniae; Legionella with hyponatremia and diarrhea; viruses), and predict patchy interstitial infiltrates that look worse than the patient.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe diphtheria (gray adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped, bull neck lymphadenopathy, tellurite agar, Elek test) and predict toxin-mediated myocarditis, heart block, and cranial and peripheral neuropathy.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe endemic fungal pneumonia (histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis) in healthy hosts, and predict dissemination to skin, bone, and meninges, and granulomas mimicking tuberculosis.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Distinguish Pneumocystis pneumonia (CD4 below 200, bilateral ground-glass infiltrates, exertional hypoxemia, high LDH) from aspergillosis (aspergilloma in an old cavity, angioinvasive disease in neutropenia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma and cystic fibrosis).

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Explain lung abscess from aspiration of oropharyngeal anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) in alcoholism, seizures, or dysphagia, and predict an air-fluid level in dependent segments and foul-smelling sputum; identify Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella as other causes.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe the catarrhal, paroxysmal (inspiratory whoop, posttussive vomiting), and convalescent stages of pertussis, its marked lymphocytosis, and apnea and pneumonia in young infants.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe respiratory syncytial virus as the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants (winter epidemics, wheezing, tachypnea), and identify prematurity and congenital heart or lung disease as risk factors for severe disease.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Trace primary tuberculosis from the Ghon focus and hilar node (Ghon complex) with caseating granulomas to latent infection, and interpret tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay results.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Predict secondary (reactivation) tuberculosis in the apices with cavitation, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and hemoptysis, and miliary spread to kidneys, meninges, and vertebrae (Pott disease), especially with HIV or immunosuppression.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Describe coronavirus disease: common cold strains, and SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 entry via ACE2 on airway and alveolar cells, loss of smell, diffuse alveolar damage, thrombosis), and identify older age and comorbidity as risk factors.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Identify likely organisms in hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia (Pseudomonas, MRSA, enteric gram-negative rods), and distinguish chemical aspiration pneumonitis from bacterial aspiration pneumonia.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Explain influenza pneumonia and predict secondary bacterial pneumonia with Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae, and identify avian influenza as a source of novel strains through reassortment.

Unit name: Infectious diseases of the pulmonary system and upper respiratory tract
Competency: Identify zoonotic and bioterrorism causes of pneumonia: inhalational anthrax (hemorrhagic mediastinitis, widened mediastinum), tularemia (rabbits, ticks), Q fever (Coxiella from farm animal birth products), and melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei, Southeast Asia).
